Reviews.108072:
I am a big fan of No Man's Sky. It's easily one of my favorite games that I've played in the realm of open world survival/crafting: a genre that is generally a mixed bag for me, personally. NMS is not without its flaws, but I find this game to be fun, charming, and unique enough to overlook many of its issues.

Pros:
-The size and scope of NMS's playable universe is unmatched, as far as I know. While many planets are similar, no two are exactly the same and there are a fair number of rare environments to come across as well. Space feels big and empty, as it should. The galaxy is really is full of strange and wonderful things and setting up a base in a cool location is always satisfying.
-The main story of the game is interesting, though it seems to most exist as a vehicle for encouraging players to explore and find new game features. It mostly hinges on your interactions with a small group of alien NPCs who help you try to solve the mysteries of existence. I don't want to spoil anything, but I enjoyed crossing paths with each character along the way.
-I love learning languages one word at a time and using that knowledge to solve puzzles and charm aliens. It just works!
-Graphics are stylish and the universe is beautiful. There is a reason the worst thing people have to say about NMS is that it is a 'screenshot generator.'
-HG adds brand-new content to the game all the time and so far there is no paid DLC or microtransactions to be seen.
-I haven't interacted a lot with the online community but there seems to generally be a positive vibe and it's easy to find people with an abundance of resources looking to help out newbies.

Mids:
-The price of procedural generation, particularly on a large scale, is that--in a way--you can never really encounter anything truly special or unique. NMS has enough variety and progression that you'll still be discovering new sights many hours into the game, but the patterns do begin to show more over time. For me, that cheapens the thrill of discovery more and more, but it's inherent in this kind of design.
-It's kind of buggy, but I think I've only encountered one or two game-breaking glitches in all my playtime, so I don't mind the bugs so much given the constant updates.
-I like the system of trading up starships to find the coolest, best ship you can, but I don't like a lot of the common ship aesthetics. Always disappointing to find really cool looking ships with bad stats because it's very hard to improve a ship's base stats on your own.

Cons:
-The first hour of the game is the worst hour of the game and that turns people off. The tutorial always puts you on a planet that slowly kills you over time, which I sort of understand as a 'throw you in the deep end' sort of survival lesson, but it's kind of rough while you're still learning the UI.
-Despite its massive size and scope, I do not think NMS is very conducive to co-op play with friends. Outside of the specific Co-op Missions and Derelict freighters, there is not much that is meaningfully enhanced by having company. When I play with friends, we tend to meet up for a bit and then fly off and do our own things because there is no way to share objectives outside of tagging markers. Even building a base together has difficulties and bugs that hinder the group experience. The game is much more prone to misbehaving with multiple players/bases around.
-Some features are more tedious than fun to interact with. NMS has a lot of menus with sub-menus and you will probably spend no small amount of time organizing your many inventories. It can also be a bit of a chore to regularly travel between NPCs for objectives and upgrades.

Overall, I'm very happy with this purchase. My interest is certainly waning here around the 80-hour mark, but I look forward to coming back to this game for future updates and expeditions. Easy recommend if you catch it on sale (50% off seems to be the regular dip).

Now that I have taken time to play this game for a while and unlock content, I can tell I highly recommend it. I haven't tried the VR version, just the regular desktop one and it runs well there.

I've always liked exploration and space themed games. I tried to get twice into Elite Dangerous and despite liking the setting a lot, I found it too complex and confusing. So I came back to No Man's Sky.

This game had a tumultuous launch, promising lots of things that people didn't get and got a lot of backlash for it. But the publishers have gone to the Moon and back to deliver more content for free to make up for it. You can have various spaceships, a freighter, several bases in different systems, pets, explore lots of planets and even abandoned freighters... Recently they have added the Expeditions mode, where you are matched with a group of players in a new planet and have to collaborate together to reach certain objectives. It's chaotic, but fun.

I recommend this game if you like exploring games and mapping and scanning stuff, because you're going to do this a lot in every system you visit, in every planet you land on. You can also craft lots of different materials, food and upgrades. Every time you craft or discover something it gets added to your log, and if you're the first person discovering a species of flora or fauna, or a planet, you get to name it and upload it to the community database. All those aspects are well designed, in my opinion, and feel really satisfying.

But this game isn't free of cons, especially if you don't enjoy management aspects in survival games, or find them stressful. There is a point where you get enough batteries, life gel, oxygen, carbon, and other elements to not have to bother about them at all or too much, but at first it's rough and can be a bit challenging depending on the first planet you spawn in. They are usually planets with hostile weather, like boiling rains, fire storms or blizzards. Having to repair pieces of a spaceship to get it ready to leave, fixing your suit, upgrading it... It all requires different materials and crafting parts, so that can be a bit overwhelming. I've found myself loving it and it adds a layer of immersion to it, having to be mindful of your resources but also reaching a point where you can just store lots in your spaceship, base or freighter, and just restock.

The exploration system feels good as well. There are three main alien races in No Man's Sky: the Gek, small reptilian merchants and traders; the Vy'keen, tall and rough looking warrior aliens bound by honour; and the Korvax, a robotic-looking race dedicated to technology and investigation which operate like a hive-mind. As a traveller, you start barely understanding them because they have their own languages, but here's where NMS offers another layer of exploration, we could say: you can ask aliens to teach you different words. So eventually you can understand 40%, 70%, 90% of what they're saying to you, and reply accordingly. These races also have standing systems, which give you positive reputation if you help distress calls, do missions for them, or help them fight space pirates that show up some times.

Now, in terms of PC specs and requirements, you need a decent system to run the game properly. Playing on a Lenovo laptop on Windows 10 I have only had the game crash once and because I was running a handful of things in the background, and didn't know it back then but had a faulty-soon-to-crash hard drive. It runs smoothly most of the time even during storms, space travelling and fights, which are the situations I can think of when you get more particles dancing around the screen. Using a Nvidia GTX graphics card, the only problem I have experienced is weird black rectangles in certain underwater reflections or sun glares when looking at a planet at a specific angle, but to be fair this hasn't happened in months since I got one of the latest driver updates. I'm still listing them here in case anyone has the problem, so they know it can be fixed.

TL;DR: good for space exploration, interesting planets and procedurally generated species, good character customisation, tons of things to do due to the size of the galaxies. If you struggle with resource management I would recommend to try the game first to see if it's up your alley. They keep adding content and community events regularly every some months, for free. Give it a try especially if it's on sale :)
Reviews.108110:
Everyone has seen the YouTube video "The Engoodening of No Man's Sky" if not you are doing yourself a disservice and need to get some good food and watch the whole thing with apt attention... Especially the end.

Here is a short review from someone who just bought the game buying it half off for $30. I would say this is well worth $60.

     I have played many survival games but none have grabbed my attention as much as this one. In the beginning it felt like an average survival game with resource management and base building. After getting used to the monotony of the beginning and getting some upgrades making the survival part more trivial I went into the main quest line. This grabbed more so than I would ever expect from a survival/exploration game. I love the characters and choices you could make. Choices in dialogue caught me by a big surprise. I actually stopped and actually tried to understand what was going on instead of ignoring the story and just clicking as fast as possible to get to the end of the main story quest. For those who don't know you don't unlock all of the games features until this main quest line is completed. 

The main story quest is one long tutorial that took me about 20 hours to complete when basically going full bore into getting it complete ignoring most other items. I wanted a nicer ship so I wanted to get access to portals (this games fast travel) to get to a planet that had one I liked. The story side railed me and actually got my attention that kept me engaged and enjoyed the main questline a lot more than I would originally imagined it could. Instead of it just being a task to complete to get to my goal it became something I enjoyed very much. Now after completing the main story and actually getting attached to characters, I could remember my goal and move on to getting the ship/multi-tool I want. 

     After getting the ship and multitool I wanted I noticed that no matter what you couldn't just have the best gun/upgrades for everything in your ship/tool/exosuit unless you sacrifice every slot in technology and storage and even then you will be lacking upgrades and have no room for any materials. This made me happy since it means people would need to actually decide what best suits them or what they like most. So everyone is different in what weapons they use and items they have upgraded. Variety always makes me happy instead of everyone just walking around with the same exact same items because if you don't use the best items you are pretty much LARPing at that point in a lot of games. 

     I made an alright base and was also really impressed with building and having a construction camera made life so much easier it reinvigorated my love for building bases. Unlike other games jumping precariously and using makeshift platforms you can free camera in your building zone which is something every survival game with building needs. There is also a full underwater expansion with sub Nautica like stuff. 

     That's about as far as I got in the first 32 hours I put in within the memorial day weekend. I am looking forward to continuing the adventure of other story line quests and seeing what else I can create. 

There are 2 bugs/issues that annoy me with the whole game. When exiting an atmosphere i get a1-2 second freeze then the game continues as normal. I have gotten used to it and after googling seems like a common issue with no way to fix. Another is the secondary's for your multitool sometimes will not activate unless you do some finagling or restart the game. these are annoying and I would greatly appreciate the secondary issue to be fixed. But these 2 problems barely hinder my enjoyment of the game.

Those 2 issues aside, Get this game. It is worth it.

Reviews.108118:
[h1]My review for No Man's Sky[/h1]
  [b]Spoilers in the story section[/b]

   Let me start this review off by congratulating and thanking Hello Games for their continuous support of the game and keeping up with their original vision for it, even after the dumpster fire of a launch it had. Everyone has already heard and said this a thousand times before, of course, so I'll just get on talking about the features of it.

[u]Story[/u]

   The story of No Man's Sky might be nothing new or innovative, as it has been tackled a few times before in the past, not just in games, but it does great things with it nonetheless. For me, it feels a bit like Deus Ex: Human Revolution in the way the story works, except that Human Revolution didn't slowly expand the story, but rather already layed it's cards out at the beginning. 
   Simple, but at the same time complex, questions of 'who are we?', 'do we even matter?' and 'are we even alive to being with?'. Sure, this is only a game 'n all, but you can easily interpret these points and apply them in real life, the philosophies and standards we live by. The way I see it, there truly is no meaning, purpose or reason in life, but that doesn't mean we shouldn't carry on with it and try our best at things, that's where a lot of people with such a mindset divide. Life might be shit in the grander scheme of things, but there's always moments of joy you can cherish, plus, you have your hobbie(s). For me, it's probably playing video games, besides other things. Now, let's not get too deep into philosophical questions, that's left for late 3 A.M. Discord calls with your buddies. 
   Talking about the game's story once more, it's great. Each of the characters have a distinct personality, which makes it more intriguing and interesting listening to them and seeing what they'll do upon finding out about the inevitable. It was also really interesting finding out that everyone in the Space Anomaly already knew about what was going on, but just wanted to lead you on and let you find it out by yourself, just like -null- did. The Atlas knowing about the 16 minutes it has left and being so afraid of it that it keeps restarting everything and releasing it's anger and sorrow that way is great. A machine being afraid of it's own termination ? Feels a bit like 2001: A Space Odyssey, which is not a bad thing, of course. Great story, loved it.

[u]Visuals[/u]

   This game has a distinct graphics and art style, almost something akin to TF2 and what not. I'd say it looks quite good, but space itself doesn't look all that good, mostly because there isn't much there to see anyways, which makes sense, but still, the skybox textures are meh. The warping animation whenever you travel to another system also looks really dissapointing, really bland and gets stale fast. Anything on ground looks good though. 
   One thing I really like is how each distinct planet has it's own subtle or massive visual changes, so much so that some planets are greyscaled or filled with rain, mist and humidity that you don't even know where you are and if you're going face first into ground.
   Lighting's in this game's good, nothing bad to say about it. Helmet reflection, glow and what not look really nice and add to the atmosphere. Same with fauna or materials that glow. 

[u]Audio[/u]

   The audio in this game is nothing all too special, but it works in deepening the atmosphere and making it feel more alive. Soundtrack wise it's a little bit better, but also nothing too crazy to write home about. Don't take this as a con or anything, because it's not. It's just not on the levels like Elite Dangerous if we talk audio quality wise.

[u]Gameplay[/u]

   Now, getting to the primary thing of the game, gameplay. This game has really good gameplay, worthy of multiple repeats that won't get boring. No Man's Sky has a lot of options to offer gameplay wise, like: being a bounty hunter, building a base on ground or underwater, exploring an infested ship, breaching a facility... and many more. All this ranging from on ground to full on space related content. Recently they added expeditions, which are these stage based missions that you have to do on a seperate save that'll give you a lot of universal rewards upon completing any of them. I did some snooping and found out that season 1 of expedition was really hard, tedious and challenging, so I hope they don't go back to that kinda setup, because it seemed like a lotta hell for nothing too special. Sounded a bit like Warframe even, sheesh. Thankfully, season 2 was way, way easier and more fun.
   One thing I wanted to talk about since I started writing this review is NMS compared to Elite Dangerous. Oh boy, oh boy, you better take some advice from HG Frontier, because they sure know much more as to what the fuck they are doing, unlike you. What the fuck is Odyssey even ? Literal early access crap. There's only a handful of things I can think of that Elite does better, that being: sound, some aspects of graphics, immersion, ship design, but that's the biggest points I could think of. Farming in ED is a HUGE problem, that NMS works around way better, making it even more fun or just an idle background thing that you don't even need to worry about. I know this part of the review isn't much about the game itself, but I had to get ED off my chest some more. God is it horrid.
   Length of this game is more than satisfactory I'd say, ranging from 50 hours up to over a hundred. I'm currently at 47 hours as I'm writing this, but I still have a shit ton of stuff I could do to keep me interested and busy. Story is not the longest, but if you don't just rush through it, but rather take it in parts, it'll be perfect.

  Overall this game was a pleasent surprise for me, because some friends of mine didn't recommend me it, while others did, so I was torn between the opinions and felt unsure when I bought it. Turns out it's a really great and solid game, with updates to come. Loved every hour up to this point and probably will every other starting on.

[b]I'd give this game a nice 8.5/10[/b]

Reviews.108136:
Pros
-HUGE play space (Like the infinite world option for Minecraft, but with no definite border)
-Full planet exploration (if you see it, you can conquer it)
-Feels like Destiny combined with Minecraft but you actually get to control your ship, even shoot lasers at minefields for minerals you need.
-Minor Star Trek vibes
-Makes you feel like you're an alien, learning words from each person you talk to until you begin to understand full conversations.
-Cool space ships
-Amazing Outerworlds-esque graphics
-You get to name everything you find.

Cons
-Not being able to escape extreme temperatures
-Limits your fuel for space flight, which can leave you stranded on a planet or stuck zooming in on a planet or station for 15 minutes to an hour.
-Having to learn multiple languages which takes lots of time from you
-Only 4 races available with 3-5 outfit pieces open for customisation (I personally would like a bit more variety like Star Trek Online, but it's okay as it is, I guess).
-Loads of hazards (swimming being one of them).

Summary: If you like space, get this game. If you hate space, don't get this game.

Reviews.108196:
To start, I would much rather give this a 'mixed' recommendation, but steam doesn't allow that and I lean towards no. I also want to really praise Hello Games for their effort in the game, I remember when this game was released and the whole shit stormed that occurred. Now five years on the game has made significant progress without the implementation of paid DLC, which is incredible, but unfortunately it still isn't enough in my opinion.

[list]
[*] [u][b] The Economy[/b][/u]
Firstly, I want to talk about the economy of the game, it works on the basis that each system has a trading type, some examples are manufacturing, research and mercantile. The trading type defines what items the system sells and also the prices at which they buy/sell items. This leads to locally produced items being sold for a much lower price than other systems and them buying certain items for a much higher price. 

Now this fine until you add in the fact each trading post comes with a teleporter, which allows you to travel back to the system for free after you've left. This allows the player to buy the cheap, locally produced items from one system and immediately teleport to another system that has a demand for the item, then sell the items for a steep profit. Rinse and repeat, and before you know it you never have to worry about money again.

This allowed me to turn 4 million credits into over 60 million credits in less than an hour, which is just ridiculous. Before doing this I was always excited to explore a planet with ancient bones or salvaged scrap to earn some money, but after I never bothered to explore these planets anymore. Exploration simply was not profitable anymore, which takes out a major incentive to explore planets in the first place in my opinion.

[*][u][b]Guilds Quests[/b][/u]
In this game there are 3 guilds, the merchant guild, the explorers guild and the mercenaries guild. What's the difference? There isn't any. They each give you randomly generated quests that have nothing to do with the purpose of the guild, I've had it before where the merchants guild keeps asking me to go to planets to kill creatures, whilst the explorers want me to go bounty hunting and the mercenaries want me to deliver a package. I think guilds should give specific quests that represent there purpose.

The second problem with guild quests are there stackability, what I mean by this is you can get 20 bounty quests over a series of systems, reset all the quests to work in the current system, and then kill two to three ships to complete all 20 bounties. This is a little broken in my opinion.

The third problem is that sometimes there is extensive delay in the quests picking up that I've completed them, sometimes I'm waiting minutes for the game to allow me to hand in the quest at the trading post.

Also, just a side note, I really thought there would be like quest line for each guild, to allow you to get more involved and connect with them.

[*][b][u]Disproportionate Gameplay[/u][/b]
I am 30 hours into the game, I am bored of the planets as a lot of the assets are repeated, this leads to a lot of planets looking the same, which makes them a chore to explore when there is nothing new to find. The economy is broken so I never have to worry about money. The quests are all dull so I never pick up new ones as I don't care about standing and I don't need the rewards. I have no reason to explore a system anymore, so I just don't, but I'm still not done... I still have to get to the centre of the galaxy, what feels like the overall objective of the game, but I'm still 700,000 years away. It will probably take me another 20 hours to get to the centre. 

The point I'm trying to make here is that I feel like the game does not have 50-60 hours of stuff to do to keep you going to the middle of the galaxy, every minute I play now is just me warping from system to system to find a black hole, go through the black hole and then repeat. It feels like a chore to play at this point. I wish the time to get to the centre of the galaxy was more proportionate to the overall gameplay.

[/list]

In conclusion, I find the technology behind the game is amazing, the procedural generation and scale of each galaxy is something I thought I would never see, but the game still feels like it hasn't grown out of a saying that was coined when the game was released. 

[i]"As wide as an ocean, as deep as a puddle"[/i]

I was a launch-day player. Like many others, I was terribly upset with how few promises this game kept. And when the devs went silent, I felt like I had gotten scammed.
But five five years later, I found myself here, grinding the latest expedition. Then my PS4 broke. With (what I thought was) only one day left to do the expedition (it was two), I bought the game for PC and spent eight hours straight, completing it all in one day. And I had a blast the entire time.
No Man's Sky is a labor of love. It always was from the beginning. It was the greatest disappointment I ever faced in a game when it launched in 2016, but now I consider it to be the biggest redemption story in the history of gaming. These devs truly care about their game and their community.
It's buggy. I won't lie. But it's fairly well-optimized, could fit on a flash drive if you wanted it to, and the community is simply incredible. If you want a linear game with a clear storyline and objective path, look elsewhere. This game is for adventurers. I've spent literally countless hours in this game.. because you can't see your hours played on PS4. Exploring systems, naming them, discovering weird new creatures, buying things from systems and selling them for profit in different ones, learning alien languages, building bases, exploring crashed spaceships, and so, so much more. Few games have immersed me as well as No Man's Sky. 
It's not perfect, but I can count on Hello Games to continue developing, improving, and expanding upon this game for the foreseeable future. It just goes to show that you can never judge a game based on its launch. Because the product of crunch time does not truly represent a game, what truly represents it is the will and tenacity of the team behind it in the proceeding years of its life.
If you like to wander aimlessly, then you're in the right place. Good hunting, traveler.

Reviews.108280:
I'm quite stunned how NMS turned out. It's a really underdog-comeback-story after the whole Launch disaster and its great. Really wholesome.
But after all this years and updates my initial impression start to crack.
The recent Expeditions breathed fresh air into it and sorted the whole jumbled up progression.
While playing them i still encounters many issues with the game that only started to form after many updates and if they just keep adding content to the game it will get worse and worse with every one of them.
To the Specifics:
NMS has a big number of features and mechanics. Non of them are very deep or integrated in such a ways that it fits in a good in a complete picture. This is due partly to the Sandbox Nature of the game. It's hart to point out the Specifics but i'll try some examples.

Trading or the idea of it. So you can Trade specialized Trading Commodities. You buy them at Stations and you have a Indicator how much Cheaper they are or how much Profits you get. Well this system seams nice and you just thought about loading up your Trade ship and flying from Station to station and make some Profit. Well scratch that whole ship part. In each Station is a teleporter that costs nothing to use. You can always teleport between stations you visited. So you just cycle through the stations and teleport from location to location and rack up infinite money until the trading commodities run out or you close the game of boredom.
Other System is Ship scrapping. With the large stack of Money you earned from Trading you sit down in a Station and buy up all landing Ships and scrap them to convert your Money to Nanites by selling Technologiemodules and you will hardly loose any because you get parts out of scrapping that you can sell. When knowing about these very easy ways to earn Money and Nanites you have access to both of the Major Currency of the game no Exploration of base building is needed anymore. You now can just Buy everything on the Stations, basic to more advanced resources for Money and upgrades for Nanites. And i assure you with a removal of these """Exploites""" this would not solve the problems they created. The game has so many ways to collect Resources but none of them are this fast and easy to pull off. Also none of them respect your time and are equal to the amount they give. Plus most of them involve doing the same activities over and over again which can quickly result in grind.
These systems are just the Tip of the Iceberg why i can not fully recommend this game.
The real Painpoints are the Inventory, Multiplayer, unexplained Systems/Mechanics, Classes, Map and Exploration Tools.

The Inventory is a disaster. It works, it stores your items but at what cost?
You have Tabs and they store different Item types and even Upgrades. Its a grid system, each item uses one grid slot. There are adjacency interactions with Upgrades but its hardly explained what they do. Even worst it seems only the Warp in know to get better with adjacency bonus. A botched System that is not fully fletched out.
Ok but now let me get back on the Inventory tabs. You have tabs where you switch your whole screen. This would not be a problem if each Tab would have its own sperted Item Type with no interactions but when you get your Exosuit Cargo/Ship/Exocraft(there are 6 of them, each with their own Inventory Tab that is not always accessible)/Freighter(And Freighter Storage)/Base Storage. But Base Storage and Freighter Storage is the same(i hope i don't lost you there). Ok now imagine you are looking for your Copper. You know you had at least 2000 of it. You start in the your Exosuit, ok here is 100 - Cargo - switch to your Ship Tab - switch to your Freighter Tab - Hey here is 20 Copper but i know i had 2000 - Now you switch to the First Storage Tab - You keep switching through the Storage Tabs - In Storage 8 is 2000 Copper. This Process will company you throughout the game. And this is already depicted with the Matter Teleport where you an access your Freighter inventory from everywhere. It's infuriating. I know Inventory management is a part of these Survival games but it can be done much better. How about one Inventory Page where each slot has a tiny little symbol on them to show to witch entity it belongs. With a search and filter function and an auto sort? Upgrades and Technologies can have their own Tab.
Overall the Inventory management is needlessly complex and frustrating. And the Main reason is the restriction that it must work with a controller. Oh god i really don't want to know how much time a player with a controller wastes in these Grids and Tabs.

With the last Updates the Multiplayer has become much more stable and playable. beforehand i we had really bad sync and lag issues. But as we could now play together we found the whole Multiplayer construct is a mess too! You can play in a group but when you want to play a mission together you all need to go to the same mission terminal and accept the same mission, manually. No Invite or Auto group system for that i'm afraid. Also sometimes the mission progress updates when your teammate does it but sometimes it does not and each party member has to do it them self.
 If one of your party member calls his Freighter you can't anymore. So no access to your Freighter inventory i'm afraid. When you land on a derelict freighter random people can also land on it and join your group. If your Setting is set to "Allow Group and Friends can do X" you will get some interesting results. You cant sit in the same Ship or Exocraft - No multicrewing so it will often happen that you loose each other while playing/exploring. Your Party member don't have access to your Ships or Inventory's at all. We tried to set up a mining base together but it failed when we discovered the freighter restrictions. I bet we would find much more restrictions and things that simply not work if we had proceed. Also there is no such thing as a "Private Multyplayer" you always have the stupid comm beacons and player bases icons littered everywhere that clutter up your UI. The whole "playing together" aspect is also a botched System that is not fully fletched out.
 
There are many unexplained Systems in the game due to the constant Content updates and no refactoring and cleanup work that is done. I already touched on them here. One we found in particular: Teleporters, there is no explanation how the whole Teleporter UI works. When do i see Teleporter bases? Why do i see them? I cant search for a Teleporter. Why is the "Group" tab full of bases of people i don't know? I think is based on the Server instance i'm playing? It's not explained anywhere. 
I have the slight feeling that the game designed in the hopes that only people play it that are so dumb they dont notice these flaws because they dont think about them. Or Children.

The whole hunt for Classes. It's one major pillar of the games motivation to "Explore" to find the best Ship/Multytool/Freighter/Frigates. But in the End it hardly matters. Well you can get good stat rolls but why? It's not necessary you just do it for the higher Numbers. And some of this search can also be done by exploiting Events and just sitting in a station.
And finding a good multytool is done by just looking into each stations vendor. They even implemented system so you can upgrade your classes and inventory's so you don't have to run the RNG mill to find "the best". Which is on one hand good but on the other hand undermines a whole game pillar. A botched System that is not fully fletched out.

We all know how this started. Lofty claims and a megaton of hype made an admittedly OK game universally hated for all that it wasn't delivering. Well, this will likely go down as THE text book case of a developer putting their noses to the grindstone and proving to everyone that they'll not only deliver on what they originally promised, but then continue to go above and beyond update after update after major update. And somehow never ask for a dime more. This is one of the few times where I've pleaded with a dev "PLEASE charge for SOMETHING. This isn't even fair anymore."

All that says nothing about nothing about the game though. It's a procedurally generated space and alien planet exploration game on a massive scale. I can't think of anything with more diversity in biomes, flora, and fauna; but there's tons of info on all that already. What I can say is that it has issues here and there. For example, I only play in VR ever since they added it a few years back and some updates have made it too laggy to function, unfortunately. I also wish the flight controls/physics were a bit tighter. In fact, overall, it's definitely the type of game where the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Because there's so much you CAN do in this game that it's hard to fault its individual shortcomings too much (except I'd REALLY like the VR to work more consistently, although I know it's not an easy feat). The discovery, the base building, the character progression, the events they add, the planetary deformation, the vehicles, there's so much. If solid combat is a requirement, this won't fulfill that too well...but if you like exploration and building, there are few games that match it.

This game has come an unbelievably long way since release.

While Hello Games still deserve some major flak for the state this game was released in, I'm now slowly closing in on 100 hours, something I years ago thought would be an impossibility.

Is this a perfect experience?
[b]No, far from it.[/b] There are still some glitches. [b]Absolutely.[/b]

There's a tonne of systems to try out, lots of things to upgrade or work on. You can play the game with friends or alone.

If you can get this game, especially on a discount, just do it.

Reviews.108420:
This is a great, but flawed game, and I hated Expedition mode.

The core gameplay of No Man's Sky is exploration-based, where you get to roam planets, collect resources, discover new systems and build bases. There is a main questline, which is more of a chore than anything, that you mostly complete to unlock more of the things that let you enjoy the core gameplay (base upgrades, easier ways to get around the universe, more crafting recipes, quality of life stuff, etc). There are a few difficulty modes that let you play the game with permadeath, or simply more damage and less inventory space, and I played around with them for the additional challenge. They are also fun! 

There's also a mode called Expeditions, and it offers some unique cosmetic rewards for completing a set of challenges within a given timeframe. It seems like a good idea in practice, but the execution is flawed. The first Expeditions was two months long, and it seemed to streamline a lot of the gameplay and give rewards that felt like significant upgrades at the point in the game that they were received. You were encouraged to explore and take your time, although not TOO much time, since you still only had two months to finish everything. 

The second season of Expeditions (Beachhead) seemed to lose sight of what actually made the game fun. The gameplay in this round was so compressed that there was little incentive to enjoy the giant sandbox of the No Man's Sky universe. While the objectives could be completed in any order, it made little sense to try to complete them nonlinearly, and this one was only two weeks long, when the first was more than two months. This meant that exploration was no longer something you wanted to do more than necessary, and the main goal was then to rush through the objectives as quickly as possible to get them done before the deadline. Beachhead can be completed in a single long gaming session, but for me, the experience was so unpleasant that I actually began to regret sinking so much time into this game. 

The main problem in Beachhead tends to be that a lot of the objectives are luck-based, or they involve warping long distances through space to reach specific locations. This is not something that is new to the game, but in all of the other game modes, there are plenty of things to distract you from how tedious this actually is. In Beachhead, you are put on a laser focused path to complete all of these tasks before the time runs out, and this forces you to sit through loading screen after loading screen after loading screen until you're spending more time watching loading screens than you are playing the game. In addition to this are the numerous luck-based missions like finding a pilot that needs to be rescued or a fixing up a crashed ship. These require you to hoard map items and then run through them one at a time in endless, tedious succession, flying from identical looking location to identical looking location until you get lucky enough to find the thing you need. It's completely unnecessary, and I don't know why RNG has to play such a huge part in a time-based challenge. 

Then there are the bugs, which are not unique to any mode of the game, but are the most egregious in Expeditions. In all modes of the game, heavily multiplayer areas of the game are very glitchy, and NPCs at the bottom of the space stations tend to be impossible to talk to without crashing your game. There are often invisible starships everywhere, that you have to navigate around, and this is a huge problem in Expeditions, where all of the players are funnelled through the same areas of the game in droves. Sometimes the star maps don't work, and you should always save your game frequently because you will generally have to reload your game multiple times per session when you encounter game-breaking bugs like attempting to land your ship and getting locked in the landing sequence with no way out, or getting yeeted out of the space station by another player's giant, bugged-out fighter ship. In the first Expedition (Pioneers), there were several objectives that had incorrect descriptions and that did not complete unless you did went online and looked up the specific way to make them unlock for you (e.g., getting an S-class gun for an achievement that asks you to get an A-class gun). In the second one, the waypoints would not trigger the objective unless you landed at the target site first, and occasionally the target site marker would disappear if you got too close to it. 

After about 6 hours of frustration with Beachhead, I gave up in disgust. I no longer wanted to play this game at all, and I regretted spending so much time with it that unlocking a cosmetic reward seemed to actually be worth the hassle of playing through a mode of the game that I actively LOATHED.

tl;dr, it's a fun game, save often because it bugs out a lot, and maybe give this round of Expeditions (and possibly all of them) a pass. Try Creative mode if you want to build megabases and don't like grinding resources.
Reviews.108421: I remember being really excited for this game's release. I remember hearing that it kind of fell flat and forgetting all about it for years before finally picking it up. I want my review to be positive because I did enjoy this game BUT I have to end it with a few problems I think the game has. One is that the "endgame" is pretty much something called ship hunting where you use galactic coordinates to go to places with nice looking ships. You then wait for potentially hours until this ship spawns in so you can buy it. The endgame doesn't HAVE to be this but with base building not quite being used to it's full potential yet and the combat being pretty nonexistent, collecting fancy ships is the best thing going. That kind of leads onto the next thing which is the combat. I remember pre 2016 waiting for this game and being told I could play a pirate or bounty hunter or something and loving the idea. You can kinda be a bounty hunter but it's just small contracts and if you have a ship that's even SLIGHTLY modded they're always going to be absolutely pathetic fights. The personal combat is not great either, with my suit mods being good enough that nothing even hurts me enough to pay attention to it. I never even made a damaging weapon for my person. They do keep updating this game and I still think it has more to come so it can always just get better and better, I just hope it doesn't always remain as the game that "could be amazing but it's quite there yet". Considering the price nowadays, I don't think anyone should turn their nose at the game though for what it does give you. Go in blind and have an adventure.

[h1]So many bugs I thought it was Starship Troopers [/h1] 

While the game has improved tremendously since release; the core gameplay loop remains the same. It's all about stop and go gameplay that revolves around resource management and inventory juggling. Gotta gather minerals, gasses and stuff to fuel your ship, life support yadda yadda...To the credit of Hello Games it is now possible to avoid mining by being a space trader and just buying your resources, but in essence all you're really doing is giving up lasering rocks for extra menu inventory juggling. It's just as hollow and unfulfilling as the mining.

Everything in this game is amazing...the first time you see it. The first ten hours are awe inspiring. The first time you have to fight space pirates is super cool, or landing on your frigate and having to repair it in outer space. But after the third or fourth time repairing the frigates becomes a chore much like being forced to fight the braindead pirates (which you're forced to do before being allowed to land on your frigate to repair it). While they've done a good job of increasing the variety of planet since the 1.0 release it still gets pretty boring after checking out a dozen planets or so mostly because there are very few terrestrial alien structures and they use the same exact prefabs for them no matter where you are in the galaxy. 

Base building and terrain manipulation was one of the first features patched into the game and it is still bugged. if you add/remove terrain and build stuff on it; the terrain will revert to it's original shape after a while (even if you don't exceed the max terrain manipulation limit). So you end up teleporting into your base that now has a mountain in the middle of your living room that you meticulously dug out just yesterday. The build mode is also lousy with little bugs and idiosyncrasies. For example you can only place trade terminals on freighter walls and inside prefab buildings but not on regular walls for some reason. Or how about being able to buy blueprints for three types of doors; none of which are in the game.

But I'm really burying the lead here. Those are the little bugs.  People have had major save wiping bugs across multiple patches. I, myself first checked the game out back in 1.0 and really got into it during the first Expedition patch. The Expedition ended and the save converted into a normal one as promised, but when the second expedition rolled around my regular save somehow got converted into an Expedition 2 save. The worst part is that the main quest is bugged preventing me from beating the game on my 80 hour save along with the Expedition rewards being totally screwed up which are account wide. For the record I have never used any cheats/exploits/save editors.

Reviews.108555:
I've always loved this game even when it first released! 
Yeah, the first version was a huge disappointment (for everyone) but it was still a lovely game. Now, a few years later with several huge updates, it has grown and flourished to a much more beautiful and engaging game. Best of all, it's not stopping. Hello Games, just keeps on making it better every time.

This is to me a very chill game and even on the first release, it was more of a 'walking simulator'. You fly to a planet, explore a bit, scan rocks, scan animals, fly, repeat. After a while you've practically seen almost all the iterations possible in this procedurally generated universe. You jump on a planet and you'll notice the same lifeforms, plants and animals. Some of them just have different colors or just a different combination. Landscapes would also start to look quite familiar. However, there's just this innate need to continue exploring. The hope of encountering something you've never seen before is always there, no matter how improbable. And, it's quite addictive.

Then came base building!
Suddenly, I was spending more hours customizing my bases more than exploring. It's a lovely way to lose hours of your life because you get a chance to be creative. You can even share your bases to your friends, or maybe a random, chance visitor.

From here on, Hello Games just kept on adding more things to do! This review will need to be updated every few months just to keep up. So, I won't delve into more details.

Right now, I'm busy with completing the Expedition events to get my Normandy SR-1 frigate (from Mass Effect games). And, I won't be surprised if the developers would make more gems like this in NMS.

Okay, there's one major thing that I just can't get over with, though: I don't like the alien races and NPCs!
I wish they made them look more like humans or at least more humanoid than procedurally generated bipedal versions of the planet creatures.

Why? Well, it makes it more immersive, at least for me. It would feel like I'm escaping planet Earth and travelling to different galaxies talking to other aliens. Maybe it's my inner Star Trek fan that's screaming to be fulfilled?

Alright, enough chatting! It's time for me to explore another planet!

Practically everything that was promised that we would have at launch of the game is there including a verbose multiplayer function to not only play with friends, but play with strangers giving the potential of making new friends.

We have multiple different play modes like Normal, Survival, Perma-death, and even a new community expedition mode which is a seasonal mode where you accomplish a specific set path of milestones and earn rewards that can be forever claimed in each of your new playthroughs of the game. It encourages gameplay around multiplayer.

This game has had multiple, free DLC additions to it and they are far too expansive to go over each one. Rest assured the $60 price tag on this game is worth it. From building huge bases, to exploring abandoned freighters and crashed freighters, playing with your friends, making new ones, and crafting this game has hundreds of hours of content you are not going to want to miss.

I HIGHLY recommend this game to you if you are in love withnon-linear, crafting based exploration games. Get it now.

Reviews.108660:
I love this game for it's graphics and modular content.

NMS is a unique cross-platform sci-fi kind of game set in a strange unlimited universe free to explore with VR support. With the 2021 addition of "Expeditions" updates Hello Games is bringing a fresh start for new and seasoned players and evolving in new exciting directions.

Go planet//system//galaxy exploring, mining resources, surviving, trading, building bases and unlocking blueprints for technology modules. Travel with spaceships or your own fleet and use portals to jump between galaxies. Follow the story and join other players, unlock achievements, earn rewards, if you choose to do so.

What makes NMS the #1 game for me to play?
It's complicated. In a beautiful way. Discover geography, flora, fauna, ships makes me come back for more. The graphics is sometimes even breathtaking.

Pros:
- Procedural generated content!
- Variety in game style, choose what you like doing (exploring, building, harvest, refine, raid, spacefights)...
- Community! Players have found exotic rare items, planets, maps and published a lot of how-to's if you search the internet discussion forums. It's a living game, get inspired by dedicated players discoveries and building techniques.
- Creativity! It's possible to be creative with the tools//modules available.

Cons:
- Missing manual. It's really complicated to understand everything you can do in this game. Expeditions updates made me understand more in one week than I did in half a year grinding and searching forums. That's why I mentioned Expeditions in the beginning, this is the most important step Hello Games have done to make this overwhelming game content manageable for new players.
- Bugs. Crashes. Mission blockers. Annoying "RTFM" moments since the FM is missing. Have patience, please report issues and do something else (like search for new planets, set up resource harvesters, weekly missions) for a while until there is an update.
- Limited variety. Repetitive core content with missions, assets and NPC bases. Seeing the same dialogues over and over again. Players can be very creative but they will sometimes do annoying things when bored.

Conclusion:
Would you recommend this game to other players?
- Yes. So say we all.

Reviews.108710:
Well, it's been a long time since I first heard about NMS and saw the teasers.  Then the disastrous launch.  And the rebirth which gave the the studio an extra life.  Then I got the game on sale, played for a while, got bored, came back a while for new content  and got frustrated, and now here we are.  NMS is, as everyone says, ambitious as hell and honest props for that.  But it's also awkward as hell.  Nearly all of the good things about this game come with downsides.  But let's get into it:

HIGHS:
* Graphics are rather nice, and it's one of the few games where I actually used Photo Mode.  They are a bit dated by this point, but not to a distracting degree.  This one comes without caveats - shocking!
* The scale of the game is impressive, as advertised.  Procedural generation at its finest.  And this does lead to some very interesting  outcomes sometimes (one of my favorites being two planets that were literally stuck together).  But...
* An endless supply of quests and missions.  But...
* The translation system where you have to gradually decipher words is a fun mechanic. But...
* Crafting/harvesting system and bartering has depth.  But...
* Ability to customize weapons and vehicles is cool.  But...
* Portal system is fascinating.  But...
* Lots of different ship designs to pick from.  But...
* You can create and customize your own base - and they look nice.  But...

LOWS:
* ...the scale of the game is an illusion.  Play for a while and you'll see the same things over and over and over.  A different skin here, different sky color there, different name for that same funny looking rock.  All the stations and all the NPCs you interact with are in the same places doing the same things.  After a few times around on that merry-go-round I put things on the shelf.
* ...the missions are endless, but you'll be doing the same things over and over and over.  Blast pirates.  Move materials.  Find a hidden base.  Loot a crashed freighter with all of the containers in the *exact same places* every time.  The first few times are fun, but it gets old very quickly.
* ...the translation system (and interaction with the 3 alien races in general) is pointless window dressing.  You don't need to do any of it.  There's no hidden lore, no story, and no sense of wonder.  All three alien races are literally interchangeable.
* ...after a certain point, you don't need money at all.  You've got more ships than you can possibly need (which are ridiculously easy to obtain - even freighters).  You've got boxes and boxes of materials, and nothing useful to build or buy.  It's a dead end.
* ...there's no point to customization.  After a certain point, survival does not pose much of a challenge, nor does combat.  Traveling vast distances is also effortless.  Not to mention pointless, as each solar system is only superficially different from the others.
* ...what good is a portal system if you have nowhere to go?  I know that there's supposedly a point to getting to the center of the galaxy, but not sure this helps.  Also, it's really hard to keep track of the addresses - the symbology is nice to look at but really hard to write down.
* ...you really don't need much in terms of ships.  Some of them look cool, and having a freighter unlocks some useful features.  But overall what's the point?  Travel is already too easy.  So is combat. 
* ...the way bases function is just a mess.  Certain devices just randomly can't be moved or deleted.  The power system, while a nice mechanic, was bolted on and is largely impractical.  The build menus are atrocious, the worst pile I've encountered since Dark Souls 2.
* Multiplayer is awful, consisting mainly of spam messages that can't be avoided.  I don't understand what value multiplayer would add in the first place - there's nothing to do as a group, no emergent gameplay, no raids, no meaningful accomplishments, no social activities.  Real head-scratcher.

BOTTOM LINE:
This game is awkward and repetitive.  It wasn't designed, it mutated into its current form because the initial launch was so bad.  While it *is* admittedly fun for a while as you explore and see certain things for the first time, enjoyment drops off very quickly.  It's Deja Vu: The RIde.  Don't bother - plenty of better games out there.  Ultimately, I think the legacy of NMS is going to serve as inspiration for other studios to do something similar, but get it right.

Reviews.108732: I love playing this game, especially the aspect of being what ever you want to be, if you want to be a Space Pirate than you can be. If you want to hunt pirates and be a Space Pirate you can be one. If you want to build your own bases and settle down on a planet you can. If you want to explore the cosmos and expand your horizon to find new meaning in the never ending galaxy. I just started playing No Man's Sky and it has been the most interesting and engaging experience I have ever had. It may be a very grind heavy game but it makes it all that much worth it when you figure something out, it means something when your able to make something from materials you looked for. Now for my dislikes which are very few and limited and what I personally want to see in the game. I feel like us as the players should get the opportunity to fight space pirates not only in space but on actual planets where they have their own bases and gang hideouts and you get mission rewards just like all the others for taking them out. These enemy space pirates should be made up of different races and they should own and claim a planet like sentinels. The only difference between the sentinels and the Space Pirates that claim planets is that you can actual clear out the space pirates on a planet and save it from being conquered by them. This will not only give you a remarkable reputation but you can get rare or decent rewards as well that you can loot from space pirate bases whether it be fuel or antimatter, or even something as simple as microprocessers or ion batteries. Another nitpick I have with the game is that we should have the option to make our own ships with different parts after we achieve buying a certain amount of ships where we are able to mix and match the parts of each ship with added new materials we could either buy for a high price or find from events. This seems like it can add a way more interesting and interactive way to look at the game and play it with astounding space battles. Also there should be more ground fire fights between the locals and the sentinels to have some sort of rebellions on some planets. It only makes sense that some races and aliens don't agree to what the sentinels are doing so I think adding ground fire fights to the mix will add a lot more flavor and spice to the game. Just give it some thought, let me know what could work and what could'nt work and why my ideas may be flawed. I would love to hear from others about these types of ideas added to these games.

Reviews.108939:
I have a love hate relationship with No Mans Sky. 

To start, it's just... the most repetitive, mind numbing, existential crisis of a game I have ever played. It is essentially "Leveless Grind, The Game, In Space." 

That section in Mass Effect with the Mako? Hello Games played those side missions and said, "this would be great if there were no bad guys and the whole game was that plus base building."

Despite the ungodly amount of procedural generation, enough to make a veteran coder wince at just the thought of it... they used such a small pallet of art assets to do it with that it invariably all looks identical. 

There are practical reasons for this. AI just isn't ready to make variations on a theme like that yet. Getting there, yeah, but not quite.

You can see this with the ships very clearly. There are about 6 noses, 3 bodies, 6 wings, 5 engines -- and each chassis fits roughly the exact same form factor. There are no racial or species or economic variables at play to diversify them, and the way the art is stylized and rendered makes them all look like they are culturally identical, like the difference between a Ford, Dodge, or GM, as opposed to the cultural difference between India, the US, and Japan. Their stats are arbitrarily attached to appearance as well, so the max level and low level could be visually indistinguishable too if not for an S, C, or B rating in the HUD. 

This problem is exacerbated exponentially by the way you acquire and modify ships. You buy them from life forms who all have the exact same dialogue and 4 dialogue options, hidden behind a language filter that you don't even need to guess is always the same, and they have apparently no bartering skills whatsoever. You just walk up, ask to buy their ship, pay a price, and they magically disappear. Damaged versions are found in missions that are likewise, all the same. You must acquire stuff to fix all the myriad broken parts, and these ships are typically almost always pretty lame (and might smoke but are visually identical to undamaged ships.)

Despite all the procgen in the universe to render planets and creatures and guns and ships from modular parts...

...every space station you visit, and you'll visit them hundreds of times... are the same.

A central landing strip with 8 ship slots. Two staircases to two levels, each with 4 shop windows.

From left to right: Suits, Vehicles, Ships, Multitools. A ship station that is good for fuckall except selling your ships for scrap at a single digit percentage of their buy value, and an appearance editor for your character that's totally free and costs nothing (can't edit appearance of ships, which even if it cost a lot would have been baller.) And a door to a room that may or my not have useless characters or carbon in it. 

Suits, Vehicles, Ships, Multitools.
Suits, Vehicles, Ships, Multitools.
Suits, Vehicles, Ships, Multitools.
Suits, Vehicles, Ships, Multitools.

Just over and over again.

The other side is also identical the same way. The races of the characters in these positions change -- and nothing else. 

Take the 45th mission from the guild guy -- it's the same shit different sky.

You win the game, all your shit is broken, and you play the same game.

Even the main quest lampoons that everything is the same because the godheads/AIdevs made it that way, for you. To see if you'd do the same thing, over and over again (not a joke.)

The main quest, I will not spoil for you, but it takes the otherwise awesome and exciting premise, and throws it into the kind of conspiracy theory your room mates come up with after watching way too many science-ism documentaries they barely understood, got high, read too much reddit on the subject of holograms that they also really didn't get, and decided Elon Musk must be an expert on the subject. It takes the chill flying in space doing repetitious tasks idea, and turns it into "the protag is the one true hero and chosen one to kill god," trope. 

And that main quest? Yeah, functionally every objective is the same holo terminal or portal or, the real kicker, seeing the same atlas station SIXTEEN TIMES.

It is... painful... to repeat the same actions over and over again. Harvesting the same stuff, even by automation at a base, is a manual task that will make you desperately wish this was Satisfactory and you could just set up a damn conveyor belt. 

Now don't get me totally wrong here, I am saying, you should play NMS and maybe even play it over something like Subnautica or Astroneers which are its genre peers and equally grindy and procgen in some ways. 

The sound effects are great. The sound track is great. The feeling of flying from planet to planet is cool. Sometimes you'll see a flashy new gun the first time in a dozen hours and say wow that's cool... only to see 5000 others just like it ten minutes later, or realize its stats are so bad it's not worth picking up and never see it again...

But there are far better and more fun space dogfighting games out there.

There are infinitely better 3rd or 1st person shooters out there.

There are better base building and survival games out there.

There are even better space to ground to space games out there in procgen universes! 

Random games aren't always fun. And NMS shows that not random enough can be even worse than too random. 

It actually makes me mad how close to a great game NMS is, but no matter how good they did, it was just doomed to never be enough due to the lack of variable verity of maps and missions, which a game this big desperately needs -- more varied missions and scenarios to emerge from the soup of variables. More varied visually and technically guns and ships.

I died more to my own plasma grenades than I ever did an enemy (never.) 

The walkers and dogs are scary the first couple times -- then you realize they, too, are it. You'll face them in the same way in the same places, over and over, and can just run away.

There are a grand total of 4 bad guys in this game. There are 4 Sentinel models. That's it. And you'll fight the exact same number of them every time, in the same waves. There are no surprises. You'll never be running out of air from damage and meet 6 more of these things coming at you in retaliation for something you did half a world away. There's no desperation. 

The gameplay loop, is seriously, just a very clearly polished ring, so obvious the main quest had to lampshade it. 

There is also no conflict between species. You learn that there used to be, you just never get to see it, which the main quest then lampoons/lampshades away again. (It would have been very cool to see galactic conflicts, but also asinine, as literally every star system is just packed to the gills with life and there's no economic reason to fight. It would only ruin the "chill ass psychedelic space game" vibe.)

So, can I recommend you play NMS? How will you know if you will enjoy it or hate it? 

You just have to be cool with the repetition. You have to enjoy the drudgery. You have to think the crafting is fun. You have to like the arguably inflated plot line and not mind that it's text only and hard to stay committed to when you're half drunk from repetitive action overload in an audio visual bombardment of colors and shapes in repeating noise. 

You can skip it and miss little to nothing. Which is to me, the biggest damnation of the game. 

The creatures, the worlds -- they do look cool -- but the variations are just noise. And noise never feels unique. 

But its worth experiencing for a day or two. Maybe pick it up from time to time to revisit your old base. 

That's its main saving grace.

No Man's Sky is visually very appealing, but unfortunately gets stale quickly and does not represent good value for money. 

I enjoyed the graphics and it was exciting to visit the first few planets. The flora and fauna are well-modelled, and the landscapes are beautiful. I didn't encounter any coding bugs while playing the game, either, which is fairly impressive. However, there are a lot of negatives. The environmental procedural generation becomes predictable and boring after the first hour or so, which is a big problem for No Man's Sky, as it is essentially marketed as an exploration game. The interaction with NPCs is equally tedious, following a basic conversation pattern with no incentive to persevere. The combat (with fauna and pirates) was far too easy to win or avoid, such that there is no real jeopardy in the game. Likewise, it was absurdly easy to make money through trading. The flight mechanics were also very poor and not enjoyable at all.

Major milestones came far too early in the game, which I felt was undeserved and unrealistic, as I expect to have to grind for the big rewards. For example, after just a few hours of play, I was given a free capital ship. The game also has no scientific realism whatsoever, which I always find disappointing. For example, your ship only needs fuel to take off, but can fly indefinitely once airborne.  Moreover, for some reason you can't buy upgrades from the same space station twice, which doesn't make any sense. 

TLDR: No Man's Sky is enjoyable for a few hours of play, but certainly doesn't justify its price tag.

This game has come a long way. It honestly blows my mind to see how much has changed since its release. I was one of the people who pre-ordered the game and can honestly say I was pretty disappointed with the lack of content at launch. It wasn't the worst but it definitely wasn't what was promised. Years later, Hello Games has done something extraordinary. With all of the updates that have came out, they have made this game into what it should have been years ago and then some. I couldn't be happier with the way it has turned out. The multiverse is as incredible as ever and I have had so much time playing alone and with friends. The story is incredible and can be done at your own pace. I started playing with keyboard and mouse and then switched to controller which I found was a more optimal way to play in my own opinion. I wanted to try out playing the game in VR because I currently have an Oculus Rift S and I must say that No Mans Sky is easily in my top 3 VR game if not my favorite so far. Being able to sit back, relax, and explore countless solar systems while flying around in a starship is one of the most incredible things I have ever done. I can't recommend this game enough even if you don't have a VR headset. 10/10 worth the wait.

TL/DR:
+Amazing Story
+Beautiful graphics
+Countless play-styles
+Very fun alone or with friends
+Awesome player customization
+Practically infinite universes to explore
+Pretty frequent updates
+Awesome vehicles (Exocrafts) to explore planets with.
++Incredible VR experience
+So much more

-/+ Lack of ship customization (It's kind of nice though due to the rarity of some ship styles. It makes exploration even more worth it.
- Limit of 6 starships (not really a problem I just would love to collect more ships. Better than the 1 at launch!)

I can't think of too many cons. This game has turned into a gem and if you keep an open mind, I'm sure you'll love it.

This is a tough review to give, on the one hand it seems like a fair amount has been added since its initial release, but, on the other every aspect of the game I came across I felt as though I could find it in another game or was very shallow (like it was quickly added to avoid false advertisement lawsuits). I don't know why it calls itself an RPG, aside from aesthetic character customisation that come pretty later on, you don't progress in any way involving skills, talents, perks, or whatever you want to call them. You do advance technology that is physically on your person, but that's pretty light as you don't add anything new, but just make what you have better. If that is an RPG then so is pretty much any game with some sort of progression.

The most customisation you get is in your base building, which is essentially Fallout base building, but in space. You acquire resources to build/upgrade bases/equipment, and to maintain your life support systems through a resource gathering system that comes right out of astroneer. To be fair, I don't know which came first, but if you are looking for casual space exploration, resource gathering, base building, and sandbox progression game, astroneer is far cheaper, and has far a more gradual and prolonged learning curve.

Apparently the game has become better because the developers sat down and added content, but I'm not sure I want to spend $70 on a game the developers decided to (I won't say finish) expand from an unplayable game to a playable game. The interactions are shallow and pretty basic, "I can't understand this thing" your character says to themselves "but through gestures I figure this out" or, nothing is said, and you just know you can buy/sell from them. There is wildlife, which miraculously wanders around a barren radioactive planet with hardly any vegetation. Your surroundings feel automated, generated, and skin deep. But at least there isn't nothing right?

It is possible I haven't given it enough time, but due to steam's playtime limit on refund requests I couldn't in good consciousness risk this much money and time to push through a game that "might get better". If you are really into space base building, go for it, but if you want an in-depth RPG experience set in space just play Mass Effect again.

Finally, they have added seasonal passes for the more multiplayer aspect of them game. You can have people join your session, but for cooperative exploration of procedurally generated worlds it seems like MineCraft has still done that better. So, if you want that multiplayer experience, where you come across other players without expecting it, and create spontaneous inter-player interactions across a vast ocean of space, you're going to need to start paying regularly for it. Which, I don't know about you, I don't want to continue to pay money for a $70 game which the developers just started to save from its initial flop of a release due to a lack of content. In other words, it really seems like the "good natured" expansion of the game by developers is showing itself as a long-term investment to start gouging players for money 5 years after they initially rushed out an under-developed game. 

To put it into context, it would be like if the developers of Cyberpunk 2077 spent years adding content to their game so that it was the product they had promised on release, only to start making their players pay monthly/seasonally for a portion of that content, which was supposed to be there on release.

The featureset is impressive, the universe practically infinite.  But for all this, Hello Games failed to do the one thing that matters most in a game:  Make it interesting and fun to play.  The core game loop is completely repetitive.  While every planet *is* "unique";  each is just a slight variation on the others, with all being essentially identical, at their core.  The storylines and quests are boring and uninspiring, and the lore is vapid and uninteresting.  The controls are wonky at times, not all keybinds can be changed (RIP non-QWERTY users), multiplayer can be very finicky, the economy is poor, and -- look, I can go on and on.
Where is the game good, then?  Why do I have 85+ hours?  Well, I wanted to see if the game got better.  Everyone said it would.  It didn't.  But at least building a base was kind of neat.  I also had a little fun save-editing after I was otherwise done with the game.  And occasionally it's nice to visit a new world.  But everything inevitably became a chore, and that usually happened quickly.
If this game is on a steep sale and you have friends who play it, then *maybe* pick it up.  But otherwise:  life is short;  spend it on games that are fun, interesting, challenging -- don't spend it on this.  Get Starbound:  it's the 2D version of what this game should have been.

While it may seem like I have played this game for only 12 hours, I have actually played this game on PS4 for over 300 hours. I was a day one player and NMS wasn't what I was expecting when it released, I still had a lot of fun with it, but eventually stopped for a while.

Then the NEXT update came along, and I suddenly got back into the game and, since multiplayer was added, me and my friend started playing together. We used to get on the game everyday after school and played for hours. Then, the BEYOND update came out, and we had stopped playing this game for a bit by this point. I tried it, and my first impressions were bad since the power system made all my bases unusable and other than that I didn't see anything new, so I didn't see any reason to come back to the game at that time. (I was still an amateur at this time so I didn't know about all the new stuff that was added)  Fast forward a few months, and Xmas rolls around and I got a PSVR + Move controllers. I had known at this time that nms had a PSVR mode, and had tried it on the PSVR headsets of other family members, and had a blast. Once I had my own, I really started getting into the game. What was once 2 - 3 hour play sessions was now 2 hour sessions in the morning and 3 - 4 in the night. I learned about all the new things beyond had brought to the table, and all the NEXT things I had missed. I finally beat the main quest-line and got a living ship. I made countless bases and visited hundreds of systems, never ever getting bored. Soon though, my NMS phase had ended and I went back to other games. Then, just over a month later, ORIGINS releases and I suddenly find myself getting sucked back into the world of No Man's Sky. a brand new procedural planet system. Many new planet types, new alien flora and fauna, new quest-lines, and much, much more. I would go on about all the new updates like companions and expeditions, but I've already spent enough time writing this review. I was never angry at Hello Games since they were obviously a small studio and all the exaggerations of the press were the main problems, but I'm thankful they stayed with the game and made it the best it could be. It's so good now that I feel like I'm robbing them by not paying for these updates! My friend never came back to this game after NEXT which is a shame, but we still chat on discord.

So, thank you Hello Games, for all the memories, fun, and dedication.
