No mans sky is a casual exploration game. The meat of the game is the planet exploration, but there is space exploration too. My evaluation of the game was distorted by the Explorations expansion. It was a seasonal event, that required a new character to be made. Up till the Explorations season I have played a normal Artemis questline character, and in 20hours I made it till the unlocking of the anomaly. It took so much because I just kept casually exploring the different types of planets. With the seasonal Explorations, a bunch of random milestones had to be completed, to ultimately unlock the season reward (a custom fighter) for every other saves too. So instead of playing the game organically, and following the main Artemis questline, I played the Explorations event.

I bought the game to play it in VR. However the user interface was not very VR friendly. Critical information in the early game was not easily accessible. On a monitor you see the state of your protection in the lower left corner, and the amount of mined materials in the upper right. In VR, you don’t see any of them readily. You have to turn your head away from the scene towards the bottom left to see the status of the protection. You have to turn your head to the upper right direction to see the amount of mined materials. Soon it gets annoying. Also reading text is hard in your log screen. A large floating window will appear before you, which you cannot overview without rotating your head to see different parts of it. I just reverted to play it on the screen. The crisper graphics, smoother framerate, and the lack of heavy optical distortions (granted, a personal problem for me with my Reverb G2) made the choice of the screen a natural one.

In the game you can explore planets. They are procedurally generated, based on a few archetypes. The stellar point of the game is the various terrains that are generated. Generally they look believable. You can explore on foot astoundingly vast areas. On this terrain are inserted varied amounts of plants and animals, and some minerals. Basic survival minerals are available on every planet. But each planet has only a small set of exotic minerals. You will have to travel to other planets to have access to some of the more exotic elements. Or you can just buy basic materials from space stations or the ship NPCs. It is a casual game, if you don’t want to gather them by yourself, you can just buy them after a bit of traveling. 

Early on the survival aspect dominates, when you scavenge supplies to stay alive. This is the part where you are not yet aware of the more advanced concepts, and will probably struggle to stay alive in more extreme conditions. Eventually however you will learn how to deal with those situations, after which they became mere nuisance, mostly due to the frequent manual replenishing of the various protections.

There are a few item types on the planets (various caches, knowledge stones, …). Soon you will be familiar with each of those. After a while you will probably ignore most. It doesn’t help that for some item types there is basically no variety. All of my treasure hunts seemed to take place in the same ruins, with practically the same layout. All the crashed freighters seemed the same, with similar rewards. Also all inhabited space stations have the exact same internal layout, the only thing that changes is the dominant alien race (of which there are 3).

On the planets there are some building archetypes. Eventually all of them will be familiar, as they are taken from a finite pool of premade resources. There are some things to grind, like words from languages, or the currencies for upgrades. Some upgrades are mandatory to access restricted areas, and unlocking them will keep you occupied.

While there are questlines in the game, or milestones for the Explorations update, it is up to the player to do whatever he likes. Some players build exotic bases, but those are completely optional. You can acquire your first freighter surprisingly easy. When you save a freighter from an attack, it will be offered for you for free if you don’t already own a freighter. You can put most of the utilities you have in a base on it. A nice bonus is that you don’t have to worry about powering them, the freighter will provide the required power. There are two downsides for building on a freighter : you cannot use a manual save point, and there is no teleport-to option. You can still use a teleport gate to travel to other destinations normally, but you cannot return to your freighter through it.

The game was incrementally expanded after its original release through various updates. You will have access to all of these updates when you buy the game. In Explorations the Artemis (aka Main questline) was missing altogether. When I completed the Explorations milestones, I stopped playing. There were still some things to pursue, like the Atlas questline, or the living ship questline, but I considered that I have already seen enough of what the game had to offer.

Your upgrade path is mainly unlocking slots for technology, and then filling them with technologies. There are different tiers of multi-tools, but I failed to observe any effect of the tier. What mattered was the number of technology slots. You can have only up to 3 technologies of the same type. In your suit that limit is for the inventory and technology tabs separately, so you can have 3+3 of the same type of technology.

There are only 2 save slots for a character. One is the auto save slot, which triggers when you leave your ship. The other is the manual save slot, which triggers when you use a save point. There are waypoints scattered on the planets which can act as a manual savepoint. You can also have a portable save point in your inventory, which you can use while on the planets. But, for example on space stations they will be undeployable.

The graphics of the game is pleasing. The surface of the planets, while procedurally generated is still welcoming for exploration. The underwater parts I didn’t like that much, there is much less variation, and the constant need for air recharge makes those parts tedious.

The game can be played with keyboard and mouse, and with a gamepad too. I played with the keyboard and mouse. Some user interface is clearly written with the gamepad in mind, but works for the keyboard too. One problem was however the redefining of the keys. The numpad+, that I use for “E”, wasn’t recognized as a valid key. I had to map that to E through Autohotkey. Also I run into a weird bug, where all the quick interaction icons were misinterpreted. When I wanted to use the incoming message function, I had to select the one on its left (the galaxy icon). Or when I wanted to summon my freighter, I had to use the settings icon on its left. If I used the gamepad, there was no such anomaly. I played the game without mods, so it wasn’t a problem due to some mods.

There isn’t much voice acting in the game, mostly due to the fact that you are interacting with aliens, whose language you won’t know at first. This is achieved through a text only interface, where the words that you have learned will be translated, while the rest will be some gibberish text. An interesting case is the music of the game. It didn’t get annoying even after 100 hours because it too is procedurally generated. As such it will nicely blend into the background, and you won’t notice repetitions.

The size of the universe is large. One milestone required you to discover 35 new systems. Around the rendezvous path, initially it seemed impossible, as everything was already discovered by someone. But after I put some distance from that path, I reached segments where most planet systems were still undiscovered. If the minimap in the top left is to be trusted, I barely made any progress from the top right of the galaxy during that.

The game was generally stable, but it might have crashed a few times.

This is a game I wish could have a neutral rating, because this game is pretty balanced in its pros and cons.  Assume it is only positive because I personally consider the pros more enjoyable than the cons, for what its worth.

That said, No Mans Sky is a game that we probably all know the history of by now.  The ultimate comeback.  The launch that sunk a million hearts, then made a million more cry in glee when they didnt abandon ship but kept going.  We could have an inspirational story, but theres a bit more to this game than a simple comeback.

For example.  The game in of itself has a very simple, grindy gameplay loop, with easy to understand mechanics and a system of choose-your-own-adventure towards playing how you want to play in a universe chock full of new things to discover that will probably only ever be seen by you in a single lifetime.  That said, NMS has a few complications with this formula.

What comes first to mind is the glitches and bugs.  Out of everything that could possibly mar my enjoyment of this game, it is the shaky realization that any moment something could freeze, or glitch, or throw me through the floor to die in space, or even crash Steam, which has happened in PD.  And yes, I did the basic checkups on it.  Saves are also somewhat unreliable, and the Network sets you to pvp immediately, setting you up for... unfortunate instances with other players.  That said, there are some ways to combat these issues, by researching, having saves ready, and of course simply turning the pvp off.

Multiplayer is an afterthought, but a welcome one if you have friends to play with.  You can do things together, and space isnt quite so lonely.  Combat is also a bit too repetitive and samey.  And while were on that, the procedural generation gets old relatively quick. There are a quintillion stars to explore, but really only ten or twenty planet types to really get to grips with, with different colors.

Its price tag is also a large detriment, costing as much to play as many triple A games, despite probably being only worth half that price.  However, after an update, the game does go on sale at half off.  Be aware that updates majorly break the game for about a week though.

However, for all those cons, it is a relaxing, quick experience to lose some hours in, and when I wasnt wrestling with the game to work, or trying to get Steam to stop hanging itself, a rather enjoyable experience.  For the quick, casual version of this game, Expeditions are definitely the goto way to experience everything this game has to offer within a quick time period.  For the rest of you, simply just do whatever you want to do, there is no time limit on anything.

My recommendation?  If its for you, then wait for a sale when its at most 30 bucks, and you will likely get a good experience out of it. ^^

The release of No Man’s Sky in 2016 was explosive. Developed by indie studio Hello Games, the three years after the game’s reveal drew an incredible amount of attention, and in turn, hype. 

The overhype of No Man’s Sky is particularly hard to dissect even now due to how many different pieces of it there were. Hello Games did objectively claim there were features in the game that were not present at launch. Some were extremely small, but others were quite large, such as the inclusion of multi-player. And many media outlets did contribute to the building excitement by expounding on the revolutionary procedural generation tech and making high claims about how the game would provide infinite replayability and was industry-defining. However, fans anticipating the game also filled the gaps of their pre-release knowledge with a lot of their own speculation and hopes for the game. This all led to a disastrous launch with thousands of unhappy fans, even going so far as for Sony and Valve to bend the rules of their refund policies. There were pockets of fans who enjoyed the game for what it was, but they were easily drowned out in the ensuing uproar that dominated the online discourse around the game. 

For many games, especially ones from a studio the size of Hello Games, this would be the end of the story. But, this was not the case for No Man’s Sky. Instead, Hello Games began a years-long process of incrementally updating the game until it lived up to the fan base’s original expectations, and has even continued far beyond that point. 

Large update after a large update has led to them adding new features such as multi-player, fleet management, base building, and a whole lot more, and it was all in the form of free updates and without any microtransactions anywhere to be seen. It is one of the greatest redemption stories in the industry, and has allowed the game to build a dedicated fan base that has contributed to the online consensus of the game seemingly growing to be that “it’s good now.” 

So, naturally, I grew curious to see just where No Man’s Sky is now as someone with no prior experience with the game whatsoever. And now, after visiting countless planets, building sprawling bases, and managing a massive fleet of spaceships, I can report back on what exactly it is like to start playing No Man’s Sky in 2021.

Starting No Man’s Sky is as overwhelming as it is exciting. Players are instantly dropped into the cold, uncaring universe with little guidance. A simple block of text gives you a small nudge towards the main storyline, and then there you are. Alone on a hostile planet with a handful of meters to manage and a clunky UI to navigate. 

Having to maintain an oxygen supply, keep the hazard protection charged, charge equipment and rebuild a starship all while navigating the new environment is a lot to keep track of, and there is very little in the way of tutorials to help the player along. However, underlying it all is an excitement for the adventure ahead. The first planets that serve as the tutorial are some of the worst players are likely to come across while playing, but even then they still spark the imagination. 

This is doubled when the player is introduced to the base building mechanics. While not as in-depth as some other survival games on the market, there is a lot here to like. There are plenty of pieces to research, an intricate power system to manage, and, perhaps the game’s biggest boon to the base building, the ability to scout out the perfect vista to build in on countless planets. No Man’s Sky only really begins to disappoint upon traveling to your first space station. An ominously large cube, the station is pretty breathtaking as you approach. 

But then, your spaceship lands inside the hangar in a parking spot designated by a lit-up circle, and you cannot help but realize that…it’s empty-vacuous even. The station is little more than an unbelievably large space completely void of character, design, or life. The idea that anyone could actually live in these spaces is laughable at best. They are so completely void of just anything at all until it resembles the shell of a spaceport rather than an actual one. There is little more than some empty benches, a handful of stalls that act as stores, and a couple of different alien species loitering about. 

It is these different alien species that make up the last piece of discovery on offer here. While exploring planets players find monoliths with strange markings on them, each one granting a word from an alien language when they interact with it. The process of piecing together the languages act as a great parallel to the player’s own growth during this early stage of the game. As players piece them together they begin to feel more at home in the universe, they gain access to the stores on the station and can actually talk to the aliens around them as they become integrated and begin to fully understand all the mechanics on offer. In the grand scope of the experience it is a small addition to the game, but what it does to help integrate and immerse the player into the world is really smart and effective. 

At this stage, players will divide into two factions: those who love the game’s core loop and those who have burnt out on the lack of driving force behind their gameplay. For those who love the game, this will most likely be their favorite stage to be in. They will have ample resources, a fully kitted out freighter to trek around the galaxy in, and a fleet of different ships to cruise around in. 

This allows the player to engage with whichever aspect of the game they want to with ease. They can go to countless planets to explore with few distractions diverting them away. They can run trade routes to continue amassing wealth until they are an intergalactic Scrooge McDuck. They can pour their efforts into finding beautiful vistas and designing intricate bases for each one like a real estate mogul. Or, they can restart the game on one of its various difficulties, including a permadeath mode for players that really want to risk it all. 

The other players, on the other hand, will have grown tired of No Man’s Sky’s relentless grind and lack of meaningful endgame content. Engaging with No Man’s Sky at this stage requires a lot of self-motivation, and it is completely understandable that many will not be able to find further goals to move towards. This is especially understandable when considering that the endgame here is more or less repeating the content and activities the player has already done dozens of times, just slightly different thanks to a procedural generation system giving it merely a new gloss of the paint. It would help immensely if the procedural generation of planets also changed the mechanics and systems that the player would interact with, ala a roguelike, but how it stands, it does little more than change the appearance of what you interact within the same ways you have before. 

This is really where, as of 2021, No Man’s Sky sits. There is a lot of potential and excitement as a consequence when first starting the game. Some of the potential is realized well, but there are quite a few disappointments throughout as well. Whether or not the successful mechanics outweigh the less successful ones is up to the player. 

For the type of player that loves exploration and finding beautiful vistas, or for a player that does not mind a bit of a grind, No Man’s Sky has a lot to offer. For other players, it may be enjoyable for a couple of dozen hours and that is it. And for other players, the clunky UI, unending resource grind, and other small annoyances will simply be too much to get beyond the first troublesome planets. 

Regardless, the tale of No Man’s Sky is one of a successful redemption that is a fantastic example to all of the other games that have launched in such a disappointing state in recent years. But it also stands as a warning to keep one’s expectations in check when

This game was totally worth the $30 I paid for it. If i had paid $60, I would have still felt I got my money's worth, but, depending on what you like in games - i dont think anyone will mind paying $30 for this. But, some might not like paying $60.

First - i enjoyed the exploration theme of it. The idea of going off into space and just exploring and identifying and cataloguing all the numerous things out there in this huge galaxy, and I like to put down roots wherever i go, so the base building is just my cup of tea, putting down small to large little outposts on various planets as i explored.

And it is heavily an exploration game, very minimal combat situations, and the ones i did encounter, they're all pretty basic. So, if you're wanting an easy going game, this game is perfect. you literally go at your own pace doing whatever you want to do within the game - complete missions, follow the story, or just explore. 

The only time that was hectic was when i first started and i just had no idea what i was doing or how anything worked - which is, really, the situation the character you play is in, anyway. You're both literally the same entity, pretty much. 

Both of you figuring things out as you go, listening to your little navigator tell you how things work. In all honesty, if you're going to die - it's going to be that first launch into the game, where hopefully you figure it out before your shields all die. If you survive that, realistically, you shouldn't ever die again. It's just not that kind of game. Yes, there are constant elements of survival, but so long as you're a pack rat, you'll literally never have issues with anything. Anything. 

You might run into some minor issues with the ONLY real threat in this game, which are the sentinels, but even those are laughable when you figure out the correct tactics to use, and you can absolutely avoid these situations, in the first place. You pretty much have to choose to get into these encounters and stay in them.

Like I said - if you're wanting an easy-going game with some light building, minor multiplay, potentially some interesting lore, and light questing (even the main story is highly optional, doing it or not really doesnt effect overall gameplay, it just gives you more lore into the reality of the universe you're exploring), then this game is for you.

If you're wanting the option for loads of action, prefer very linear games, or a heavy story, this game likely won't deliver. It's simply too sandboxy without being a real sandbox.

TLDR 2-Point Summary
#1: Procedural magic appears among the sameness. 
#2: No Man's Sky is nowhere near as much work as the game you're currently playing.
---
I've put somewhere north of 800 hours into No Man's Sky. One hundred+ of these are due to the first Expeditions season.

When I began playing in the Spring of 2020, I was looking for something less intensive than my current game, and to be honest, that's the best description I can give you. No Man's Sky: less intensive than the game you're playing.

Don't get me wrong, No Man's Sky is full of surprise, jump scares, risk and loss. But those are only accessible, oddly, when you just play the game. For a procedural space game, it seems to be able to tell when you're grinding -- and refuse to pay out.

There's a lot to be said and a lot to explore, but if you're like my brother Chris, you see through "proc" like Neo in the Matrix, and the suspension of disbelief is gone. If you're like him, No Man's Sky is probably not for you.

One thing you learn when you play a lot of games is that patterns emerge across any playstyle. If you're acquisitive, you'll find your particular route to success, on a continuum of passive to active. The continuum is directly controlled by the player, thus the PvE elements are only as challenging as you like. As a consequence, No Man's Sky can feel like easy inventory Tetris. A Passive player can just as easily cross all the gates in the story. In fact, until the relative innovation of the Expeditions Gameplay Seasons, there are few reasons to ever risk one's life, or even a scrap of inventory.

If you've gotten this far, you might be looking for advice: first, become Zen with dying many times.

Background: I'm terrified of Space. Ever since I was young, I've been petrified of being locked in a capsule, blowing out my last breaths as spiders of veins pop across my neck. It's a nightmare I've had since the very first time I saw Steve Austin crash his rocket capsule on a black and white tv.

The first time you launch into Space in No Man's Sky, leaving the comfort of terra firma, it's disconcerting. With a full field of planets ahead, there's a real sensation of losing your place. Of never finding it back to your start planet. It's absurd of course. But there are real feels.

When you first resolve, you're crippled, with a starter Exosuit. Far from shelter, a ship, help of any kind.

In Survival Mode, you'll die thirteen times on your dangerous planet before you can read the pop-up about feeding your Life Support. On the way to shelter you'll die another 13 times. Once you reach your ship, that Zen I mentioned will kick in, and the link you used to have to dying will be broken. It's humbling. It's freeing.

Instead of a weapon, you're given a Multitool, which makes the implications of this game extremely family-friendly. At no point during my first playthrough did I kill anything other than a pirate -- in self-defense -- unless the mission compelled me. The Multitool has the capability of deploying a scanner, a shield, a visor that can find resources, can mine great chasms into the soil, and can fire offensive or defensive rounds in various ways.

When you begin there on your Starter Planet, you get a small MT with limited capabilities. As you start to shop around, you'll see there are loads of styles and many different varieties of tools, all with their own characteristics. And then like everything else, you realize the tools are procedurally generated, right down to crystals in the handle, or color of the body. Or whether it's a pistol, rifle or alien tech.

When it comes to tech, almost every portion of the MT is upgradeable. You can add a shotgun feature with the Scatter Blaster, or install an upgrade to add 20 rounds to its magazine. Upgrade your scanner for range, rewards and cooldown.

[b]Governed by Class[/b]

Like the Multitool, your Starship is capable of surprisingly numerous upgrades, add-ons and modules that can change the way it fights, hovers, scans and takes off. Not to mention, every Starship in No Man's Sky is capable of Warp, which can move you to a new system perhaps thousands of Light Years away.

Also like the Multitool, Starships have a Class designation from C to S. C-Grade is the lowest, B is medium-grade, A is top-grade and S is Superior. The cost of an S-Class ship can be surprisingly affordable, but generally the grades describe a fairly steep gradation in price. An A-Class Shuttle with 28 storage slots can cost 2.2 million units, while an S-Class with 34 slots can be around 6 million. That's because there are Class benefits that add up to extra powers or strengths for your ship.

[b]A conceit, or a wish you make to yourself[/b]

Being a participant in self-deceit is how an outside observer might consider traditional Role Play. The self-deceit you must realize is that after some time, when it comes to proc, the parts and pieces will all align and you'll find yourself going "it's all the same."

This conceit is threaded through the rather nihilistic storyline, which in no way compels one to continue. No Man's Sky is almost a "take it or leave it" experience. The game would rather not have you play if you're not into it.

You will see common creatures whole Galaxies away. You'll see similar ships. You'll see a lovely tailfin in a weird place in a far-off Galaxy. But then you'll realize it's just a tailfin.

If you ever played one of those face-switching games as a kid, you'll know what I mean. Flip the card and put the googly eyes in place. Flop the mouth for big, sexy lips and a full mustache. Parts and pieces.

Spend enough time in Space Stations and you'll see those pieces and parts, in different concatenations, wherever you go. And after a while your mind sort of reels, thinking of all the diversity inherent in an admittedly closed system such as this one. After all, the Universe limit is 255 Galaxies. The inference is real: this is all a simulation.

That's not a spoiler, by the way. You'll see the sameness in the species you encounter, the differences only in gesture, visage or costume. If you focus on this sameness, the illusion dissolves. But then, that's sort of the point.

[b]The sameness extends to Planets[/b]

This effect occurs with planets as well. Your Star System can have as few as two celestial bodies, and as many as eight, including natural satellites. The planets themselves are procedurally generated in No Man's Sky, so when you venture into a system where it says "First Contact," this experience is being made for you. This is why it's so satisfying.

And this is why it works.

I'm afraid I can't explain much farther without adding too much value to the game, getting into partial spoilers and potentially upsetting the critical balance. No Man's Sky is about making something magical emerge from utter sameness. Cold, bland, sameness. There is a greater metaphor there, and as you discover your umpteenth System, you'll think about that. The magic that can be derived from the same old stuff.

Hello Games has done a wonderful job with this game since its release! I was holding off on buying it because I'd heard it was absolutely terrible at launch, but the developers have been working hard to deliver instead of writing it off, and they're still working on adding more to it. I originally purchased because I wanted to support that attitude and the hard work they put in, but now I've played over 24 hours in the last week! The best way I could describe it is if Minecraft, Elite Dangerous, ARK, and Hollow Knight had a polyamorous lovechild they then worked together to raise to adulthood.
It has the vast space travel and exploration of ED, giving everyone the chance to discover new worlds nobody has ever seen before, the simplicity of Minecraft in crafting and control, the building system of ARK as it was intended, and an engaging story that makes you genuinely feel for the characters involved. All in a procedurally generated universe where every planet, moon, and star is fit for a magazine cover (once rendered in.)
If I had to gripe about anything, I'd say the loading screen to start up the game is pretty long, but I did make the mistake of installing my copy on a hybrid drive instead of my SSD.

Let me preface this that I'm a massive fan of that mid-late 70s to mid Eighties Sci-fi cover book aesthetic (Chris Foss/Fred Gambino/Peter Elson/Ralph McQuarrie/Roger Dean/etc etc) and this game definitely manages to evoke the aesthetic a lot of the times while being its own thing, nor is it trapped too much in 70s (although honestly I wouldn't mind it if it was even doubling down on it more).

But unfortunately as an actual [i]game you play[/i], the gameplay loop consists of the following (if you're ignoring the main quest). Fly to planet. Fly around looking for a resource you need maybe/some landmark/etc. Mine needed resource. Refuel/upgrade/sell resource at one of the space bases/poke randomesque wildlife/and fly around same-y looking areas. Compared to something like Subnautica which has a very solid exploration loop (keep going deeper, you'll find more stuff to upgrade!), base building (You need something to find stuff/etc), and map design, No Man's Sky flounders. No Man's Sky gives you a wide variety of ways to get around (Skimmer/Motorcycle-esque thing/Dune Buggy/Giant Mecha/Trundling big truck-esque thing) but ultimately none of them are as fast or as useful as a decent class spaceship with recharging take-off fuel. The whole gameplay loop is more or less like this. You CAN have a huge fleet of spaceships that go on adventures, but you just get some text updates and some cash (or they die, or their ship breaks, and you have to do some of the most tedious repair job exploration game-play things I've done in my life). You CAN build a huge sprawling base, but other than a few core elements and people, the bases are useless and just serve to either house containers for more resources. You CAN visit endless randomly generated planets, but after you've seen a good 10-15 of them, you feel like you've seen them all, Once in a while you can find a funny animal and feed it, it becomes semi-friendly and it poops. That's your interaction with the life in the galaxy.

There's no cool dead cities, there's no incredible space jungles, or weird atmospheric giants. It's just same-y looking rolling hills and maybe once in a while floating rocks. There's a small bit of a plot, but it's not really gripping at all. There's a bunch of aliens, but they don't have anything to say. There's a bunch of random missions a la Skyrim/Fallout 4, but ultimately it's just more useless credits once you have a multitool/spaceship you actually like. The spaceships you can fly around are kinda neat, but there's only one scale of them. You can't pilot anything larger than a single seat spaceship (classed as fighter/small shuttle craft/"explorer"/and the rare exotic) unless you consider a freighter as "piloting", which makes the space battles limited and dull.

I genuinely want to like this game, like I said, I really like the aesthetic (some of the glitch planets are pretty cool), the music, and what it could be. But ultimately as an engaging [b]game[/b] it still completely fails, even with all the updates which serve more or less as distractions from the core loop of "travel to other planets, mine their resources, mess around in the inventory to make things". As an interactive screensaver that you kind of interact with and look at colorful same-y looking landscapes, or build bigger and more useless bases, it's a nice distraction.

In short, it's like an excellent mix of Elite Dangerous and Subnautica. To break it down a bit longer...

Having played Elite Dangerous for a good chunk of time, I can sort of compare this to Elite. The problem I've always had with Elite though is that it has a lot of good ideas but many of them are half-baked and seem thrown in. This game is like Elite with it's ideas fleshed out. The game is extensive, featuring fighter-like ships, planetary vehicles that range from mechs to a tank to a submarine, capital ships and freighter armadas, all of which are able to be owned by the player. Planets are randomly generated and the possibilities for them are vast. I have not found a single pair of planets that look alike in nearly 50 hours of gameplay (And having visited probably close to 30 planets).

Social sections are also done in a very engaging way. The universe is a vast place and you are unlikely to run into other players by chance. That being said, I have stumbled upon many abandoned bases built by players, which do well to make the galaxies feel lived in. You can also use portals to quickly travel to specific locations. I've made quite a bit of use out of these so I could travel to places with a lot of players, or where players have found something interesting that I wanted to see.

Additionally there is a social hub that includes the ability for matchmaking where randomly generated missions and rewards are given out every few minutes. This allows for the downsides of a massive player space to be sidestepped and has lead to some of the best moments I've had in this game; building bases  or exploring the depths of a nearby underwater planet, all with other random players in the game.

All in all, I never played No Man's Sky on release but recently heard from fans of the game that it had really turned around since then. I bought it to try it out and while I can't speak to how much better it is than what it was, I can say this is a very well made space game. I would absolutely recommend this game to anyone who's looking for an excellent single player experience, with room for friends to join in.

It's a fun, relaxing, casual game. Don't go in expecting any kind of depth though.
There is a lot about this game that I like and a lot of things that I wish were a little bit better. 
In my 60 hours of exploration, I didn't really find many different species or planet types. It doesn't take long until you start seeing same species on every other planet with only very slight variations. Also don't go in expecting to find anything like a hostile tyranid world or anything like that. An overwhelming majority of creature are incredibly docile and passive. Even a planet type called "The Nest" is nothing special at all. 
The exploration part of the game is really strange. When you arrive to a new system, it says that you or some other player have discovered it, but in reality, there's already a station there and everywhere you go there are signs of activity from people before you. And they all use the same style of machinery, buildings, terminals, etc. 
The combat is very easy and simple. I didn't even bother upgrading my ship's weapons or shields and still managed to kill every enemy ship, even the "difficult" missions and high alerts, with barely any effort. I'm not even a good pilot, the combat is just effortless, on the ground or in space. 
It's better to do the story missions first, because if you adopt the skyrim approach of abandoning the main stories from the get go and try to catch up later after you've explored, upgraded and etc, then you'll run into the problem of doing missions for no reward, since every npc will give you blueprints that you already have.
On the topic of NPCs, none of them matter or are memorable. The game kind of wants you to talk to every npc at every station and learn specific words from their language, but that gets super old super quick. I wish the ability to click through and skip the "dialogue" was faster. Collecting words is really tedious.
I like the Exocrafts, but for some reason you can't scan things from inside. Like it'd a difficult thing to put a scanner on a giant mech. Imagine you're walking in your mech underwater and see something that you'd like to scan. Guess you gotta get out now. Oh joy.
I said that this game is simple, but some of the mechanics are incredibly convoluted. Some things you can only figure out by accident or by relying on a wiki article. Wondering how to get an Atlas pass? So did I and the way I got it was by blindly stumbling upon it. There was no indication prior to it and the solution felt counter-intuitive. 
Often times I'd find myself wondering if my game was bugged, if I'm not understanding something or if it's working as intended but the design choice was bad. I read online that the derelict freighters are supposed to be always different, but somehow managed to do the exact same one 4 times in a row. In different systems no less. Why is the exact same derelict freighter in different systems? I still don't know if it's a bug, if I messed up or if it's supposed to be this way. Google searching gave me no answers. 
Graphics and music are fine. The story is a bit meh. 
Overall, for an indie game made by a small studio, it's still a very good game and very fun. Just get it during a sale and don't expect too much.

Reviews.109524:
[h2]General Thoughts:[/h2]
While vastly improved from the state of its initial release, almost five years later their proposed roadmap has led to what still feels like an early access title. Limited, repetetive content, severe performance issues, and buggy multiplayer all lead to an underwhelming experience that's not worth the asking price. For all their talk of quadrillions of worlds, this game feels devoid of meaningful content, especially compared to other games of its price range. If it were more polished, with a little more depth, No Man's Sky could be the definitive open-world space exploration game, but as it stands, you'd be better served seeking out more polished spacefaring experiences elsewhere.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
No Man's Sky offers a vast open expanse of interesting and unique worlds to explore, claim, and name for all to see, with a variety of ships to pilot, varied beings to interact with both sentient and otherwise, bases to build, fleets to command, and an intriguing story for a single player to pursue. The first impression of all of these elements is solid and promising. Some of the ideas stand out as particularly unique; learning the languages of the various species, for example, is a cool idea.
Unfortunately, all of these elements are crude in their execution and they give a distinctly incomplete feeling, which I largely attribute to the fact that so much of this game has been left to procedural generation rather than properly curated game design. By the 20th space station, the sameness of the encounters becomes inescapable. The quests are extremely basic and formulaic (Find building, activate terminal, done). The dialogue and NPC interaction is minimalist and repetetive (try to understand NPC, choose a word, done). Over and over I'll complete my objectives with a distinct feeling of "...That's it?"
Multiplayer... exists. This game is certainly better with friends, simply because friends offer something to interact with that has depth and real unpredictability: you can talk with your friends about whatever you want, and none of the NPCs will suddenly decide to try to kill you for hyucks, and space battles are certainly more interesting with a large collective of people involved. To the game's credit, multiplayer is easy to set up, something that seems to be a holy grail nowadays. Unfortunately, multiplayer suffers [i]heavily[/i] from the bugs and performance issues that otherwise plague the game. Not fun Skyrimmy bugs, either; more "my base that I spent 10 hours on is underground now" bugs. 
You'll notice I have almost 70 hours of play in, and you may fairly think, "Clearly it wasn't [i]awful."[/i] Firstly, a [i]distressing[/i] amount of that time was spent in just trying to get the damn game to be playable (see "Additional Thoughts" below"). Secondly, a lot of that time was spent in anticipation, feeling as though I must still be in a sort of introductory portion of the game and that it will take off once the game really opens the taps. That never happens. Thirdly, at times the game absolutely crawls. For example, when you send your fleet on quests, some of those quests won't be completed for 24 hours. [i]Real time.[/i] One quest I was doing told me that I had to wait for 2 hours before the quest-giver would even give me my next task. In addition to these arbitrary waits, many quest objectives are aimless and/or grindy; "acquire this object" doesn't give you any clear idea as to how or where to acquire it, and I just had to toodle around the galaxy scanning and mining and hoping I'd get lucky and stumble on the thing I was looking for. It was a slow, plodding, frustrating 70 hours, punctuated by the occasional "Oh this planet is cool".
Overall, the gameplay as it stands is what I would expect from an early access title, not something in a final game: a promising skeleton that should be fleshed out into a fuller, deeper experience before release. Unfortunately, the game has been released and [i]significantly[/i] updated and expanded, and still here we are with a promising skeleton.

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The game, when it's rendering properly, is gorgeous; vibrant colors, diverse planetary environments, interesting and varied flora, fauna, and fungi, creative character design, wondrous space structures, and so forth. The starships you'll acquire have individuality. There is clear artistic vision and creativity here, and that it's executed procedurally is a technical marvel.
My only major complaint on a visual level is that the game does not capture the scale of stellar space well. Star systems in No Man's Sky feel almost claustrophobic with how close everything is. You'll always find every planet on the same side of its sun, for example, and in almost every system you will have to fly [i]around[/i] a planet to get to one behind it. You can clearly see neighboring planets filling large real estate in the sky. Space is not so small as this; these star systems are "micro-systems" in the same way that Skyrim is a "micro-country" that you can walk across in a half-hour. For me at least, this defeats the sense of the vastness of space.
Unfortunately, the game struggles to render its visuals well, and it doesn't seem to be consistently tied to the adequacy of the PC; many users reporting unplayable jank have [i]very[/i] capable hardware.

[h3]Audio[/h3]
The soundtrack is good, but not particularly striking or iconic. It fills in certain moments well, with spacey ambience and energetic combat music. There's no voice acting, but the aliens make alien noises that apparently are supposed to be words that you can learn to understand. For the most part the sound effects are clean and effective and add to the sense of atmosphere—for example, on some planets, you can hear particulate in the atmosphere rattling against your ship as you fly—but there are moments of odd and obnoxious anomalies, such as a planet I found myself on that sounded as though it was constantly exploding around my ship, which on-foot exploration could not explain. Overall a sufficient sound experience.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is told primarily through dialogue boxes, reading character speech and having limited ability to respond, and I don't get the sense that my responses make much of a difference to the story or even the individual interactions; perhaps one or two dialogue boxes change in response to a choice I make. I get little tidbits of lore through interaction with various structures and NPCs, but it's not a cohesive experience.
The story in this game is... vague. 70 hours in, I don't really have a strong sense of where the story is headed or what even my goal is; I've just been doing what I'm told by entities who speak in vague and cryptic terms using broken and often nearly unintelligible speech patterns. The game's mystery is so thick that it results in more confusion than intrigue. It would benefit strongly from introducing an overarching goal or concept early on to tie the narrative together; as it stands, I feel aimless even as I follow the directions and quests I'm given.

[h3]Additional Thoughts[/h3]
A major part of my recommendation against this game is that it game performs [i]abysmally.[/i] No $10 game, let alone $60 game, has any business running this badly. For me and many others, it borders on unplayable unless you're brave enough to dig into your settings files—and I couldn't even get [i]that[/i] to work because the game kept resetting my changes every time I started. I won't conjecture what is actually the problem—I'm not an expert on game optimization—but if you Google "No Man's Sky lag/stuttering", you'll fall down a rabbit hole of frustration, confusion, and misinformation. If you decide to try this game, and you experience these performance issues, get a refund before you dump hours into trying to fix it, because there's a good chance you won't have fixed it before your 2-hour gameplay limit is up.

Playing for the first time on PC in 2021, this feels too buggy to recommend. Even without the bugs, I'd probably be on the fence: there are too many little annoyances that distract me from enjoying what could be a decent procedurally generated space exploration game.

First, the bugs. Nearly 5 years in, I'm surprised how many bugs I've run into in just a few days of play. Every game session has ended with the game hard-locking, often after alt-tabbing despite running in Fullscreen Windowed, necessitating a full reboot. I've gotten stuck in my ship unable to leave or fly around. I've had missions get bugged so either scanning doesn't work or quest markers don't show up or quest objectives don't get completed. Portable items used in missions often become non-portable requiring either destroying them or restarting the game. I've had my inventory button perpetually default to my ship inventory and get stuck that way. I've had enemies get stuck in the ground or clip into structures in ways that I can't fix (ie kill them). I, myself, have clipped through space stations and fallen through the world a few times, dying in the process. The Pulse Drive is usually not usable near planets or space stations, but about 5% of the time it bugs out and works anyway. The games portals sometimes show me only the portals I've been to and the ones in my system. Other times I see portals for a whole ass-load of people I don't know and can't travel to as the worlds usually don't download. Though when those portals do work, the structures on the other side don't render. Did I mention every session ends when I quit after the game locks up?

There are other bugs that I've encountered, but I'm not going to nitpick every graphical glitch or hiccup. It's procedurally generated on a massive scale and those issues are bound to happen. On the other hand, there are some head-scratching usability decisions by Hello Games that I just can't stop thinking about.

When it comes to item management, items stack in your inventory spaces. But some vehicles/containers allow certain (unmarked) items to stack higher than usual! Instead of giving vehicles/containers *more* inventory spaces or allowing certain items to take up fractional item spaces, you'll frustratingly find items that don't move, space for space, between your Exosuit and another inventory. Furthermore, not all inventories work the same way! Your Exosuit and various vehicles all have inventories that you can stack, rearrange and organize to your hearts content. But try to build a base and you'll find *chest inventories* don't let you do any of that. You can one-click-move items in and out with the game auto-filling container slots from top to bottom, but there's zero ability to rearrange and organize already containered items. In a game that has so many moving pieces and items to keep track of, you want to create predictable item behavior, not whatever this is. 

Playing on PC almost requires significant control remapping and I'm just not sure how Hello Games managed to land on the control scheme they did. By default, flight controls are set up for players with a controller and a thumbstick that snaps back to center. Flying M+K with the default scheme is maddening. Detecting and painting target locations while moving on foot requires WASD + holding F to detect and also holding E to paint a target, which is at best uncomfortable. The number keys, by default, don't do anything. They don't even select the different firing modes for your Multi-tool (that's cycled with G). You *could* set them up manually (if you can find the setting) to switch between *different* Multi-tools when you get them which won't happen until several hours into the game and isn't all that useful even then. Until then those are just wasted buttons. Scanning on foot requires pressing C. Scanning in a vehicle equipped to do so requires you press X to open a menu and then select the type of building you're scanning for and then click to confirm! Why do this?! Lastly, when in an inventory, you'll need to press E to extract loot from certain items. Q, E, A, and D also toggle between your different inventories and the pages of items therein. Venture a guess how often the game knows you're pressing E to extract and not E to change inventories in the following scenario: you've moused over the item you want to extract AND it's displaying the tooltip prompt reminding you it's 'E to Extract'?

It's not a high percentage.

I can't leave without mentioning the Sentinels. Having not progressed the story very far, to my knowledge Sentinels are a robotic galactic threat, everyone pretty much hates em and they're no good/very bad. They come in a few sizes, with the smallest ones patrolling planets in varying density and, like the cops, will come harass you if they think you're up to no good. Attack and kill the sentinel(s) and they'll call for backup.

Indefinitely.

Like, actually forever.  There is no securing an area. There's no winning a fight. The fight only ends when you disengage and let the alert timer run out. Most modern games have, for good reason, shied away from endlessly spawning enemies except as a means to disincentivize the player from some action. Here, however, sentinels will just *attack you* when they catch you doing one of the only actions that matter in No Man's Sky: collecting resources from a planet. For some resources, the game just spawns a bunch of sentinels as soon as you've started collecting and will keep spawning them, wave after wave, until you back off and disengage. This feels bad! For new players, every fight escalates until you can no longer hold your own. Collecting resources can pull you into these 'unwinnable' fights which feels like a waste of time. There's no sneaking around and evading the sentinels while you collect certain resources. There's no sense of accomplishment by beating a tough enemy. There is only fighting them until you're dead, run away, give up, or maybe until there's only one left alive that you can ignore while you gather your space cactus or whatever. This feels unintended and it's a pretty near-sighted implementation of never-ending enemies. Why not have a wave-cap that increases with the Sentinel Presence rating of each planet? Because eff you, that's why. 

Forgetting the bugs, the odd interface decisions and, now that I think about it, a whisper thin newbie onboarding experience and what is No Man's Sky really? It's the monumental vision of galaxy-scale procedurally generated content with a few billion worlds to explore and gameplay that ... kinda falls flat. The technology may be impressive, but at the end of the day, you have to look at a vertical slice of the game. What are you actually spending your time doing? You're exploring surprisingly similar-looking planets to collect resources, occationally doing a little (unsatisfying) fighting, and you're crafting materials to expand your toolkit. It's gameplay that sounds better as bullet points on the back of a box than it is to actually play.

"You can mine asteroids for precious metals!"

"Buy any spaceship you see and trick it out with custom parts!"

"Explore a galaxy, system by system, planet by planet! Fly to, land on and explore worlds seamlessly!"

But those actions quickly feel insignificant and tedious. The possibilities are broad, but the content is sadly shallow. No Man's Sky falls into the same trap so many open world games fall into: unimpactful exploration.  There's a hecking lot to explore but not a whole lot to actually see or do. Hello Games executed on a wild vision, but I'm left wondering when I get to the real fun part. Collecting resources and crafting kept me humming along just fine for a few hours, but I'm now certain there isn't anything else coming. If this is it, it's a no for me dawg.

 And then I remember about the bugs. Major Yikes

This is for myself for future reference to get Oculus quest 2 over airlink to run smooth 90fps ( with dips to 87 here and their) with only 8 percent reprojection according to FpsVR and 10 percent headroom for detail,Nvidia control panel set Vsync to off,power to high performance, In steam vr turn legacy reprojection off, Super sampling down to 1872x1888 for both steam and game, that is default res for steam when oculus is set at 3712x1872 by 90hz.
In game turn down detail or to off on options that allow off and set Anistropic x2, turn VR body off as well can be janky when using jetpack, so just have hands on display.
When the game is running go to Task Manager, go to details, set vrserver.exe,vrcompositor.exe, OVRserver_x64.exe and No mans sky all to high performance, this is the same as with half life alyx to avoid stuttering due to oculus not working right with steamvr at the moment.

RTX 2070 S, Intel i7 9700k ( not overclocked due to testing ) 32g ram, normal HDD not running off my SSD.
And oculus quest 2 running over AIRLINK stutter free.

Keeps getting better and better!
Fun planets, building bases, carriers and now pets (although I didn't really feel the need for one).

Simply following the storyline kept me occupied for a long time and aside from that there's still lots to do (for which I wished there were proper sidequests for guidance). I also really like the Nexus, where you meet and see and the different players and can visit some of their bases.

Multiplayer needed an update and I think Expeditions is a good step forward. Personally I wished for a better coop experience (quest sharing among other things).
Space combat is obviously not as fun as in other space games. But the game makes up for it with good gameplay mechanics. Just getting from A to B, landing, taking off, calling or switching ships don't feel like work - which is good, because I want to play a game, not spend hours simulating docking procedures.

Due to the random generation of the planets and places of interests some places start looking the same really quick (like in Minecraft). There's hope (and yes there is, as they push out ~3 major updates per year) they will improve abandoned outposts and enemy hotspots so it looks less generic.

I came to this game pretty late. I did not play at launch so I didn't experience a lot of the launch woes that apparently existed. All I can say is that this game is one of my favorite ways to spend time casually, and it made the COVID-19 quarantine of 2020 bearable in so many ways. I find it incredibly peaceful to fly to planets, harvest goods, run trade routes, outfit bases and so on. There's lots to do and it's okay to take a long break and come back which is important right now for me. 

I also really appreciate this game as a big Star Trek fan and in many ways this game feels like the Star Trek game I never got. It's all about the exploration and so many Trek games are more about the combat and strategy. There are many times that I wish I could have NPC followers to go exploring with when piloting the Freighter around like an away team. Full disclosure, I have not tried the newest game mode with Expeditions but I'm hoping it scratches that itch when I do.

Overall the game is well worth the price, if you really enjoy exploration in games than this one will not let you down.

Some cons and/or criticisms:

Some of things are vaguely spoiler-ish so tagging them as such...

[spoiler]
Eventually you really see a lot of the same patterns repeated on very different worlds. Even though you have a seemingly infinite amount of planets to explore you eventually notice that every hostile plant basically looks the same despite the fact that other lifeforms vary pretty wildly planet to planet and regardless of weather patterns or whatever.

Reviews.109696:
What a ride!

Pre Aug 2016
Leaving your stable career for a startup. Selling your house to support a tiny team of six people. Hawking your passion project at E3 and then suddenly being strapped to the front of a hype train you have no experience steering. 

Trying to build this game while fending off lawsuits, having your office flooded, and having three kids. Stepping up to be the face of your company and your game with introversion/social anxiety and no PR experience, with media companies jostling to get a piece of you and your game. While you're drowning, Sony swoops in with an offer that could make them millions. Incredible! More publicity couldn't be bad...right? 

Now the eyes of the world are on you. You start to realise that you won't be able to make the deadline. You're recruiting for your team as fast as possible and it nearly triples in size, but it's not enough. Now Sony is breathing down your neck with a contracted date. 

If you ask for more time, people will expect more from the game, but if you don't, you will have nothing to deliver. The dread in the pit of your stomach is constant, the anxiety overwhelming. And when it hits, you become the centre of one of the biggest gaming hate storms to date.

If I were in that position, holy ...

2021 - not an abandoned software. Unlike many, many other projects NMS has not been dropped for a NMS2.

It's not perfect, but it should be way better than "MIXED". I wont argue about the price tag, since NMS has been in so many sales. Get it when while you see fit it to your budget liking and you wont regret it. Especially if you want a chill coop session wit your friends. If you want quicker progress, don't complain - mod it or edit it. It's not a MMO nor a GTA official server with forced circumstances ... 

HAVE FUN, with all that has been added in whole freaking five years.

The concept is good, it is very immersive and you can either pirate, farm, build bases, explore mine. It is an open game without limit, although it is not great at anything it is good at everything. I have played it it for a few months, and have looked forward to playing it on my days off. whether it be completing missions, upgrading equipment or just exploring.

On the downside, it is painfully slow in the personal scenes, eg talking to NPCs, and is bugged still, whether it is loading incorrectly where nothing loads correctly and sometimes buildings and ather avis do not appear until a few seconds/minutes later, and sometimes never. Worst still, it can crash at anytime, losing you game time, unless you are aware, and save progress at every opportunity, such as enetering and leaving your starcraft to create a restore point, but even that get's tedious. However, I was prepared to put up with that for the fact that the game was so good.

However, and this is the deal breaker for me, they decided to come out with an update called expeditions. Was it to fix the bugs and the glitches and the slow NPC scenes? Sadly no. This update was to give more emphasis on multiplayer missions. Personally I am not, and never will be interested in that aspect, and never will be, but I can take it or leave it, so if they left it that then I would be happy. Apparently they were not happy with the game being good and playable so they decided to make it harder for solo players.

They changed the missions so instead of having a choice of maybe 9, you were limited to 6. You used to be able to accumalate several similar missions in different galaxies and complete them all in one go earning you all the awards, but not now. Each mission has a specific location and not necessarily in the galaxy you are in. When you select a mission it now only takes you to an approximate location so you have to get out of your craft and scan for the exact location (which in itself is not always accurate) then either walk or to fly to the location (PS, at the time of writing, the locate missing person mission is bugged, and does not work). So you have to spend a lot more time earning credits and nanites to get upgrades, which in my opinion is not an improvement. If I enjoyed walking round aimlessly, I could shut down the computer and leave the house, and I could get a pie and chips on the way.

Another way earning credits was to buy goods at a space station at knockdown prices, and fly to the next galaxy and sell them for a profit. They have now stopped that as the next galaxy also is selling the same items at knockdown prices so no profit to be made there.

The companions upgrade was a nice diversion, but there is a limit to how big they get. I reached that and so am no longer interested.

Overall I think it is a great game, and would be good for a new player. For me, they killed it with the expeditions update, and wish I had the option to undo the update, this is no longer the game I paid for, or enjoyed playing. What is more of a concern is that the developers have been criticised in the past, and stuck to it and designed a very good game, despite the flaws. Now they seem to be intent on self destruction, as, instead of fixing the bugs and crashes, they bring out updates that make the game less attractive. I used to play it about 20 hours a week, I think I probably only played it about 20 minutes this week, and only to check up on my companion. That is how bad it is now.

You could buy the game, and enjoy it, but be prepared for the bugs, and the fact that the game you buy today, may change for the worse in the next few months, and without your decision. I would not take that chance

As a kid, I have always been fascinated with all things extraterrestrial. Stars, planets, aliens, all the good stuff; the only thing that came close was my fascination with dinosaurs and oceans. In fact, I think most kids are this way. And as such, when No Man's Sky was revealed, I thought it would be my biggest childhood fantasy realized. But at the same time, I thought it was too ambitious of a project to be possibly carried out on PC, in 2016. And I was right, it was a disaster. "Lucky me," I thought, "saved myself 60 dollars."

Fast forward a couple of years and I stumble upon NMS once again, on a Steam sale. The price was good and the Sunday was a real yawner so far, so I bought it. And I played it. For 15 hours straight. No Man's Sky was everything I hoped it to be, and more. In the greatest redemption arc in the history of gaming, the players were fed several DLCs, DLCs that EA would charge another 60 bucks for, for free. And in 2021, No Man's Sky has everything - countless stars, planets, systems and galaxies, randomly generated worlds that you can explore with your friends, in real-time. And they all have their own, randomly generated dinosaurs. Oh, and oceans. Worlds covered in oceans. Who needs real life anyway? Real life sucks ass.

I went into this game with the lowest of low expectations expecting the worst. I was extremely excited for this game up until launch and from there it was a no go in my books. From my personal experience this game was joked about and overall viewed as what not to be for years. Recently I had a couple friends who had played for a very long time introduce me to the game. They had me make my first save as a hardcore character and overall babied me from dying about 10 times within my first half hour on the game. While feeling annoyed with the game and continuing to think it was what I had heard for years I finally lifted off my first planet. I really struggled from here to find out how to make money while my buddy was making millions in the same time I had accumulated about half a million. It was kind of at this point I decided I wasn't going to quit and instead see this game through and have a real first hand opinion on it for any of my friends that wanted to try it in the future. 

The game took a turn for me when I found my niche. I got a couple scanner upgrades and spent the next two days doing nothing but exploring as many planets as well as doing main story here and there. I found that this game really enables you to profit, and or have fun with whatever it is you enjoy about it. I was always told the diversity between planets wasn't really there. While there could be more for sure, there is some crazy stuff out there in this game. There is enough diversity to keep even someone who just enjoys exploring engaged. This game surprises you with the main story, it isn't going to win an oscar but the story in itself is unique and fun. I truly believe the best way to experience this game is to never look at what this game was but to instead look at what it is now. This game offers something for everyone to enjoy. Whether you want to be a space pirate, an explorer, a trader, a bounty hunter, or really any of the other titles you can give an activity, you can make your own fun out of nothing in the world they have so far. After you've had your fun in normal mode, survival, hardcore, and creative there are expeditions which ended up being the most appealing part of this game for me. It reminds me of Diablo or Path of exile seasons where you can start up fresh and meet goals set out and have a brand new journey however you decide to do it. 

Overall this game is worth your time and money if you like anything about exploration, and space. 
If you're unsure of yourself take a look at some of the content people like SurvivalBob, Jason plays, and whatever the youtube algorithm fancies that you click on. 

I write this mainly for my friends to see if they ever click on the game briefly to consider it. But I really hope this can help one person go in with a positive mindset and really give this game a go.

This is a weird one. Depending on what you're looking for it may not be what you're expecting, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. When I first tried it I clocked 30 hours and gave up -- the procedurally-generated planets got boring, the story was uninteresting, and I kept asking, "what's the point?" But I later gave it a second chance and it kind of clicked.

This is a sandbox game where you set your own goals. It gives you a giant playground and nudges you in a few directions, but it's ultimately up to you to decide what to do.  There is a "main quest," but it's (imo) quite boring and is only there to string you along with learning crafting recipes and introducing you to the various aspects of the game.

For me, the fun came from building bases, hunting down S-class starships and gear, and figuring out how to make enough money so I could stop shooting lasers at rocks all the time and just buy anything I wanted. The game has a gratifying RPG-esque grind, and to me it's been a comfy "chillout" game to turn on for a few hours each night and slowly work towards various goals.

This game isn't Mass Effect or Star Citizen; it's more like space Minecraft. It's not a linear adventure where the fun is handed to you on a silver platter. You have to enjoy crafting, exploring, and figuring out things on your own. I think creative and escapist types tend to feel most at home with this game.

I have played this 290 hours, yes. I tried all the content as it was released. Everyone knows the story of the bad release. Everyone knows how crappy and buggy it was. I won't discuss that part of this game's history.

After creating a basic empire and automining platinum for days to turn into Nanites and buy basically every premium item and upgrade available...nope...I wouldn't do it again.

Let me say here that the power creep is real. If you're starting out, play in solo mode. Players can one-shot you easily in the early days. And those early days are critical. You will grind for about 50hrs or so just to get decent gear, space to carry items, a nice base, and a good freighter.

Everything you do in this game is grind. And the grind has very little payoff.

I participated in the game's "main" storyline. It's one of those 'pick your bad ending' plots which isn't really worth putting a spoiler alert on. It really is that forgettable. There was no real connection established with the game's other characters. We learn very little about them through interaction, and you can probably hope to care very little in retrospect.

Derelict freighters are a slog, and they're the best part of the game. Go from A to B to C. Kill monsters. Turn on heaters. Read logs. Things onboard. Captain regrets not heeding warnings of the crew. Loot loot loot. Repeat. Every freighter is the same aside from the type of monster that's aboard.

There's very little variety in the planets. Bountiful Planet A is basically the same as B as C as D. They did put some interesting looking visual effects like "Shattered World" and "Capped World" but these add no depth to the explorative process. They're just there for flavor. Once you've scanned everything, and mined what you need, there's no reason to stay. There are no unique NPCs to find. No challenges to face. I'm told there are massive sand worms now. Okay. What do they add beyond their existence? 

Ganking in Expeditions is a problem. Remember I said you can get one-shotted by griefers? Well imagine a mode where someone can park a starship over your head and just kill you over and over again. Big fun right? No. Oh. And you can't escape. Cause you only have starter equipment and they have 30 days of grinding in.

It's just all pointless. The grind doesn't get you anything of value. The content does not create story. It's just a sandbox. And there are tons of other sandboxes out there that do worldbuilding as well. You can unlock better ships and more storage space, but it's not in service of anything important, and the Expeditions mode which gives that progress purpose has no pvp flagging, no phasing out with high level players, and no cooldown timer after a kill has been made. An amazing game that continually gets better. I have never experienced anything that made me feel so small, and appreciate that notion so deeply. 

What can be said about the troubled launch and redemption story that hasn't already been said before? There can be no doubt that the creatives at Hello Games have poured their hearts into this title, and continue to. No matter how much you explore, there is always be more to find, and new content being added so regularly that it isn't even the same game now that it was [i]six month[/i] ago, let alone a year (or four) ago.

The visuals are so compelling; so many beautifully-terrifying and just-regular-beautiful sights to behold. With so many planets, you may well be the only person to ever see them. It's just one rare and wondrous thing after another. The music is brilliant. The writing is terrific (though the uninitiated may wish to note that there is no spoken dialogue, all text-only). I really enjoy every single game mechanic and I even think the UI is very clever and useful once you get the hang of it.

The community of players surrounding the game are a breath of fresh air, as well. Where a large volume of other games focus on destruction, competition, and are generally rife with "toxicity," the NMS fan-base is overwhelmingly made up of players who want to build for the sake of building, help for the sake of helping, and share for the sake of sharing.

If you like exploration, space battles, ruminating on the nature and meaning of existence, base building, playing with friends, cooking, inventory management, playing alone, mining, crafting, midnight drives, Lovecraftian space horror fiction, swimming, farming, economy crashing, interplanetary culture, empire building, peacefully gazing at alien butterflies, or going for long walks, then there's almost certainly something in this great big universe that you'll enjoy. 

And if not, maybe it will be added soon.

I’ll start by admitting that I didn’t play the game when it first came out, I instead got it a few years ago.  It’s commendable how much the developers have worked to improve this game without asking for any additional payment. However I don’t personally enjoy the game much. Despite the dev’s efforts, the game is rather grindy. Most of the game ends up consisting of collecting resources to become more efficient at collecting resources. Once you’ve played for 5-10 hours, you’ve seen most of what the game has to offer. Besides story content which offers a bit more interest, most of the side missions are also repetitive and grindy. You can get lost in base building, but this aspect of the game ends up feeling at odds with the whole galaxy exploration stuff. While there are teleportation networks, it feels weird to spend time building a base despite the game pushing you to keep going to new galaxies. There’s a lot of replay-ability in a sense because of the procedural generation, but since the core of the game doesn't change in any meaningful way, there's no hidden depth to get lost in.

Coop does exist in the game, but it feels limited. All of the quests (story and side) are tracked per person, meaning you can’t really work with other people on the same job (besides sharing resources). There are missions you can do together, but this isn’t until later in the game. Otherwise, there’s so little you can meaningfully do cooperatively that it feels like you’re both just playing a single player game “along-side each other”.

The game is still being updated, meaning they’ll probably eventually add something that’ll make it more worthwhile for me. But right now, I really can’t recommend this game unless you’re already a fan of open world crafting games. If you’re already good at making your own fun, then you’ll probably like this. $60 seems like a bit much to me. Maybe $40 if you’re really into this genre. If you’re not sure how you feel about the genre but want to try the game, maybe wait for a sale even lower.
