Reviews.110042:
I've been playing for about a year now since I picked it up during last year's summer sale for a ridiculously cheap price. This was years after its disastrous launch, so I wasn't around to see how most of the major updates changed the game. This review is for people interested to see if the game is worth playing at all. I know you've all probably heard different things about the game, so I tried to compile my entire experience as an average player right here.

[b] [i] I found becoming space Jeff Bezos in No Man's Sky to be very fun. [/i]
[/b]

Maybe I am just easily pleased, but I never really got bored of visiting planets in system after system. I hear a lot of people complaining about planet diversity, and while the game could still be fleshed out greatly, I haven't gotten bored. I think this is mostly to do with the fact that there's always something to work towards. For me, it's all about scouting out new ships to trick out using the units I've gathered from selling goods and from finding loot (you can own six total), but there are tons of other things that players can spend their time on. Base building is a feature that I haven't bothered to learn much about seeing as I have only three, littered about on planets that I thought looked neat, although there is no limit to the amount of bases you can claim in the galaxy. Some player bases I've visited are insane though, with people spending many hours designing perfect, intricate systems to farm goods and make hundreds of millions of units per hour. 

The tutorial is not extensive. I learned about tons of useful mechanics that saved me loads of time many hours into the game. There is a certain charm to this because it is inherently fun to feel like you are learning new things for yourself rather than having advice tossed into your lap, but I can see how this might frustrate some people who don't want to spend time doing things inefficiently or switching to youtube tutorials (of which there are hundreds).

The story fits the game. No Man's Sky is not meant to be an epic saga with character arcs and crazy plot twists. Instead, it sees you journey through the galaxy to confront the Atlas (god) and learn about your origins as a Traveler. At every step of the story (and in every other corner of this game) the writing is very good, and the lack of voice lines never bothered me... I think spoken dialogue would not fit the quiet, lonely aesthetic of the game. The story works well because it is not the primary thing to do (you can just ignore it if you want, although some bonus features won't be unlocked for you) which meant that I found myself on frequent detours to complete other missions and found space Amazon.

I really like the multiplayer aspect. There is a giant spaceship that you can summon called the Space Anomaly which is essentially a big lobby of players gearing up and splitting into groups to go on missions. I would highly recommend trying out a mission of the week with a random group. How these work is that everyone (and I mean EVERYONE) will be transported to a random system that the devs picked to do whatever task it is for that week. Seeing the hundreds of bases that people built in a few days will always be entertaining for me, and being flooded with messages that clog your screen as soon as you step out of your ship is a great contrast to the rest of the time when you're absolutely alone. The community is great. Visiting bases, checking out ships, and showing off Freighters is very cool, especially with people you've never met and will never see again.

There are tons of other features to talk about that would require an essay-length review. Here are some things I skipped over: 
Every ship is unique, every animal is unique, you can rename anything you discover, buy a Freighter, warp directly into a Freighter attack, find an abandoned Freighter, learn alien vocabulary, find enormous planetary trade depots, find archaeological dig sites, learn crafting recipes, fight giant two-legged robot monsters, crash economies by flooding the market (this was nerfed), build a base underwater, build a base hundreds of meters in the sky, find volcanoes, die on extreme weather planets, feed animals, tame animals, show off pets on board the Space Anomaly, summon any exocraft you want in any system for free if you have the right Freighter upgrade, get a ship that is alive, get a ship that looks like an octopus (exotics), melee attack and jetpack at the same time to go extremely fast, scan plants, animals and minerals for money, reach the center of the galaxy, get a refiner that is INSIDE YOUR INVENTORY, find abandoned space stations, and TONS OF OTHER THINGS THAT I FORGOT.

Yes, some planets look the same. Yes, you can't land on asteroids. Yes, systems are separated by a sneaky loading screen. But there are so many great aspects to this game that I really don't care.

This is the sort of game where you'll only ever need one save file. In my case, I have spent my entire 100 hours of play exclusively on my starting file. The new expeditions update offers a different mode of play that requires you to start a new file, so I haven't really gotten around to it (although I've heard that some of the loot from the new mode can be used in other saves). This game can be an excellent way to relax if you let it, and I'm totally set out to spend another 100 hours on my save.

All in all, my experience with No Man's Sky has been extremely positive. If you want to chill out and wind down at the end of the day (or keep playing until 5am like I have), then this game is for you. Don't even think twice if it's on sale.

The devs deserve all the respect in the world for sticking with this game.

This game is simply amazing, albeit it has some small problems. The developers are champs and constantly update this, to make the already insane scale even more insane. There's so much to do, so many up- and sidegrades, so much to unlock and explore and experience.

Which is one of the problems, without Google and the wiki, you are pretty fucked. Playing this game blind is extremely difficult, as not a lot is explained. The new Exploration mode is actually a good place to start the game, since the milestones (goals) give you a rough idea of what you can even do. But even then they are often too vague and you might not even have any idea where to start.

The other big issue is Coop - it works alright, but there are no vehicles you can take together, the base building is often glitchy where it doesn't load in correctly and apart from the Nexus missions, there is no real focus on it. 

That being said, I spent 170 hours in this game before I stopped playing and felt like I have done 'mostly' everything (spoiler: I didn't), and now have come back and am enjoying it again. The game feels great (even though it's slightly buggy here and there), and gives you a great sense of scale and speed. 

A definite must-buy for anybody that wants to have a space crafting exploration game.

Overall, everything is just "meh". For spaceship, you get a starter ship you probably won't like and instead of being able to change it's parts (AND COLOUR!!!) to the ones you would like to get different looks, stats and utilities, you need to jump from star system to star system hoping that this time you find one that has the mix of parts you like. It triggers me just thinking about it. You can't even get rid of your boring default armament to put in the weapons you want to actually use as default.

The space fights are pretty much all the same and ultra easy once you figure out how it works (as long as you are using a controller). Especially once you get good upgrades for your ship. just stock up on some nitrate and refill your shields before they break and you can go for hours. The most infuriating thing though is how spaceflight feels like atmospheric flight. as soon as you let go of the gas you loose all your speed, so no drifting or pivoting on yourself to shoot backward and other cool space flying manoeuvers. 

ground wise, you get told to destroy the sentinel before they call back up, but they call back up whatever you do even if you one tap them when they are not alerted. 

The creatures and planets are cool at first, but after a bit it starts to all look the same. There's a feeling like nothing is unique since everything is a mix of everything. Some plants and minerals are all the same yet every time you got to scan them to "know" what they are for every planet you visit.

It's fun at first, building a base, getting some ships and getting rich to get more stuff. once it's all done though, you got no other reasons to play. Unless you want to create yet an other cool base or whatever with some friends.

It's a decent non-serious game that would be ideal for young teenagers though. If you're an adult looking for some fun in space, I'd recommend looking for something else (I keep thinking I should've got elite dangerous instead).

I remember getting hyped for this game from a Colbert interview back in the day. When it came out, I heard the complaints and decided to wait. Now, years later, with the price of the game you get an insane amount of content. I haven't even begun to touch it. I play mostly in VR, and the port is solid. I wanted a chill VR game I could play from my couch, so I don't even mind not  having room-scale. Actually flying my ship is incredible.  I spend a lot of time just looking for cool ships to buy and stick on my freighter. You can do so much base-building, exploration, and honestly just walking around taking pictures. The cons of VR are that the set-up can be tricky to get right and have it not stutter.  I'm on a GTX 1660ti and it runs pretty smooth, but most of my settings are "standard". There is a "shimmer" effect from the countable edges in the game blinking in and out of existence I haven't found a way to fix.  Honestly if they spent some time to optimize the VR portion of the game it would probably be top five games I've ever seen.

In flat screen it's just gorgeous.... 

The recent expeditions update is some of the most fun I've had in a game, ever. It really showcases the multiplayer (and the multiplayer bugs). In that mode everyone starts out on the same system and works toward a point in the galaxy by achieving milestone goals and meeting at rendezvous points. Each comes with a reward unique to the expedition, and they last three months.  I just finished the first, and I hope they do more because it is crazy fun to run into other people, see what they've created, and then break off the beaten path and find my own stuff.  In this mode I had one of the coolest experiences I've ever had in a game. I warped back to the starter system after I had finished most of the expedition goals just to see what was there now. On the way into a space station I ran into another player flying out, and he was immediately attacked by pirates. We took the pirates out together and, since I have no chat functions in VR, we just sat and looked at each other in space for a minute. It was a strangely powerful moment.

Biggest criticism: no ramping difficulty.  If there were more to the combat this game would be unprecedented.  But hey, it isn't that kind of game, and you can' have everything in one game... can you?

While it is fun and pleasant to look at, you find yourself in a vicious rinse and repeat cycle.

Graphically this title is artistic and pleasing to look at, over all a great immersion-ish experience.

Sound engine is good, no complaints but there isn't much to play on deep immersion.

Soundtrack is flawless, a balance between background and foreground engagement and is relaxing much as that of the MineCraft OST.

Storyline is good, it is naturally interesting making progression less of a chore and keeps your yearning for the next chapter.

Quality of life is where this title starts to be weighed down, this is one of those "Wide as the ocean but deep as a puddle" situations. There are countless planets to explore and hubs to visit but as you spend a couple of days playing it is obvious the wildlife is just slightly changed between systems. Plants, Animals and rocks are exactly the same but with different names which is disappointing. 

Character customization is somewhat limited but there are some cool combinations you can have.

Overall this title is not worth it's full price of $60 but instead something more of a $30-45 range *not on sale*. Though this title is enjoyable and why I would recommend it,  one should only buy this while on a 50% sale.

Alright, this game is very good, BUT you should think through if it's for you. It is a non-linear, open game, it's quite enjoyable to just wander around exploring, and to just go with whatever you feel like doing at that precise moment. For anyone that expects a more concrete and guided experience, this game will feel boring. There's a ton of stuff to do, but you shouldn't stick to anything particular. The visuals are amazing by the way.

Some people find it grindy, but I think that after some time you develop several ways to gather resources much more efficiently, so don't go farming too much at the begining. Just relax and go with the flow.

They say this game was terrible at launch, and that's probably absolutely true. The thing about the procedural generation is, it isn't really a premise for a game, but a means to achieve it. As such, the game feels much more like a canvas for many amazing ideas, and surely the developers are trying to add them with regular content updates, but there's just endless room here. Honestly, a single planet is already large enough that I would like to spend weeks exploring it, too bad that would take a whole other game developing. It does have infinite potential for modding.

Buggy, but fun. Don't let the occasional "fall through freighter floor until you die" or "the game won't let me talk to these pilots or freighter captains for no reason" put you off, it's worth persevering.

When the game works, it's fun, but needs some serious work.

None of the "simple" build parts will power things like trade terminals or health stations, and there is no way to connect them to the power grid apart from attaching to a powered wall. You have to get to the Anomaly, and research prefab structures just to power them. The game NEVER tells you this. This is both unintuitive, and bad design.

The variety of things to see and obtain is quite large, and visuals are amazing, but the combat seems kinda meh despite being one of the primary gameplay elements. Ship controls for mouse and keyboard are very mediocre, and the disparity in ship damage to ground compared to ship-to-ship basically renders ship-to-surface combat nonexistent, as any ground weapon will massively outperform the ship weapons. (Why? Doesn't the ship have "more powerful" weapons? Why can't I just mount my 2 spare multitools to my ship to make it useful in surface combat instead?)

Rate of text and clicking through is wastefully long and boring, as is the "learn a language" mechanic. It takes WAY too long, and the auto-translators are worthless because they don't actually teach you the language, they just translate text in dialog that has nothing to do with anything.

Terrain modifications do not persist through sessions, and sometimes not even through teleports/warps. Sometimes part of the terrain modifications return after you leave and return to a system, but never full terrain alteration.

Oxygen gets depleted from your life support system, even if you're on board a pressurized ship, on a paradise planet, or anywhere else, and doesn't regenerate when in oxygen-rich environments. Makes no sense, and just wastes time and effort to force the player to harvest and refill their oxygen supplies.

There is much more, but this should give you an idea of the sort of things that need work in this game.

All that said, I do still recommend this game, despite its MANY flaws and issues.

Reviews.110256:
Spoilers ahead.

[spoiler]You wake up, a simulated lifeform in a simulated universe. You bumble around doing whatever until you either run out of things to do, or get bored and quit.[/spoiler]

That is the entire plot of No Man's Sky. Well, that and a blunderbuss loaded with tiny fragments hinting at this and that, so vaguely that it is a very real possibility that the writer hadn't quite worked out what all of the little hints are [i]actually[/i] pointing to. That thing where you just throw out some random foreshadowing and it doesn't really make much sense but you figure people will just assume there's some great, rich narrative and deep lore at work.

There are some disturbing developments, sure, but yeah. Overall, not a gripping tale of emotional investment. Some emotions, yes, but mostly negative ones... despair, futility, directionless drifting.

You can explore endless random planets, but they all kind of look pretty similar once you've visited a dozen or so. Endless random star systems, but again, deja vu will set in. It's that Starbound thing where, sure, you [i]technically[/i] have a million billion places to go, but they're all made up of the same pieces. It's not as pronounced in No Man's Sky, but it's still there. On some level, you always pay for procedural generation with blandness, just as you pay for tailored world design with effort and some degree of linearity.

There are three alien languages to learn, and... well, if you don't, certain parts of the game - related to acquiring manufacturing blueprints - will become much more of a dice roll than an informed selection of the correct choice from a console you can actually read. This is a problem as you learn one word at a time, and it takes ages to learn enough to have a chance at grasping the gist of a console message. That, and as mentioned, three languages... each with its own word for yes, no, not, to, for, carbon, metal, and so on and so forth. Along with zillions of words you'll never use and rarely hear from NPC babble.

Oh, and there's another language related to the [spoiler]simulation computer[/spoiler] itself. Which one would imagine you'd already know, or could quickly be taught. But nope, you have to gather it word by word.

Sure, all of these things sound like they could be fun. They should be. But somehow, they kind of aren't. Things feel like a hassle, there's no real goal to anything besides "get to the middle of the universe and start a new universe" which is a [i]massive[/i] chore and, based on player reactions, seems to be a huge anticlimax as well. You can build a base if you want, and staff it with weirdos who seem to be copy-pasted straight from Planescape: Torment's Dak'kon - apparent strangers who inexplicably owe you some kind of blood debt they can never repay, and thus offer eternal servitude. Which makes no sense in the context of the greater plot.

You can communicate with other "travellers", i.e. NPCs with some written quote-unquote "story" dialogue and their own little story arcs, which... pretty much universally end in exhausting tragedy, making you wonder why anyone would play this game. Perhaps it's meant to be like Russian literature - super depressing, but then it wins prizes for being deep? Not what the world needs right now, though. Not by a long shot.

If all you really want is a sci-fi playground where you can bumble about and do random things for no reason, then there may be some appeal for you here.

For most people, though, I'd recommend you give it a miss. A hundred hours in, it's not worth the price, time, nor effort.

Reviews.110264:
Not a game for everyone. Exploring is fun and relaxing, if you treat the game as a chill sandbox to relax with your friends in (or solo) it's good, but the core game loop and systems aren't great. The building is competent but not really crucial to the progression in the game. The combat is mediocre at best and enemy variety is basically non-existent. The planets are neat to explore but there's not much reason to really explore any one planet all that much. Stuff like the cooking system and creature taming system feel half-baked and lots of the features in the game are redundant. 

With all of that said, I have enjoyed checking in on this game occasionally since release. I enjoy the (mostly) relaxing nature, the atmosphere, and the writing. If you're okay with a game with little combat or solid progression you'll find something to love here. 

It's also worth mentioning that the VR in this game is great. The performance isn't the best, but the sense of scale and just experiencing planets in VR is a lot of fun. I don't think VR is the best fit for games which require long play sessions and are slow paced, but luckily all of your saves transfer between regular and VR modes, so you can play on your monitor and then switch to VR to see your bases, cool planets etc. 

Finally, the most recent update has been great for someone like me who has played the first part of the game 1,000,000 times but never gotten to the endgame. It gives you concrete goals to check off to gain really powerful rewards.

No Man’s Sky has come a long way since it was first announced and released. It started out as a basic space game with limited gameplay. It has since become a much better game. It is mostly as open world space game (PVE) with some co-op. Since the original release, the game has improved significantly. They have flushed out the “story” and main quest line. Added base building and economy. The game has a decent amount of replay ability. 
This game is very progression based. Once you finally complete all the objectives, build all the bases you wanted, explored lots of planets, it can become stale. This fact is overshadowed, however by the updates to the game that add more content. These updates decrease this problem significantly. 
Overall, this game is very polished and feels mostly complete. The planets and biomes look stunning and full of life on earthly planets and completely dead on others. There is a wide variety of places you can go with little restriction. You can even name planets and solar systems! This game has risen to my favorite space game overall. 

Pros: 
-Interesting worlds and biomes promote exploration
- Objectives teach you how to play the game 
-Easy to learn 
-Crafting items and mining are fun and easy to do
-Local economy makes mining interesting 
-Based building allows you to make a variety of builds
-Easy and stable to run (ran on nividia 1060 and got 100+ fps)
-no DLC (everything in base game) 
-no microtransactions

Cons: 
-Heavily progression based (once you complete everything, explore enough, get all ships: it can get stale)
-gameplay is a bit repetitive (when mining) 
-early mining and inventory management are challenging
-low amount of combat 

TL:DR If you are looking for a space game this is it. It is similar to space engineers, but simpler and easier to understand. A beautiful game to look at and co-op is not forced on the player. Overall, a great game and I highly recommend you play it. However, I would recommend waiting for a sale as $60 is a bit steep for a 1- year old game.

I am reviewing the game as a new player who started playing in 2021 after Expeditions update. I have mixed feelings.

+ huge and interesting world worth to explore (you never know what you will find)

+ it's very relaxing game
+ free updates

Cons:
- optimization (it has really huge CPU load!)
- player's actions have zero impact on the galaxy (no wars, no territory control, no economy relationship... every system is totally isolated)
- world feels empty
- very simple AI
- too many possible exploits  (Who's idea was to store saves locally in multiplayer game?!)

I feel a little conflicted about No Man's Sky. I have many hours logged, but most of them are forgettable. I'm glad I own it, but I'm not entranced by it. It's unique, but it doesn't stand out. It offers a feeling I don't think I can get anywhere else, but I don't crave it, and it rarely satisfies me.

I believe the key to enjoying this game is forgetting about time, forgetting about goals, and focusing on the moment right in front of you. You have to enjoy the colors, the feeling of exploration, and the feeling that you [i]really are[/i] discovering new things.

However, after long enough, I always find myself stepping back and realizing how that's all it is -- [i]a feeling.[/i]
I'm not exploring a new place, I'm exploring a similar procedurally-generated place. I didn't discover a new creature, the code created an amalgamation from modular assets. I didn't solve a new problem, I just chose the right action from the options. I'm flying my ship, but I don't know where I'm going. This breaks the illusion.

As I've continued playing, I started believing that the game was designed this way purposefully, but I also wonder if it was just convenient to build on that weirdness after Hello Games couldn't make it believable enough.

No Man's Sky relies on crafting basic ingredients into usable components. I found myself getting frustrated by collecting RNG blueprints, which I often required in order to construct the items I [i]did[/i] set goals to make. This would often make me feel like my progression was stunted, however finally getting a blueprint I needed didn't impact the experience very much, if at all.

The most unusual thing I find is that, depending on your perspective, everything I've described can be seen as either good or bad, and for this reason I'm giving No Man's Sky a positive review. It makes way onto my list of "unique things that didn't exist yet."

I came into the game right around the NEXT update (mid to late 2018). My girlfriend was one of the many people who pre-ordered this for PS4 so I was well aware of the state of play at launch. Here we are now, 12 updates since NEXT and 300 hours deep. If you're brand new to the game and unfamiliar with its backstory, grab it. There's never been a better time to play and its going to continue to grow. Full price might be a little too steep yet but its also not completely unreasonable for the content there.

If you've been keeping tabs and are still on the fence, I still highly recommend it but here's my feelings on it:

Pros:
+Visuals are amazing and continue to be improved upon
+Storyline has enough weight to get a fair amount of hours in without overstaying its welcome
+Wide variety of mission types/activities to satisfy most people
+Newest update Expeditions brings a fantastic "new save" experience for both new and old players
+Devs are still working on free content updates almost 5 years since 1.0

Neutrals:
=The menu/inventory system is a bit on the overwhelming side at first
=Missions can be repetitive
=The Class system for weapons and vehicles could be a bit more noticeable
=No variety to stations and buildings
=Some things I'd like to see might not be possible with the game's engine

Negatives:
-There's always a low level awareness of the game not running the best it could
-Content updates are great but I'd gladly wait longer if it meant bugs could be fixed
-Procedural generation could stand to get some new ideas thrown at it for more variety
-Still feels like a "single player" multiplayer experience

Wishlist:
*Starship and further freighter customization
*Story mode multiplayer/better shared experiences
*Better planetary events (damaging meteor strikes, earthquakes etc)
*Re-imagining of the water aspects of the game (water falls, rivers, hydro power for bases)
*Ability to sleep to recover life support systems/shields and also pass time

Reviews.110794:
They say it's good now, but I couldn't enjoy it.
Here are some of my salt points:
Health and Hazard replenisher stations cannot be powered (at least not at the tech level you start out with + it being researched fully)
Scanner isn't a toggle, you have to keep the scanner button held down.
When on a mission, the scanner is subdued by default in favor of a signal antenna, which is annoying.
Scanning itself must be held down. Holding down keys is not good for tendons.
The game faked me out a few times by telling me to mark an object of interest while in the spaceship with 'e' but 'e' lands the spaceship even if the prompt to hold it to mark the object is on the screen, it's a lie.
I claimed a broken ship during a story mission,  and that turned off the marker of my previous, main ship. 
(Yet I think in multiplayer, markers are put on all ships of your friend, not sure, can't remember, but I think it's like that)
Anyway, I knew that you could summon your old ship with 'x' and going to a menu.
However, for some ...completely absurd reason, I couldn't summon the old ship due to it 'being broken'.
Turned out, by claiming the new ship, which had broken engines, the other ship also counted as broken, and only when i repaired the new ship I could summon the old one.
Markers, again, disappear, they only show up for your active, currently selected ship.
Furthermore, despite this highly annoying situation (which also ate through most of my oxygen and salt reserves as I was groping through a hostile planet), the game is made in a way that if you teleported to a base or a space station, your ship would just wait for you there no questions asked.
But a marker is too much to ask?
In fact, I find the marker system highly annoying in general, they are both intrusive and slippery at the same time.
Might just be selective perception but when i want the markers to show, they don't show (because of height differences) so I have to spin around like an idiot trying to find it (also, you can only mark one thing at a time...)
And if I don't want markers, then they are everywhere, especially in clusters of metal fingers and co.
While making a base, with a base computer (which costs resources) you can choose to deconstruct the base computer and get resources back.
But if you choose 'delete base' from its menu, it disappears without giving you anything, another newbie trap.
The jetpack and running is pathetic, maybe it gets better with upgrades but boy is it PAINFUL.

All in all, I am frustrated a lot.
The game has nice points too, but I'm a control and interface/user experience freak and these kind of things chap me extra hard.
Someone who doesn't mind clunk/needless strain and button pressing that might not be an issue.

But I don't like it. It takes me out of the game.
Which is a shame, cause there is good stuff in it.
That said, I cannot recommend it like this.

---[TL:DR]--- 

As one of the players from the release date of the game years ago, experiencing lots of "ups and downs" with this game... In its current state however with all the free updates and continued development over the years, if the game is [ON SALE] and you might enjoy it, then why not give it a shot!



---[Review]---

Being there playing release VS its current state is crazy to think about (50% Unplayable, save corruptions and extreme amount of missing content...
However this is now the game that was hoped for looking back at what they said should be in the game unfortunately it took a very long time to get here! 

What you'll find now is a decent game, Its not a ground breaking title by today's standards but its one to remember. There's plenty to have a go at if you enjoy exploring for the sake of it, I tend to find No Mans Sky relaxing with a bit of spiciness thrown in occasionally but there are a few things that might feel a bit repetitive for most players the longer one plays...

However being able to go solo then drop in at any time to a friend is great!

I would imagine not everyone will enjoy this game, but on the other hand many still could in its current updated state.

Will admit though the standard price of $80 AUD is extremely high, as lets be serious, its a older release now (late 2016) and its had its challenges in the past... Would strongly suggest picking up ON SALE! 
As of current review (6/4/2021) the game is half the price above, a lot more sensible.

Anyways playing it again, I'm enjoying it so decided to finally review it 5 years later ahaha.


NB: Thankfully the dev team has kept determined working on it, updating and adding large chunks of gameplay rather than ditching development and diving away from No Mans Sky!

Reviews.110880:
I originally recommended this game at 41 hours and spoke of how the campaign for it was very dense and entertaining for hours on end. I am re-reviewing now as to critique the playtime at the endgame.

It is my belief that many games attempt to strive to get a long-term dedicated player base. This game is highly effective in my opinion at bringing in a very dedicated player base, but they rarely stay for a long amount of time due to the lack of end-game entertainment and content.

SPOILERS BEYOND THIS PARAGRAPH

There is an immense amount of missions, which from now on I will refer to as the 'campaign' of normal mode. I found the campaign to keep me glued to my seat for hours on end, grinding through the progress and achieving more things. I received much reward for my grind which I was very happy with. There was no lack of entertainment on that front.

In the end game however, we see that once the player is complete with the campaign, they are left almost exclusively hunting for ships, items, etc. or left to reset everything when the atlas path is complete/the galactic center is reached. It seems like this game relies on the hope that players will want to do it all over again so that there does not need to be endgame content. I believe strongly that this is a mistake. 

While I am not fully knowledgeable about game design, I do believe competition can do a great deal at keeping players in the game long term.

I find the joy in playing this campaign similar to the joy I found playing the GTA 5 campaign. I found the campaign to this ever so slightly less engaging, possibly because its a choice to do everything you do, whereas in GTA you are mostly thrown into heists, precarious scenarios, etc. Unlike GTA, I found the end game of NMS to be very very bland. A player is left with the choice of resetting everything with the only reward being the choice of galaxy, implying that the true reward should be exploration. While it does sound poetic, the RNG can only go so far in maximizing the entertainment of your exploration. By the time you reach the galactic center, you would have likely already explored and seen most of what there is to offer. The GTA endgame (online really) even keeps players playing WITHOUT the campaign, which is a huge testament to how entertaining it is. While I do see Hello Games attempting to shift to a multiplayer experience, it is still highly limited and seems like it mostly relies on your ability to come into the game with a lot of friends with a copy. There seems as if there is very little friendship-making opportunities. In GTA heists, somehow, it is easier to make friends than with missions at the nexus. This could possibly be due to the fact that high collaboration is required for heists, whereas missions require NO collaboration and people frequently prefer to do them on their own in order to avoid awkward silences if the mic opens up, which is set to automatically do so.

For some reason, it was so much more satisfying in GTA to grind for a yacht or bad-ass vehicle for example. I think much of this was to be able to flaunt it in a very small map where players will frequently view your wealth and fear your power.

My comparison to GTA may in many cases not be very fair. The player-bases are very different, but I do believe that NMS has the potential to be comparable to other open-world exploration and mission games. There is clear drive towards a multiplayer experience, but I believe there is a lack of collaboration and competition which draws from the game's ability to facilitate long-term player entertainment and in-game friendships.

I also noticed I was able to obtain money and nanites very easily, but found it immensely difficult to obtain ships I liked. I believe this discrepancy should be balanced to some degree, whether the resource obtaining is nerfed, whether the ship obtaining is buffed, or some lesser combination of both. 

THINGS I'D LIKE TO SEE:
I genuinely want to see this game develop into something top-tier. I originally came into this game expecting a space game, but this is not a space game. It is a game of lore and exploration. It's much more of a sci-fantasy than a sci-fi. With that being said, I expected some basic manipulation of worlds. I think sentinel facility hunting resulting in a peaceful planet could be interesting as well as taking trees/plants from other planets. I would really love the ability to be much much more creative with the world and building.

I would love to see in the game is an improvement in building. Currently, I feel like bases are limited in size and complexity. Currently, cooler builds can only be possible through glitch building or outside editors. Mid-game, I expected to be spending a lot of time in the end-game building amazing bases. However, it takes an ETERNITY to build something relatively basic. I never got around to building an amazing base as I hoped due to this. I would love to see snap angles that are sharper than 90 degrees as well as more axes to flip on. Currently, you can only rotate.

I would love to see some reward to entering a new galaxy. Galaxy change functions as some sort of 'rebirth', so there should be some sort of high reward for it. I don't believe that keeping your ship etc. is not the right choice. Maybe some sort of exclusive items would be in order.

Exotic worlds ONLY HAVE TROPHIES. There is no reason to be on an exotic world if you have seen the same type of world before other than to use it for building with trophies, which is already very limited. I believe there should be some sort of story to the worlds.

Finally, story improvement. I really thing some sort of mandalorian-style conquest and story that can be entirely encapsulated on a planet would keep a player entertained for a long period of time while slowing down the progression of the game, resulting in higher net entertainment. There is typically no reason to explore beyond your local area for a longer period of time if you would like to progress the lore or gain resources. You can get cartography maps anywhere in the galaxy, so exploration per planet is not unique. In summary, I hope for randomly generated storylines, key locations, etc.

---

Side-note: I originally bought this game because InternetHistorian hyped up the comeback story. This hero story should not define the game and its current ratings. I believe this game is rated higher than it should because of the comeback hype.

TL;DR - This game has a great campaign, but is falls short in its multiplayer experience and long-term player entertainment. There are many things that Hello Games can do to improve and they seem like they are trying to reach that long-term dedication.

Reviews.110887:
This is the perspective of someone who never bought/played the game until 2021

The good:
* Getting your ship running again was a fun challenge
* Leaving the atmosphere of a planet for the first time was epic

The bad:
* Bugs - Within my relatively short playtime, the game locked up several times. By locked up I mean the screen froze. I could tab to other applications so it wasn't that my whole computer locked up. I'd eventually get a message from Windows to either close the application or wait for it to respond. It never did. Also, the module upgrades you buy with nanites are a sort of randomized loot I guess. However, my first module upgrade had a missing description. So I don't even know what it did and it took me several hours to get to that point. Kind of a let down.
* Combat - On the surface of a planet, this mostly consisted of either me firing on defenseless animals or being attacked by sentinels. The sentinels are similar to the police from GTA, you get "wanted" levels for taking resources from a planet. If you manage to kill the initial wave of them, a more challenging wave comes. So it appeared that the point was to just run away if you were attacked by them. In space, if I sat for more than 10 seconds to just look around I would get scanned and attacked by hostiles. These have the same mechanic of increasing in difficulty if you kill the first wave. So again, it seems the point is to get you to just run away. This left me confused as to what the point of having combat in the game is. With other games you fight the enemies in an area and get some type of reward that lets you fight more or tougher enemies and it is usually a core mechanic. However, here it seems like combat is more of a nuisance. There is little point in engaging enemies and the controls aren't satisfying enough to enjoy it even if there was.
* The first base I built using the basic components they give you. One of the first things the main quest has you do is to place a teleporter. That teleporter appeared to be about 25% taller than the base I constructed. It let me place it anyways and it clipped through my roof. It just adds to a feeling of it being poorly implemented. If the game drives you towards building something in the first few hours, shouldn't the basic building blocks that they have you use work together?
* I visited three planets. I couldn't really tell you the difference between them. I was the first player to "discover" all three. When I landed on the 2nd planet, I saw what looked like the same herp-a-derp plant I discovered and named on the 1st planet. However, it was supposedly a completely different plant that just used the same or similar texture.

I gave the game long enough that I can't request a refund. Have buyers remorse and no desire to play it any further.

I never played this game when it first came out.  I read all the reviews about how it was terrible.  I revisited when I heard they revamped it and it started getting good reviews.

Now, the game is still terrible compared to other similar games out there.  Unpolished and uninteresting.  
*  I was presented with a choice of game modes, regular or survival.  But regular also has survival elements?  Which do I choose (Answer was definitely regular)?  
* The interface is frustrating  do I zap this target with LMB or use e?  who knows!  its random
* The interface is frustrating. If you have a menu open you still see keyboard shortcuts for other parts of the interface that don't have focus and therefore won't work (eg press x, top right still shows interface buttons while bottom-middle build menu is open, top right won't react to hotkeys anymore).  
* The interface is frustrating, why is everything "click and hold" to interact and not just click?  Is this a console thing?
* The interface is frustrating, why do menus drift around the screen when i'm moving my mouse?  is this a console thing?  
* Which objects contain which resources is random and unintuitive (this one has carbon, this one has oxygen, no clear indication why).
* There's nothing interesting about gathering different resources, ferrite vs carbon, the process is all the same.  
* No clear explanation for whether I should purify, eg my 90 Na purifies to 45 purified Na, but which one gives more total value?  No idea.  Who thought purifying was an interesting mechanic and not just tedium?  
* I'm often told to gather resources but the scanner doesn't show any nearby, so I have to wander randomly.  
* The visor-scanner icons are useless, i have to mouse over every icon to see the text details on what I'm looking at, because so many resources use the same icon.  

This is the type of poor experience I would expect from an early access game, not one that has been around and been worked on so long.  I normally don't document bad game features so thoroughly but this was laughably bad.  

Do not buy, there's a million "explore/gather/build" games out there that are 10x better.  Valheim, 7 days to die, etc

Gostei muito do jogo. Acho que o tema é muito bom e a jogabilidade é muito boa também. Eu sugiro alguns pontos de melhora que levariam o jogo a um patamar alem do atual. Isso iria dar ao jogador uma visão melhor do que ocorre ao seu redor e uma imersao mais fluida:
1) O modo de interação com os NPCs é antigo, pode ser atualizado para um tipo de interação desta época.  
2) A movimentação está limitada a posição de pé e pode ser melhorada. existem pontos baixos que ficam inacessiveis. E a mudança de 1a. pessoa para 3a. pessoa está muito trabalhosa, muitos jogos utilizam o botão de rolamento do mouse. 
3) O modo de marcação de pontos de interesse é muito limitado. Isso faz que se perca muito fácil pontos de interesse já encontrados. E força a criação de milhares de bases sem necessidade.
4) O engine IA das criaturas está muito simples. Apesar do visual, a movimentação e interação é parecida para todos. Acredito com que com uma movimentação melhorada, seria muito mais interessante que as criaturas não gostassem do explorador. Principalmente porque ele afeta seu habitat.

Independente dos postos apresentados, eu recomendo o jogo.

The development story of No Man's Sky is quite a story. It was one of - if not - the most hyped game before its release in 2016. The CEO and trailers made promises of an infinite world that is randomly generated in every one of its aspect. People were very disappointed later upon realease for what was basically an empty universe with little to do and loads of bugs and glitches. "Unique" alien lifeforms and minerals and plants were the same from planet to planet with slightly different colours... The community and critics took down the game in flames... However over the years that followed, they relentlessly patched the game and added large amounts of contents and generally managed, against all odds, to flip the general opinion into a very positive one. Personnally, I think the CEO really is passionnate about the idea behind his game and really wanted to materialise his vision into a game. He very poorly managed the hype that was building around his game and then struggled to resurface after the debacle that was the release (something we're all too familiar with these days, aren't we). But he succeeded in making a great game and reconquer his community. Today NMS is even one of the main contenders for the Steam [i]Labor of Love[/i] award year after year. As of today, the dev team is very much still active and they just released a new coop game mode and constantly tend to their game. It's not perfect by any means but if you're into randomly generated stuff and looking for a great sandbox with the sensation of an infinite universe while being able to build cosy or even grandiose bases in a multiplayer open-world, then NMS is for you.

A Caveat.

This game does what many other huge, open-world games do - simulate living a life in an alternate universe.

Do what you want! 
Be who you want!
Go where you want!

Skyrim is similar, but this one is in space with ships & tools & elements & aliens.

It's incredible really. The work & creativity & sheer scope of these games is mind blowing (I grew up with an SNES... games today are like magic by comparison). The creators of this game have done great work. And the tools that enable us mere humans to create virtual worlds like this are truly something incredible.

No Man's Sky might be the largest & most complex virtual world ever created to date. Thanks to procedural generation it could be theoretically infinite.

However... the problem with making ever more vast & detailed & full worlds is this: now what?

I already live in a world. I have a home & places to explore & people around me to meet & talk to. I don't need a game with which to do those fundamental actions. Once the novelty of:
Travelling (in space).
Building (on other planets).
Talking (to aliens).
Working (gathering space elements)
Sight-seeing (other planets & space)
Etc...

Once the novelty of doing very regular and boring things but in a unique context, wears off... what do you have? Why am I doing these things? Why is this better than my real life? Other than being easier to succeed & having an accelerated improvement curve (look, I own TWO space ships now!) games like this often miss a key element.

I need purpose. Motivation. Story.

A reason to play beyond living a dual life full of chores & commutes & collecting stuff.

NMS has a vague story so far as I've played, and some vanilla missions. What little story there is takes the form of infuriatingly vague and slightly poetic scraps of prose often interspersed with static so you can't really glean the meaning. After this many hours played I feel like I should know SOMETHING about this vast universe, the people in it, the political climate the history, my own character, something. But I have only hints of fluff. It's frustrating and makes me feel like the creators of this game didn't have much to say about this huge universe they created.

In such a vast game, the story is diluted. The larger the scope of a game, the more impactful the story must be, so that it's not just a puff of smoke in the wind. 

(And yet, if NMS had been more in-your-face with their story, the players who just wanted to live their space life wouldn't be happy.)

My character is nameless, with no memories or personality. Perfect for those who want to slip into that character & make their own way.

But take Shepherd from the Mass Effect games. He/she has presence. Impact. Substance.

It's ok to like games which stay out of your way & let you live your best (space) life. NMS does this well. And for the players who want a great life-sim in a galaxy far, far away, NMS is an excellent contender.

For me, I don't need more chores or travel or checklists & recipes. Instead of mining elements in caves, I could be pulling weeds in my garden: same concept, but the latter has real world benefits.

~30 hours in & I already know 90% of what this game will be for me. That's ok. Some of it is fun. But a player could oh-so-easily sink many hundreds of hours into this game, and if I'm going to do that I need more substance. A long, drawn out, expensive path of upgrading my equipment, just isn't fun enough.

NMS is an incredible game, I'll probably play some more in fact. But one benefit of maturity is that I understand better, the kinds of experiences that interest me, and what I want from my leisure time. Sometimes it's to pass some lightweight time in a cool setting, seeing the sights, doing neat things. And sometimes it's to have a capital-e Experience that makes me think or tells me a story. NMS is perfect for the first option, but way too diluted for the second. And that's mostly ok.

..

Now if we get past the aimlessness and you say that you just want to live your own adventure in this vast universe.... I can't avoid warning you about a MAJOR flaw in this game. Navigation is an utter mess. If I can travel across planets, across solar systems and across the galaxy.... holy smokes the game better make navigating this endless space a smooth experience. It doesn't.

- There are no planet or real system maps.
- You can place save beacons that add a permanent pip to your HUG. But you can't name these things, so once you have more than a few on a planet, good luck determining which is which.
- You can note the latitude and longitude of locations, but once I'm using that to navigate, a game has already failed.
- You can lose track of the location of entire planets and easily forget which is which.
- You can visit landmarks, leave to find needed resources and then have no clue how to get back.
- Pips on your map that you visit and 'activate' them, don't get removed or changed on your HUD, so I find myself going back to the same item more than once in a complete waste of time.
- Certain markers seem to come and go on my HUD. Sometimes the space station is a yellow cog looking symbol - easy to find - other times it's totally absent.

If you do some research online you can find tips on what to do. Namely place a save beacon, note the latitude and longitude, the planet and the system on a piece of paper, and use that to find it again... but oh my gosh is that ever a pain in the neck.  Why on earth they don't let you name beacons or mark pips with symbols, or let you have more than one custom waypoint (you can easily accidentally unset your waypoint and therefore can't rely on it) is beyond me. Navigating is honestly a major turn off in this game and I hate unnecessary travel.

---

These 2 main criticisms are enough that I'm probably not going to play this game very much. As a parent I have to be careful how I spend my time. I still rate this as 'recommended' because it is very cool in many ways and I think other players would enjoy it.

Reviews.111358:
It's hard to recommend this game for any one thing it does, but the whole package is massive and varied.
 
I can't write a review without spoiling too much of what makes this game great.
[h1]Positives[/h1]
[list]
[*]Co-op - It might not apply to you, but it's really hard to find decent co-op games.
[*]Space sandbox.... I mean that alone for me was enough to want to check it out. 
[*]Evolving progression. This is the part that's easy to spoil, so I'll just say the list of tools at your disposal and what those tools can do grows as you progress through the game. This is true for for mobility, combat, mining, crafting and pretty much every other aspect of the game.
selection.
[*]Sense of scale is captured pretty well. Planets feel huge, star systems feel bigger, universe feels massive.
[/list]

[h1]Negatives[/h1]
[list]
[*] Atrocious save system. Your progress is saved when you exit your ship, or interact with specific save points, that are not too common. Early on in the game, while I was slowly walking on foot for hours without any means to save, a crash cost me a about 90 minutes of progress. Worst part is, I didn't even know how to save until I googled it.
[*] The game is relatively slow as pretty much everything takes time: dialog (slow to appear), walking, mining, crafting and even basic actions, such as picking up....oxygen.... I would prefer to cut some of those times down, as some really feel like a waste of time.
[*] Sandbox (the negative part). Complex sandboxes always have unique bugs, that are close to impossible to fix completely. They also often lack direction for the player. I doubt most players will have problems with either, but it's worth pointing out.
[*] Exploration is rewarding, but never rewarding enough to max anything out. Utility and fun of exploration runs out fairly early in the game at which point you'll probably have to shift to a more grindy/efficient methods for cash and stuff.
[/list]

No Man's Sky has come a long way since it's horrendous and unfinished launch in 2016. 5 years later, almost all of the features that they initially promised are now in the game in some capacity on top of hundreds of other features that they never promised, all of which have been added free of charge. For being made by a small studio, No Man's Sky is a testament to how far a game can rise and how successful an initially poor product can come. I want to touch on a few things that stand out to me for the sake of this review, so I'm going to split it into positives and negatives.

Positives:
- The game let's you do whatever you want, you aren't locked into playing a certain way
- Expansive and dynamic solar systems, including rare resources, ecology and cross breeding/gene splicing
- Base building/exocraft construction
- Multiplayer nexus with daily missions for exclusive rewards
- Starship and multitool diversity and customization 
- Consistent update cycle

Negatives:
- Very repetitive gameplay loop
             > Get in ship, fly to planet, land, scan ecology, get in ship, fly to planet, etc
- Buggy 
             > Texture issues, saves being corrupted, random crashes are all still present after 5 years
- Not enough variation between planets
              > After you visit about 8 solar systems, you've seen every planet type

I really enjoy the game, but I've seen many of my friends leave the game after playing for about 10-15 hours because they find it too repetitive. I completed the main story in about 30 hours and after that the rest of the side quests feel very trivial by comparison. The recent expedition update provides a good way to get people to come back and earn rewards through gameplay, but there is still a while to go before No Man's Sky can truely become a self-sustaining game. If you really enjoy space/adventure games, this is going to be a great purchase. If you dislike games that put you in a constant loop of grinding for materials, you may want to watch some videos on the game first before putting your money down, because even though the game is constantly getting updated with new things to do, the core gameplay loop has remained the same.

No Man's Sky offers a refreshing, content-rich, and immersive experience. It's easy to get lost in the game and sidetrack from the main story line missions offered by the game. The beginning of the game allows the players to progress and develop the intuition without being overwhelming, and mind the fact that this game can be overwhelming as you progress through the story and explore more. It fulfills its duty as a space exploration and as open world survival, going above and beyond with unique world generation that differs in every star system, with the ability to live and base essentially on any planet or moon.

This game is well refined and bug free for the most part. The issues that have risen with the game have not inhibited my gameplay experience or caused some tragic loss to my items/base, and there is a peace of mind knowing that this game remains supported by Hello Games and actively updated on a reasonable basis.

I have played using both VR and non-VR. My experience on VR has been immersive and almost complete. I have lost myself for multiple hours at a time being able to experience the universe No Man's Sky has to offer with my own two hands. Flying my starship in this game using VR has been very enjoyable with adequate flight controls. Typical tasks like mining and building also remain enjoyable experiences with the ability to control my multi-tool and use both hands freely thanks to VR. It performs reasonably well too. Note, keep anti-aliasing off however if you plan to use VR for performance reasons. Also, if you're having trouble swimming, switch your movement control direction. Overall, I can recommend this game to VR users.

As for non-VR, I'd say the experience is just as good as on VR, if not better. The graphics in this game are beautiful and the experience is still maintained with plenty of great game mechanics and intuitive controls. It's not a very intensive game to run, so you can expect to get high fps on high/ultra graphics settings. 

The music being generated randomly too is great, very pleasant to listen to when exploring. Money making is diverse and there are plenty of paths a player can take spanning from selling resources to bounty hunting to raiding freighters to more than I can cover. Starships and freighters are customizable with plenty of different models. 

The game is multiplayer. Parties are up to 4 players, and up to 32 players can be in the same star system. You can join another player's system by joining their lobby. You can also warp to your friend's bases.

All in all, I can recommend this game to anyone with an interest in space exploration, survival, and sandbox.

At first I was very confused, but about 10 minutes in, I was much less confused. The graphics are beautiful, so far the concept is very good. I like how the game is fairly easy to navigate, and the tasks are easy and clear to understand. I like the survival and exploration aspect without much risk of death, as well as the base building. I'm pretty picky when it comes to games, but the fact that I played more than 20 minutes of No Man's Sky means it is definitely a good game. I played for 4 hours straight, and the only reason I'm not playing more is because it's 4am and I need to sleep. I'm looking forward to waking up so I can play more.

UPDATE: Just a bit over a month later, I now have around 200 hours in game. I have to say, I'm incredibly impressed with the game's ability to keep me engaged. The only games I've reached 200+ hours in have been Pokemon games, Minecraft, and the Sims 4. I own hundreds of games. This game is truly a work of art. I played a little bit on PS4 back in 2016 and I have to say, they really turned things around. Major props to the devs for that.

Things I really like:

Exploration
There's always a better planet out there, you just have to find it. Finding paradise planets that are a colour you like with fauna and flora you like is a pretty amazing feeling. Finding planets with the stablilized reality glitches is also pretty fun. I have yet to collect them all, but I'll be pretty happy when I do.

Starship and Multi Tool Variety
Early game, you're limited to the cheaper starships, but once you get more money, you can find the starship that you want. You just have to do some looking. Same with multi tools. Upgrading ships and tools you really like is also quite fulfilling.

Plotline
Although the story was somewhat difficult to follow until closer to the end, I liked the existentialism that was in the story. They definitely could've made things better, but I liked how near the end SPOILER your character starts to question everything and eventually finds out the truth that everything's a simulation. SPOILER OVER

Post Game/Side Quests
I like that post main storyline, if you have a quicksilver item you want, you really have to work for it. Quicksilver is somewhat frustrating to get compared to the other materials and currency in game. It's a bit of an added challenge that's rewarding and exciting.

Community
The online community is super nice surprisingly and there's actually not too many toxic people. Especially the community on Reddit.

Things that they could definitely improve on:

Base Building
I really love building things, and most games I play involve building of some sort. I've spent at least 50 hours in game building bases, and sometimes rebuilding them. My first base was somewhat large, however not nearly as big as other bases I've seen. I ended up having to remove most of it due to the terrain coming back, and I learned the hard way to not use the terrain manipulator in bases. It also deleted a bunch of parts. Now, I'm careful to make sure I don't change the terrain while building. I wish this could get fixed though, I'd love to have my base be partially underground again. I also think that some of the building mechanics are a bit off. My game also lags a ton while building, which is frustrating. I also wish they'd add more decorations, but I'd rather have the terrain stop being glitchy first.

Lag
I'm running the game using a GTX 1060, i7 9700, and 32gb RAM, and was experiencing huge amounts of lag. Initially, I thought it was my GPU, but it was only running at about 7%, with my CPU and RAM around 20%. I used the Nvidia GeForce Driver optimization and that made it worse. I had to play around with settings for a very long time to fix the lag since it was so bad my game was practically unplayable for a few days after the recent update. The settings I'm using now are all over the place and don't really make sense. For some reason, having anything set at standard lags out my game.

Overall, I would 100% recommend this game. It's got something for everyone in it. The lag and glitches are a major downside, but the pros far outweigh the cons in my opinion. Here's to many more hours in game!

[h1]A certain class of gamers will get lost in No Man's Sky for hours thanks to the countless discoveries, but it's depth is somewhat shallow, and many design choices keeps it from being legendary.[/h1]

[b]No Man's Sky launched as a near failure.[/b] Sean Murray of Hello Games and Sony HEAVILY marketed the game, selling it as an ambitious, revolutionary, incredible space faring experience that was expected to mesmerize and awe it's audience. Instead, NMS was an unmitigated mess, lacking many promised features, crashing regularly, and was sold on an overhyped lie. [b]It became a perfect cautionary tale for players to not become overhyped by heavily marketed games, but Hello Games was able to make many improvements to NMS to this date.[/b]

[h1]No Man's Sky was able to partially scratch an itch I had to get lost in a fantastical, science fictiony space universe and just explore.[/h1] [b]Exploration is the most critical aspect of NMS, as some other aspects of the game are disappointing, annoying, or partially underwhelming.[/b] However, Hello Games does a decent job of giving you breadcrumbs to lead you into other discoveries of the world. Gathering resources to help you survive the elements allow you to explore more, earn units and the premium currency, nanites, by discovering alien creatures, plants, and minerals. You'll find yourself running out of inventory space with resources, encouraging you to work towards building a base with storage containers, completing quests to earn the exocraft vehicles, repairing starships, or hunting down drop pods that increase your inventory. Until you reach the end game, there's always one more blueprint, one more multi-tool or starship upgrade, one more inventory slot, one more next tier of starship or freighter to get to make your journey to the center of the Galaxy or the Atlas path

[b]The quintilion planets of NMS means the game world is practically infinite. It's honestly too much, but I suppose that is the point of NMS, to show that would be foolish to explore everything, and that every player can experience their own set of planets and stars completely uncharted by others.[/b]

[b]NMS has a robust variety of creatures, plants and rocks, but you will soon start to see repeating patterns in certain creatures, especially in birds and fish.[/b] Planet variety is strong, such as mountainous planets, volcanic planets, planets that look like deserts or winter tundras, planets based on hexagonal shapes, planets based on bubbles, planets based on weird rock formations with light pillars, or planets with strange, giant, mechanical, octahedron objects that look like they could be underwater mines if they weren't floating or buried in the ground and many more. There are lush, Earth-like planets, or barren Moon-like ones. However, many planets look similar or you will notice failures in the procedural world generation as waypoints and cargo crates are unnaturally clipping in the middle of cliffs

[b]The lack of true civilization is strange and illogical.[/b] There's no such thing as cities or villages, but most locations to land at are small "factories", settlements with two TINY houses, trading posts, or their larger cousin, the Colossal Archives, which the big, hulking towers only offers a giant computer that rambles off a bit of alien lore. [b]It makes no sense that there are space stations, frigates and freighters, spaceships, and multi-tools, but no place that actually makes them....they just exist and everybody just seems to have them.[/b]

[h1]The center of the galaxy quest ending is notoriously terrible and the Atlas path is obtuse, so NMS is a game you play for the journey and the infinite world to explore, and not for its ending. NMS is better suited for mellowing out, and discovering photography subjects, base building, or hoarding resources and star craft.

At best I recommend No Man's Sky on sale, due to play-time potential, but numerous issues. The current product at least more closely resembles a $60 product then it did at launch[/h1]

[h1]Below is a list of my many annoyances with No Mans Sky[/h1]
[b]- Unfair start:[/b] You could start on a planet that is literally killing you due to heat, radiation, or toxicity before you've even had a chance to learn the controls

[b]- Un-removable Message Terminals:[/b] You can place messages on large floating computers for other players...but you can't remove them, even on your own base

[b]- Base building jank:[/b] Only some parts can snap to some parts and you can't snap parts to a grid. Only certain building structures and snap to each other

[b]- God D**ned grenades:[/b] The Plasma Launcher shoots grenades that hurt enemies and destroy/harvest resources without changing the terrain. The Geology Cannon shoots a larger explosive that does the same, but resources are less harvested and leaves holes in the ground. Both have resulted in 98% of my deaths as they explode on contact with enemies or terminals you just exited dialog with.

[b]- Freighter/Starship Hunting:[/b] It could take forever to find the ship or freighter you want and players rely on Wiki's and subreddits to find what they want, instead of the in-game systems. Even if you do, you can't edit your starship colors or shape, and there is a bug when recoloring your freighter that still isn't fixed in 2021.

[b]- Nanites:[/b] Nanites are a secondary currency to buy various upgrades, blueprints for upgrades, base parts, or upgrading the class of your Starship or Freighter. 200+ hours in, completed the main quests, and finding ways to get loads of nanites, I have yet to earn enough nanites to up-class a starship or freighter. I have enough to up-class a multi-tool from B to A, but not from A to S. My multi-tool is an A-class I found early in my run. 

[b]- Kinda bad Interface:[/b] The UI is a bit annoying to deal with as a PC player, such as not having the ability to type a number of a item you want or the fact that using the quick button to send items to storage cubes and other inventories doesn't stack items properly, wasting precious slots

[b]- Instability:[/b] Game stability has been improved over years, but expect the game to potentially crash when landing on a planet, going into certain areas, or loading from a death

[h1] No Man's Sky: Review 2 (24/05/2021) [/h1]

No Man's Sky was a game that only god could imagine. A open universe exploration game with background story and planets that felt alive - or so we thought... I look back on the start of this games era and frown, I want to forget that crappy game that I watched every YouTuber try their best to enjoy because this was £60! And since then, the team has been working on the game, taking care of it like it's their actual child. And now, nearing mid-2021, the game is more than what it promised to be. Space exploration, Eco-systems that feel truly alive, and more that was not promised from the start. 

[h1] Is it still worth it? [/h1]

If you looked at this game back in 2016, and were disappointed, I believe this game deserves another shot. It still fits the vibe of 'slightly grindy', but it is a very worth playing game. Personally, I started playing this game before it's 'Beyond' update, which I believe changed this game forever. New things to note that are now a integral part of No Man's Sky:

- Companions - literal pets - literal baby aliens!
- A hub area similar to Destiny's Tower which can be used as a meetup area and a place to start challenges.
- Living Ships.
- Interesting story, kind of...I mean it's slightly interesting.
- Avatar customisation.
- Real Multiplayer.
- Sand worms! They're cool to see around on desert planets!

That's just a bundle of random new things that could interest you, but if you would like to know more i'd advise looking at the patch notes for the new updates :D What i'm trying to say is, this game is very fun! If you wanna give opinions on the game in the replies i'd love to hear :)

I honestly hated this game when it came out, like many people did. There are review from some people at the time who really liked the bleak, lonely and monotonous atmosphere that the game produced, but I was not one of them, and I admittedly felt pretty cheated, and had put the game down until a few days ago. In between I'd started up a couple creative mode save files to check out some new updates, but that wasn't a useful way to see what had fundamentally changed about the game. Now that I've been playing on a new normal mode save for as many hours as when I first bought this game in 2016, I can say that while the very core of the gameplay system remains mostly the same, the entire game as a whole is different. Planets used to be identical aside from a change in color palette. Now they're different, varied and wild. Flight controls feel smooth and immersive, fully embracing the fantasy premise of exploring space in a sleek starfighter that this game was initially built on. Space stations feel alive and bustling, as opposed to the desolate form they once had. I feel a drive to explore this game like never before. Instead of giving up when finding out what waits at the center of the galaxy, like I once did, I now want to build up my trading fleet, fight off pirates, catalogue strange animals and build a base on a tropical dream planet. This game has become even more than what I bought it hoping it to be, and I'm glad that I've picked it back up again.

--Update--
I had stepped away from this game for a while again but lately I've been obsessed with it. It just keeps improving, and at this point I'd say that the multiplayer community is one of the biggest selling points. It's easy to find coordinates online for various player inhabited systems and it's well worth exploring and joining in.

No Man's Sky is a game for those who are in it for the long haul.  Things take time and patience but the rewards for your troubles are worth it.  

The game has you beginning on an unknown planet all alone.  Not knowing who you are or what you are doing there.  You are sent on a mission of self discovery which will send you across the Galaxy in search for answers and in doing so you will come across some weird, wonderful and dangerous things.  You will also learn to build a base and expand it with many different gadgets and vehicles until you potentially have a massive structure to be proud of.  Once you have finished that base....you can build on any planet you like and leave your mark for other travellers to find.

No Man's Sky is a game of discovery and exploration.  I found a strange sense of relaxation but also slight Loneliness while I explored the vast reaches of space.  The many planets and solar systems that I have found and named, along with the wildlife, plant life and various rocks etc  all add to the sense that you are alone in this vast Universe...But you are not alone...

Perhaps the real shining light of No Man's Sky is the community behind it.  Occasionally you will come across other Travellers that are exploring just like you.  But when you summon the Nexus (A huge Orb shaped ship that is essentially a multiplayer hub) you can venture inside to find many other players talking and helping each other out.  Many times I have come here and been given something of massive value for no reason at all by a completely random player that I have never met.  And this is a testament to the type of community that really make this game what it is.  

Not once has a player ever approached me with aggression.  If you are looking for that...then this game isn't for you.  Most players here just want to help each other out and team up to complete a team mission from the Nexus Hub.  Fly together, Explore together and sometimes fight together or even show someone your favourite base that you have built.  

Graphically this game is pretty especially when weather effects start kicking in during a storm.  It never gets old when you land on a new planet and get out of your ship for the first time to see a fantastic view of the land ahead which then calls to you to explore on foot once again.

This is a great game that you can play at your own pace.  I Highly recommend it to anyone who likes to sit back and enjoy a game that you never feel the need to rush through.  

Explore, Discover, Create, Build, Travel, Connect.   I hope to see you out there some time fellow travellers :)

I've followed 'No Man's Sky' since it's abysmal launch. I thought the company would just disappear and we'd never hear from them again. Instead they kept developing the game and releasing updates, bringing the game ever closer to those broken release-day promises. It has now reached a point in its development where it has fulfilled those promises, three years late, but better late than never and there are more updates slated to be released this summer.

I've now played 15 hours -- most of that with a friend -- and I've been thoroughly enjoying the game. Fifteen hours isn't nearly long enough to experience everything the game has to offer and I'm still unsure of just how much depth there will be once I reach the mid to end game and I've researched all the technology and acquired all the fancy ships, but here are a few of my thoughts.

CONS:
The game is quite a grind. *Everything* requires resources to function: suit oxygen, radiation/toxicity shielding, mining laser, terrain deformation tool, ship shield, ship launching, ship warping, etc... This makes logical sense, but it means a large portion of your very limited inventory is taken up with resources to power your ability to continue obtaining resources.

Planets are very much the same, though each planet has different biomes to break it up. You will see the same geological formations time and again.

Flora and fauna have the same issue -- you'll see very similar creatures over and over. There are only three or four types of 'aggressive flora' that are found on every planet. There are underwater geysers that are the same in nearly every body of water on every planet.

The interface feels a bit odd, like it's a hybrid between a console game and a PC game. It seems to work equally well with keyboard and mouse as with a controller, but two different UIs for the two different control schemes might have been a better option. It's not terrible, it just takes some getting used to.

I bought this on sale for $30. It's worth $30, but the full price of $60 is too high in my opinion.


PROS:
There are some lovely vistas to see. The graphics aren't great, but they're adequate.

The building system seems pretty decent. I'm still trying to move beyond the basic, wooden building modules, but it seems promising. If you've played 'Ark: Survival Evolved', it's similar. You discover or buy blueprints for crafting various devices and structures and then can place them if you have sufficient resources. Also, thought I've not done it yet, you can build underwater, which I always think is cool.

I've found it interesting and fun to explore strange, new planets and discover new technologies. This has been especially enjoyable with a friend.

There's mod support. Nearly all the cons I've mentioned can be fixed to some extent with mods from the community. There are mods that improve textures, mods that improve the shaders, mods that add hundreds of new animal and plant types, mods that make biomes and planet generation more interesting and varied, etc...

The game is still being actively developed. Unlike certain other developers that abandon their game and customers when they botch a release, Hello Games has stuck with this game and, in my opinion, has become a shining light of what a game company should be... now that they've learned from their past mistakes.
