Claiming that this is a bad game in 2021 is like screaming into the wind, but after trying it once again years later, I must yell regardless. Simply because Hello Games did the right thing for the game, people are more than willing to overlook that they have added MORE of the things that people complained about initially, but their good nature has blinded people to the irony within. 

Aside from the game not being what was initially promised, the most prominent complaints on launch were bugs, horribly tedious tasks, and awful inventory. It's frequently stated that these have all been mostly fixed, most notably the repetitive tasks and inventory systems.
This couldn't be farther from the truth, yet because a change was made, people either choose to ignore the reality of the situation or simply don't notice that the game has doubled down on those issues. 

The inventory has been expanded slightly, and only slightly. This might be something good were it not for the fact that they've also increased the amount of materials needed to craft almost anything at all. Not only the raw quantity, but the complexity. Where as the game initially required you to harvest 2 materials to craft 1 component, you now must craft something to refine materials into OTHER materials. They've effectively turned 2 requirements into 5, all of which eat up inventory space. 

As for the repetitive nature of the game, most notably having to constantly refill your ammo, oxygen, toxicity shield, and the 3+ components for your ship, they've also increased the complexity required for this. Instead of your default tool being able to mine ores and plant alike, you must now also craft an entirely separate tool to harvest ores, one that of course needs its own fuel. They have, at the very LEAST, doubled the amount of components and time needed to do even the most barebones task within the game. Somehow though, simply because changes were made to the game, people now decided that they're better despite being in every possible sense worse. It's as though adding more of what people hated persuaded them that things were somehow good now. 

If you're looking to get a comprehensive tutorial in game that doesn't involve mandatory base building, forget it. If you want to take to the stars, the tutorial is not how you learn the essentials of the game. It will walk you through the boring nature of base building, a process that,  yet again, requires the insanely tedious process of harvesting, converting and crafting over and over again. For something that was such a highlight of complaints, it amazes me that so many more steps were put into the game to drastically hinder progression. Most of this would be genuinely fine if it weren't for the absolute lack of inventory space that you have. The display is almost intentionally misleading in game, as it displays how many units of something you can hold, yet ignores how many actual spaces you have to store other items. When in game, you'll notice what looks to be a jaw dropping amount of space; a resounding "99999" slots. Surprise surprise, after harvesting 15 different things though, you're down to 0. Your ship starts with a laughably small inventory as well, meaning you're still just as limited as when the game first came out. How people thought the inventory system was fixed is beyond me. The process of base building is made unnecessarily lengthy thanks to the need to craft one thing after another just to get the most basic things going. If you're planning on skipping the base building segment of the game, you'll also end up lacking out on advanced technology within the game. Essentially, if you want to play this game to just explore planets while still making progress, you're straight up boned. 

Clearly, I don't like the fact that they've expanded on the crafting systems within the game, but my point of contention stems from everyone saying this were made BETTER. Despite all the content added to the game, it takes twice the amount of effort, all of which is spent doing the most boring bits of gameplay, to get to literally any of it. The game is still weirdly buggy and still, after all these years, has the issue of stuttering. The inventory has been made actively worse, despite being changed for supposedly the better. The progression of the game is entirely stunted if you just want to do what you paid for. Traveling through the stars.

This game is an amazing look into how PR can make and break a game, no matter if it's still fundamentally broken. Make people upset enough and simply choosing to do the right thing will make people rave about it, despite the game still being a bad game. 

If you're looking for an absolute time sink because you truly have nothing to do at all, this game might be perfect for you. Hours upon hours will be spent dealing with a full inventory, refilling unnecessary systems, and crafting things that only aid to filling up your inventory. If you need something that's fun within the first few hours though, you're immediately going to learn this will not provide that.

No Man's Sky, A game developed and published by Hello Games, Launched 13th of August, 2016.

I have longed for a game that would allow me to take to the stars, fly amongst the raging balls of fire, the spiralling rocks and visit worlds untouched by man. I have played countless Science fiction games in hopes for this dream. And so i was obviously drawn to No Man's Sky. It's promises of grandeur and its visual style spoke to me on so many levels. But did it deliver? At first not even in the slightest, but this game has been in development for a long time now and perhaps its now finally at a point where it can be evaluated as it should be.

I would like to mention here that everything below is purely based on the game itself, I believe the team at Hello Games are doing a considerable amount of effort to make this game as good as it can be and that is a mindset that can only be praised.

[h1]Story 1/10[/h1]
No Man's Sky or NMS as i'll refer to it on going isn't entirely based on a storyline, so it makes it hard to write this part. However the game doesn't really deliver any kind of information at all, as to how you came to be, where you came from or even a story of the universe you are flying through. The relatively small amount of information you are provided only seemingly leads to more questions. Not that questions aren't a good thing for a mystery and to build suspense but that's where it ends. Beyond the standard amount of information you'd expect, this game is devoid of any semblance of history, lore or world development.

[h1]Gameplay 3/10[/h1]
[b]+ World Design:[/b]No Man's Sky doesn't provide a whole lot of gameplay mechanics so this section is going to be relatively short, However it does a few things particularly well and a few things pretty dismally. The world design however is pretty amazing. I understand that the worlds are procedurally generated but the algorithm used to build them is pretty sensation, the worlds are vibrant and full of things to explore.
[b]+ Mining:[/b]I love a game that has a good mining system, especially when its crucial to its own mechanics. NMS has made Mining it's fundamental game mechanic in that you need to mine to do pretty much anything, from fixing your ship and ensuring you won't die, to making money.
[b]+ Scanning the environment:[/b]This game has plenty to look negative toward, however i really enjoyed scanning creatures and the environment to document my travels. It felt like a great idea and never really got boring, i wish there was more of a reward for doing so than just a cash prize. But as a whole it felt very interesting, discovering different resources on a planet.
[b]- Movement:[/b]NMS essentially has you moving constantly, finding resources, traversing landscapes in search of points of interest. However the mechanics here are flawed and clunky, Movement is heavy and sloppy and feels unnatural. The sprinting is almost useless as you can only really sprint for the space of 1 meter before you character collapses from the strain, and the jetpack has almost no forward propulsion only upward and even then its extremely slow and clumsy.
[b]- Enemy Diversity:[/b]I use the phrase "enemy" extremely loosely here as there aren't really any enemies, the sentinel robots patrol planets occasionally and attack you if you bother them too much but there really isn't any fundamental combat set up here and the enemies aren't really worth the effort in fighting.
[b]- Endgame/Purpose to Play:[/b]The game doesn't really have one, it has you progressing through this world for a seemingly endless purpose but with no reason. You can continue to build a base and upgrade your ships but there is really no purpose to it. Somewhere around the 20 hour mark you will have experienced everything this game has to offer and for a game of this scale and scope that is pretty sad.
[b]- Hazardous Environments:[/b]I understand that in any survival game, the fundamental premise is that you are in a dangerous environment and that you have to survive. No one can argue with this mechanic, However in NMS you aren't really given a chance to survive, you awaken on a planet of random designation, that is in someway hostile to you. You are immediately subjected to an ever draining life system that will eventually kill you unless you can find the resources to repair your ship and to keep your exosuit functions running. I like this until you reason your character is a brick on lego wheels and that you can't traverse any sort of distance on foot without almost dying.

[h1]Visuals 5/10[/h1]
NMS is a beautiful game, and it was far more beautiful at its launch. It hasn't aged extremely well although it still isn't ugly. The graphics are overtoned by its vibrant colour schemes and amount of information it throws at you almost immediately. It has a significant amount of graphical options to help alleviate even the minor discrepancies you would have, but even at Ultra this game isn't all that stunning. It looks good for what it is, but it's not breath taking, not compared to other games of this genre. There were no minor or major graphical issues in this game running it at Ultra. and the frames held steadily well above 60FPS.

[h1]Audio 7/10[/h1]
Suprisingly i have very little negative to say here. NMS has provided a beautifully designed OST to compliment its game play. The world sounds alive even if you can't really see it at times which can be depressing. But the sound effects here are on point, everything you do feels impactual and connected to the world, Flying sounds intense and that first take off is stupendous to hear. Overall a sensational audio presentation here and the developers should be extremely proud of it.

[h1]Overall 4/10 "Mediocre"[/h1]
Whilst No Man's Sky has had a lot of work put into it, to make it the game it should have been 5 years ago now. It's probably reached that point. However in that time games have exceeded it's original promises and have excelled at it exceptionally. It's overall mechanics and graphics are outdated and despite the the effort here to make it a great game i just can't see it becoming one. The developers are a dedicated and passionate team and the work they have put into NMS is evident from the moment you launch it. However the game isn't really worth the price, and probably not even on sale.

I paid $24 bucks for this game and I don't regret a penny of it. (In its current state, Atlas 1.3, it is still NOT worth $60 bucks/ full price) 

It has entertained me for hours, its challenging yet its peaceful, it’s frustrating yet it easy. You cannot just easily progress or buy everything, you've got to work for it. Yes, sometimes you have to be repetitive... but its gets easier as things go on. 

If you had doubts about picking this up just ask yourself "did you enjoy Minecraft?"  If the answer is yes, this is a very advanced version of Minecraft... in space.

You must spend hours slowly farming resources, which will in turn make gather the same resources a little bit quicker later. 

If it’s your first time playing, DO NOT start on Permadeath or Survival. You will die... A LOT.

You need to know what to look for, how to look for it, and how to efficiently farm it. This game is about efficiency in the long run. There are multiple paths to take after you start off as a crash victim and repair your ship. You can be a galactic trader, explorer, pirate, or much more. Though the depths of each of these paths is now as deep as some would like, they can still be entertaining. (Pirates kind of go the path of GTA where each sentinel you kill brings harder and harder sentinels after you... until you run away or die) 

Traders work their way up from small ship to Freighters, which cost millions of dollars, but allow you to own multiple ships and have a mobile farm and base. 

Explores can keep it small with a variety of ships which allow them to quickly traverse the never-ending universe naming as many things as they want after themselves. 

If they ever get the multi-player figured out, this game would make an AMAZING MMO universe. 

I will say this, if you're looking for a game that has instant gratification (AKA a game you can completely figure out or conquer after 5 hours of play), this is not a game for you.

Reviews.176352:
Edit: WOW this review is old as balls. Yeah uh this game is fully worth the price now, and then some. GET IT. 

I'll start off with this: Wait for a sale. This is a 30 dollar game, not 60.

So, No Man's Sky set the world record for roughest, most lauded start in the history of gaming, bar none. It was the fault of both sides, really. The developers hyped it up way too much, and the players actually believed the hype. I heard of No Man's Sky years ago, where it claimed it would deliver a seamless, no loading screen environment of exploring space. I said cool, and went on with my life. When it released, it was gifted to me, and I played it. I noticed it seemed a little lackluster, and then the salt showers started. I was confused at first, but then I found out why: I'd successfully avoided years of unbelievable and undeliverable promises, the infamous hype. I just shook my head, sighed, and hoped the developers would try to redeem themselves. Then they got investigated by some trade agency, their office doors closed, and I thought that was that. Pity, the game looked like it had potential.

And then, out of the blue, the game updates! And it's a good update too!

With that out of the way, here we go!

So, since everyone and their unfortunate mother seems to know how the base game goes, I'll be brief. You're an intrepid little explorer (and I do mean little, you appear to be quite short) out to explore the galaxy and make your way. Exploration comes as landing on planets and scanning the local geology and lifeforms, which you are rewarded for. You jump from system to system, finding more planets to explore and space stations to visit. It's all procedurally generated and pretty predictable. You can upgrade your handy dandy multitool, which serves as both a mining laser and a weapon, be it a machine gun, shot gun, or grenade launcher or all if you so desire, and your ship, which you can replace either by finding new ships or purchasing them from other sapients. You're protected from the environment in varying degrees by your exosuit, which you upgrade much the same as the ship and the multi-tool. All of this via the resources you search for on planets.

And that was the base game. Pretty cut and dry, which is the reason for the salt. There was something of a storyline to complete, but it was very shallow.

Now, however, they've really started to revamp the game. You can have your own base now, which you construct, and crew, with your findings in the galaxy. It opens up new forms of equipment for you, and can be customized to your designs. They also worked on the procedural engine, so critters, planets, and ships are a lot more varied now. You've got space freighters which you can land on and chat with the captain, and apparently hire! For what, I don't yet know. I've gotten a construction specialist, a scientist and an armorer on my base so far, and if what I know is right, it's the farmer who deals with freighters. I'm pursuing the main storyline, something about an all knowing entity called Atlas, and it's kept my interest so far.

So, all in all? A good game to grab in a sale.

Reviews.183904:
Edit: Hello Games has worked tirelessly on this game and it shows. What was once an empty, aimless experience has grown into a full, beautiful game. Some of this may be due to my own expectations being tempered, as it definitely still has some samey-ness between worlds, but there is enough variety and enough of an actual GAME here that my experience with it recently has been a positive one. I am keeping the original review below to emphasize that I feel changes have been made for the better that address my previous issues. 

I really wanted to love this game. For a short time, I did love it. There are still times when I feel like I do. However, there are some deep flaws that need to be addressed before No Man's Sky is something I can truly call a good game.


[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]

- Exploration: ...for a time. New worlds and alien creatures are wonderous in the beginning. Also, looking up at the night sky and seeing other solar bodies in your system is pretty awesome.

- Soundtrack: The music throughout the game is very well polished.

- The Languages: It's neat that you do not understand alien races from the get-go and piecing together what they are saying over time is a nice concept.

- Near Seemless Transitions: It's still fun to hop into your ship and fly into space without loading screens getting (obviously) in the way. The same is true of the inverse.


[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]

- Exploration: ...after a time. Upon exploring enough worlds, you'll start to notice repeating patterns. There are the same few presets for what x kind of creature can look like or what y kind of tree might be. The sense of newness fades and exploring feels less like finding something completely new and more like discovering close relatives to what you've seen before.

- Conflicted Sense of Self: This one is hard to summarize. The game seems to want to be two things at once: a tranquil exploration-focused game and a resource-management game. The problem is that they conflict with one-another in terms of how the game feels and is paced. It also doesn't help that, after time, neither of these game-types holds their fun.

- Handholding and Console-itus: Simply put, a lot of things were dumbed down or not optimized for PC. Several mods are must-haves just to make things (such as flying your ship) feel like it should have from the start.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


No Man's Sky feels like a bunch of ideas that never really got fleshed out. Mods have helped tremendously to fix problems the game should never have had, but they do not fix the core issues that plague the experience.

In order to substain the sense of wonder, the game either needs to be more focused (with more resource & quest-oriented content) or more varied (to continue to find completely new things beyond the first few hours). As is, the content that is there does not justify it's purchase.

So, regretfully, I cannot recommend No Man's Sky. :(

I belive Jim Sterling said it best in his review stating "As vast as an ocean, but as shallow as a puddle" While I avoided the hype train and went in to this with minimal expectations in hopes to enjoy it in my own way and avoid dissapointment, I wanted to like this game, I really did!

For the first 8 hours I actually did, I had spent those hours on my first planet "ooOOOooing and aaAAHhhHHing" at the odd animals, beautiful colors, all while collecting cool technology, learning a new language and eagerly collecting materials to make a great ship. I then decided to head up to the space station, get my stardrive and move on to the next system and experience the other wonders the game had to offer.

It was at that point I realised there was nothing else the game could offer me, 18quintillion planets, became 18quintillion reskinned recoloured repeats, I found nothing that set apart any of the planets in any major way that had any real impact, none of the planets I visited left any sort of memorable imprint. aside from heat, cold and poison, they where all pretty much the same. The animals while different and frankly absurd, still contained parts and bits I had previously seen, it got to the point where I didn't care about the animals, I found the interaction with them pointless and tedious.

The interaction between you and one of the 3 only species in existance is shallow and repetitive and with keeping in tune with the rest of the game it lacks any real substance. Want to talk to an alien in their ship? knock on the window to bring up a portrait to ask 1 of three questions....every single time.
I could go on but I would just be repeating what has been said in other reviews here and almost every review on the internet has stated so I'll just close this up.

While I can appriciate what Hello Games has done with NMS and wanting to give us a game we wanted, but sadly I think they lost sight and fell victim to the sheer size of the what this could have been. Aside from the lies from Sean Murray and the missing features, it's the core of this game being everything is procedurally generated is what did this game in. The whole experience feels soul-less, empty, and unrewarding. I read so much that this game was going to be a memorable experience, it will for sure, but it will be memorable for all the wrong reasons. 

The only way I could ever reccomend this game is if it was on sale for $20-$25 TOPS, and the modding community really came out with some solid content to make this a real game, otherwise there is no way I can recommend this game in any form.

Alright, so after a few years after I got this game on release and was completely disappointed with pretty much a game that delivered 1/10 of the original promised content I recently downloaded it again and oh boy! This is a completely new game to be honest and it is already better than any other space game I have. 

I know I am late to the party, and I managed to start and complete a degree while taking a break from this but hey, I am back. Seriously, you can throw everything out of the window and just get NMS. I really like how engaging the environment feels with the insane amount of creatures, side quests, random things you just find all the time. This is exactly what I thought about when heard "procedurally generated" and a clam of infinite variety, but this is the first time I see an implementation that works insanely well and is actually bringing true uniqueness and not just a slightly altered skin or texture. 

There are lot's of positives in this game now, but I really want to comment of the major one: for this huge amount of content present I really like the fact you are not forced to grind for hours to get anything unlocked and most of the time I just find myself bombarded by new items/blueprints/quests/resources and I don't think there was a single moment where I just had to waste time trying to collect some extremely rare resource or farm for experience or whatever to progress - if you don't have something, you can literary forget about it for some time, go and do a couple of side quests or just explore and you will most probably get the needed resource along the way. 

I really like how complex but at the same time simple this game is. Somehow NMS managed to create pseudo-space sim which feels extremely engaging and exiting at every moment. It's been a few years since I've put a scathing review for this title. Back when it was a cobbled-together piece of junk that aimed to swindle consumers out of a lofty 60$ for entry. It started it's life as a shallow, buggy pile of junk. Worse still, this title told the Video Game Industry that it is 100% possible to make a broken pile of junk and release it anyway. No Man's Sky was interesting for just long enough to skirt past the Refund window, then you would start to realize that yes. This is it. 

The following updates were, improvements but something to be said about polishing turds. This game, still deserves everything it got in those early days. It was indeed a scam.

How does it fare today? After news started to circulate about how NMS was being built and how Hello Games was forced to create the game, it became more clear as to how they were forced to hype up a game they themselves knew wasn't going to be feature complete. Over the years after release, the team kept their heads down to keep fixing this game, adding promised features, listening to feedback. All without a single paid DLC. 

This game now starts to shine on it's own. It has redeemed itself in the eyes of many, including my own. I still feel the 60$ price tag is steep for it's age.

Edit: It's better now


I decided to give this game another chance, it's been so long since it's been released and I paid so much for it I figured why not? It'd be nice to see how it plays now that they've had time to polish out the bugs and other issues.

Oh boy. Hoooooooo BOY was I naive.

Upon reinstalling the game and launching it, I configured the options, as you do. I immediately set my resolution to my monitors native value. What? Why do I need to restart the game? It's 2018 and I'm playing a game that forces me to restart every time I change a graphic option? Alright, whatever, I'll set the other options while I'm here. I change my FOV to 90 to avoid the headaches and motion sickness a lower value brings. Huh? That's funny, it seems like the values in the menu STILL aren't correct. 90 is actually more like 60. Why isn't this fixed? I upped the FOV to the max of 100 and managed to make out about 3 pixels in startling detail, so zoomed in was my view. Well they didn't fix that, but I can still correct it in the config files, annoying but it only has to be done once. Perfect.

So I restart the game and begin playing. Everything goes fine for about an hour, and I'm actually having fun. I stumble across an enourmous pillar of solid gold, glistening under an alien sun. I'm going to mine this and buy myself a god damn planet, I tell myself. I grind away at this pillar, filling my inventory to the brim with spoils before returning to my ship to store it all and start another run. You know when you have something so planned out that when it goes wrong it takes a few seconds for you to comprehend what's happening? Your brain stops for a second before it goes "well fuck, that'sgone rather poorly somehow." That's pretty much what went through my head as I fell through the map. Yes, that's right, somehow I fell straight through the terrain. The best part is that you don't even die instantly, there's water down there in oblivion, so you simply have to let the cold ocean of hell take you very very slowly. Many days later, when my character had finally expired, I respawned at my ship. My cause of death was listed as "suffocation." Apparently "bullshit" hasn't been coded in yet. A nice little marker taunted me, telling me to come and retrieve all my hard earned gold from a few kilometers under the world. Furious, I returned to the gold pillar, determined to leave with SOMETHING of monetary value in spite of the games best efforts. on my way there I saw why I was able to fall through the map. A massive square of terrain simply didn't exist. It hadn't loaded at all. This shouldn't be happening in a US$60 game, let alone one that's had so many updates since release. By now I was positively INCANDESCENT, and mined a few units of gold before returning to my ship, giving the portal to hell a wide berth. 

I was back, I made it to my ship and was ready to leave. I didn't have as much gold as I'd hoped but at least I could get off this gods forsaken planet. I nearly ran my father over when I was a boy. He got me to reverse our family car as he wasn't able to at the time. I didn't know how sensitive the throttle pedal is in a car and I shot backwards, miraculously not hitting anything. This is exactly what happened once I took off in my ship. I started flying out of the atmosphere and released the throttle once I was clear. As soon as I did this my ship HAULED ASS in reverse at -200,000 units. I spazzed out all over the galaxy before getting it under control by accelerating again. Against all odds I made it to a space station where I could sell my gold before leaving for the next system. As I exited the space station, my ship shot backwards yet again, through the space station and into deep space. However this time, because I had gone through the stations auto dock zone, I wasn't able to accelerate. Infact, I wasn't able to do anything, all my controls were disabled, and I was stranded hurtling through space at close to the speed of light.

I write this from my cockpit knowing that I will die here. It is highly unlikely that my ship and body will ever be found but if it is please, I implore you:


Do not buy this game.

This is Martyr Chief Hajaar signing off for the last time.

ORIGINAL REVIEW: I can't remember the last time I was so disappointed with a game at launch. I survived Star Wars:Galaxies and a number of questionable launches of other games including Eve, but No Man's Sky has to have plumbed new depths of software that wasn't ready for prime time. 

More fool I, perhaps - no open beta, tightly lipped team, but so many promises! And I wanted to believe, I really did. 

It took me a while to be able to play this game; I have a Phenom and Hello didn't do a beta or clearly test on AMDs because the game didn't work, and those of us with AMD Phenoms had to use a workaround using an Intel emulator in order to play, (player suggested workaround too), at a reduced framerate. I should add Hello was HORRIBLE with communication - Sean (the owner), posted they were working on a fix and then went dark for 48 hours, no updates on where they were, no status of the fix, until finally some people on Steam boards saw a build pushed to experimental, which got you farther but not to the planet. Enter the emulator workaround, then FINALLY more info from Sean they were going to make people happy with a fix, but still no concrete info on it. The final injustice in all this is apparently Hello is already working on another game! Despite this 'premium' title not containing the features promised, despite its problems and unfinished feel, they've used my money to move on. I feel cheated. 

The game doesn't deliver on what it was promised - it feels more like a sandbox or alpha game, incomplete, than a $60 title. You hunt around and salvage parts to repair your ship after being stranded on a planet, attune to a mysterious stone, maybe encounter an alien or two, and then go to a station to sell. 

There are so few NPCs that it feels the place isn't populated. You should get nudged for a mission that will grant you a hyperdrive, (I haven't yet), but if you pre-ordered you already have one, so it doesn't make sense. I repaired my ship, found a trader on the planet I was on, then found a station off planet and interacted with a device in the wall and sold some ore... and then what? Your cargo bay is small, stacks are 250, there is no inventory and no direction. 

It looks okay - I mean procedurally generated terrain is fine and all, but I can't play it. I don't mind open world games like Skyrim - there you have content, quests, NPCs, etc., but No Man's Sky doesn't have any of that feel. It is a boring game with poor support at an expensive price and I cannot recommend it, despite the fact I try my hardest to support small studios.

UPDATED: 2021

I have been playing this game off and on for a while now, and really like some new things they've done.  I hesitate to change my review to recommended because there are still some significant issues with it, but since I'm playing it, I sort of feel forced to.

The biggest issues are with multiplayer, and they are not insignificant. My SO built a base underground to surprise me whilst I was offworld, and when I came back he showed it to me and it was horribly glitched. Stuff that he built didn't exist for me but he saw it, ground was there that had been cleared, clipping things he had put in. Leaving and coming back and resaving fixed none of it. These are terrible bugs (loss of information/data). It basically makes multiplayer impossible/tedious/not fun. Also annoying? Surveying a new planet together and not having the weather in sync (he'll get a storm and it will be sunny for me.)

Even in single player there are issues with terrain/build priorities. I can't tell you the number of times I've come back to my base, only to find the uneven ground that got flattened by my base building has reformed and swallowed or clipped into my buildings. It's really freaking annoying. 

I'm also not the hugest fan of the storyline, I think it's a bit hokey, but the biomes and worlds are terrific, and I love looking at and finding ships. Using Nav Data to get maps to explore locations is fun, because you don't know exactly what you'll encounter. There are some freaky (but cool!) creatures and you often really get the feel of alien exploration and there are moments of stunning beauty. I have to say to community I've interacted with at the anomaly has been really nice. 

I wish they would concentrate more on bug fixes and quality of life instead of pushing more features, because I would be able to enthusiastically recommend it then. It has moments of genius, for sure, especially if you have a hankering for space exploration games.

No Mans Sky, a beautiful procedurally generated universe with infinite possibilities. Or so I thought.  Explore and fight your way through thousands of solar systems, like most people had me sitting on the edge of my seat with anticipation. I could not wait to get in there and see what amazing discoveries that I could find.  Unfortunately this isn’t exactly the case and I was soul shatteringly disappointed.

You start off on an unknown planet not knowing where you are or what is going on.  As you explore and gather resources you learn that you are not alone.  You eventually find out that there are a few other races that you can interact and trade with to help you on your journey to the center of the galaxy.  What they don’t tell you is the nps never move around or show any real signs of life.  There are no major cities anywhere just little cookie cutter buildings that all look the same and take on 7 forms; trade station, monolith finder, crashed ship finder, exo suit upgrader or blueprint finder.  They come in a whopping 3 different colors and styles but essentially all look exactly the same.  In all of the 18 quadrillion planets there are a total of 4 races.  That’s right 4.  You only ever get to really interact with 3 of them and they are all are emotionless stationary drones who all behave in the same manner.  The only thing that changes is sometimes they look a little bit different.  There is absolutely no character customization.  You cannot customize the way your ship looks.  You can craft parts to go in your ship to make it a bit faster or shoot harder ect but essentially that is all.  I had a ship that only had one wing on it, it had a wing on the left and none on the right. It was very very ugly but I needed it to get to where I was going.  

You earn money in the game by collecting and selling resources.  Then you can use that money to buy other resources that you might need or to buy a ship with more inventory space. Or you can find a crashed ship and take that one for free.  Unfortunately once you have upgraded your exo suit to max and you have a ship with 30 or more slots you find that money no longer has any purpose.  You aimlessly fly from one system to the next exploring the beautiful planets with the 7 little cookie cutter buildings scattered randomly on them.  Or you can follow the pre destined travel of the race called the atlas which guides you to the center of the galaxy. Sometimes the planets are hot or cold or toxic or radioactive and you have to craft a shield to protect yourself from the elements.

But after enough time goes by you find yourself getting very bored with the repetitive droning on from one place to another.  Sometimes you will encounter hostile ships that want to kill you or you can be the attacker and take out cargo freighters at a loss of reputation with one of the 3 other races.  There are sentinel robots that will sometimes attack you and are very annoying because they are like flys that follow you around everywhere you go.  But pretty much all this game is: you fly around collecting stuff so you can upgrade your suit and ship so you can fly to another place to gather more resources so you can upgrade your suit and ship and this just repeats over and over until you are bored.

I would say from an exploration standpoint this game is very beautiful to look at.  But they did a very terrible job at adding any real substance to the game.  The story is shoddy and the npc interactions are lame. This game needs a rethink and a lot of work to be better. It is not worth 60 dollars in my opinion.

UPDATE: 2021 Just played this game again.  Its still boring.  It still lacks content.  Its still a grindfest. I would love to get my money back.  Game not worth what it costs.

After all the updates, 5+ years later, this game is 'good enough'.  And actually fun to play.

I like this game, it is fun, but it is definitely not worth 60 dollars.  It's, in essence, a mix of Minecraft and the Space Stage of Spore.  I would wait for the price to drop and for them to release their (allegedly) free DLC before buying it, but it is definitely worth playing for the experience.  I'll write what I liked and didn't like about the game and you, the reader, can draw your own conclusions.

While it is very exploration oriented, I felt like the constant need to gather materials to power your ship or to fund you explorations limited it's potential.  The gathering materials is interesting at first, but quickly becomes rote once you have to grind for things, or are searching for a material but can't find it.

Discovering animal and plant lifeforms and the many different plants is something I kind of just do if I run across them.  I don't go out of my way to do any of that.  That in itself, the struggle to discover everything living on the planet just to get that "100% completion" is a boring chore.  It's a neat mechanic, that is also VERY reminiscent of Spore, but even in that game I didn't waste my time scanning things.

I found the highlights of the game to be discovering new planet types that you hadn't run across yet, the interactions with the different alien races and the dynamics among them, and the spaceship combat.

Discovering a new type of planet is fun in that your expectations can be defied-- you go to land hoping to gather a certain material, and instead end up with a planet that extremely hot and will kill you in seconds if you leave your ship, or the planet's robot guardians are all murderous and try to kill you, or the wildlife all teams up and tries to eat you.  Or, in between where most of the planets are borderline uninhabitable, you'll find one that is incredibly beautiful and is almost a paradise.  Something about it immediately captured my immagination.

During my first few hours playing the game I focused on interacting with one of the alien races, which was neat, as there are a variety of uniquely designed encounters and environments in which meet the different alien characters.  There are even two recurring Alien characters, who act as your patrons of sorts, who follow your journey throughout the universe.  There's no real dialogue, aside from alien gibberish, and most is done in text to be read, reminiscent of old RPGs (and Spore).  You can learn the aliens' languages, and it'll translate what the gibberish says on the screen, so you'll get a better idea of what the alien is trying to tell you.  Where I was guessing how to answer the aliens at first, once I'd learned words through interactions with other aliens or through exploring the worlds I could make more informed descisions as more of what was being said was revealed to me.  It's pretty cool, although definitely shallow at times, so those who were looking for indepth interactions with characters will definitely be disappointed (although I didn't know this was even going to be in the game, so I was pleasantly surprised).

Lastly, the starship combat.  It's, frankly, kind of tacted on, a sort of last minute thing with simplistic controls.  It's very uncomplicated, and you'll feel underwhelmed at first, as your ship is as weak as your enemy's, and just two or three foes is enough to kill an unprepared beginner pilot.  But once you upgrade your ship, or get a new one, you'll definitely see improvements.  Once you're able to chew your way through eight opponants there's definite satisfaction.  I enjoy it just because I don't have to stress over to many things when fighting, you'll only be using the jointstick and two or three buttons if you use a remote like me, and there's no penalities for dying.  Yeah, this game is pretty darn easy.  You're going to have a hard time dying, and if you do, there's no real punishment for it, so I sort of wonder why they put it in-- there's a Dark Souls-esque 'gravesight' left behind where you can reclaim any and all lost items.  If you were hoping for a hardcore sci-fi experience, this isn't it.

My only question is where you find the giant robots featured in the gallery on the store page.  I want to fight those.

So, in short, I reccomend it, once the price goes down.  Really, if you're excited for it, just wait.  Be patient.  This game's been in development for like half a decade now, a few more months or so won't hurt.

I have to make a dramatic revision to my old review.  I can recommend this game now.

It still bears saying, I bought this game at launch.  I was disappointed by a broad range of unfulfilled promises during the original development period, but still squeezed my money's worth out of it. It even put me on a planet where I couldn't find any sodium (the mineral that recharges your hazard protection)!   I got mad at that and assessed the game as not worth purchasing.

I came back this past weekend, and while a new game still starts on a hazard planet, it's balanced and teaches you about hazard maintenance and will make a new player really appreciate the eventual 'garden' world they'll find.  The old magic felt like it was back, along with the new magic of base building and exocraft.  While I have not indulged any multiplayer stuff, if you're a single player type that wants a rather relaxing, at-your-own-pace space sim, this game has finally at least achieved that.

Reviews.218524:
"No Man's Sky is a game about exploration and survival in an infinite procedurally generated universe." is the Steam description for this game, but for some reason barely even scratches the surface of what this game is about and what its been through.

I don't make stupid long reviews for games because no game I feel has ever justified me writing a long review about it, because really they just don't. They either suck or they don't. No Man's Sky, however, I feel deserves a giant review after everything its been through. Obviously everyone knows what happened with this game. It came out, it sucked ass, and was the laughing stock of the internet for months on end. Not even I, as someone who actually did play the game when it came out (Hi Wade) can in any way try to justify what happened (for some reason people try to defend the state of the game in 1.0, I have actually seen this.) 1.0 was shit. Like, REALLY BAD. 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 were not anything impressive either, the mechanics made no sense, the game was ugly, and the planets were unfathomably ugly and borderline incomprehensible. (but the later updates WOAH they were good, ill touch on that later.) But the incredible thing about ALL of this is that for some reason, 5 years on from launch, they still give a shit. Other devs seem to have tried this, and never succeeded. Primary examples and their fates are: Anthem with its support dropped. Star Wars Battlefront 2 with its support dropped. Artifact with its Support dropped. Fallout 76 which is still terrible LOL. Lawbreakers with its support dropped. Cyberpunk 2077 (THE BIG ONE) with its fate TBD. There's been a new term thrown around the video game industry lately where people say a game will "pull a No Man's Sky" and yet it seems no game has actually pulled this off in the same scope other than the one that coined the term.
Hello Games has shown this was not some one off project they would release and never care about again or update a handful of times and call it a night, this game is their passion project, which is why I appreciate it so much. They turned this game into so much more than its ambitions at launch ever hoped to achieve, and the majority of content promised at launch but was absent for some reason has actually been implemented. (multiplayer, sandworms, unique ship and weapon stats, etc.) Things never even mentioned prior to launch like base building, a multiplayer hub, community missions, and so much other random stuff is present now too. Every update has been free as well, not a fucking DIME in microtransactions or DLC or any of that bullshit. Hello Games wants their game to be good, and they want to add stuff that people want, so they sit down and they ACTUALLY DO IT. It may sound weird but I think some devs treat their games the same way artists will treat paintings or drawings, you're never really done with it sometimes. You'll see something that needs improving in a tiny piece of the picture and become laser focused on that one thing. Hello Games is sorta like that.

Some of my friends don't understand WHY I like this game so much, and they have a lot of reasons to question me. I think what it is though is how I literally grew up playing Minecraft. It was one of the only games I ever played for a long period of time starting when I was only 12. This game is exactly like that game. It's that niche feeling people enjoy of surviving, building, discovering, creating, and just doing whatever the hell you feel like. I'd build stuff for hours when I was a kid playing Minecraft, but when I grew out of it, nothing took its place. When I played this game in 2016 for the first time I played for like 2 hours then never launched it again, didn't think twice. I checked out the 1.1 and 1.2 updates but they never got me into it. 1.3 however, actually got me interested due to it actually having more fleshed out features and cohesive objectives. I didn't really realize then exactly why I liked the game so much. but after all the major updates (literally dozens of them) I know why. No Man's Sky is Minecraft in space. Building, exploring, surviving, fighting monsters, playing with friends, etc. this games unintentionally mirrors what Minecraft used to do so well. Of course this games not for everyone, you're not smart for pointing that out. It's repetitive, it lacks goals (debatable after introduction of story mode and the brand new expedition gamemode), and can be very grindy. Yet for some reason, Minecraft has all those things too (and even less goals) but nobody draws the comparison and the whole internet foams at the mouth over Minecraft TO THIS DAY. (Dream is a loser.)

ever since 1.5 aka "NEXT", this game has been on an absolute roll. Almost every update is pretty top tier ("Visions," "Exo Mech," and "Companions" kind blew though sorry) with updates being SO BIG that they were labelled as 2.0 and even 3.0. (3.0 Origins is the best update objectively.) I was so unbelievably hyped for 1.5 I could barely sleep the night before its release and the update even managed to live up to they hype. For some reason though people are just obsessed with old versions of the game (1.0 through 1.3) or still never shut the hell up about how much better the pre release looked. People caught up with the old versions are blinded by nostalgia. Sometimes I wonder that if the game released looking like how it did pre launch, would people have actually still liked it?

Creator of the game Sean Murray once said that a Valve employee told him "What you do now is more important that what you say." I think more people should probably apply that statement to a lot of things.

TLDR: space gam fun lol Buy No Man's Sky

I've never hated No Man's Sky, but I did think it was overpriced for what felt like a very limited space exploration game. Over the past year, I've been noticing updates. Some of them are good, just it wasn't enough for me, but I saw that the developers still want to fix their mistakes and make sure they deliver on what's promised. Would I still pay $60 for this game? Being me. probably, because I'm an impatient person and won't wait for sales. Although it's probably not worth it to an average person. 
They have a sale almost every time they've made a big update to this game, and I have a feeling they're going to keep doing that. So I would recommend waiting. 

Anyways, it's good that they haven't abandoned this game, and for anyone who already owns this game and is looking at the reviews for some reason, try it again, I'm sure you won't be disappointed.

I originally purchased No Man's Sky back in August of 2016. Initially, the game was very disappointing and really did not live up to its hype. Multiplayer didn't exist, worlds were very similar, flora/fauna were strange and unappealing, my computer was dying and barely getting 20fps, and it just wasn't a great experience at all. I stopped playing for several months. 

However, since then, Hello Games has been surprisingly good at providing new updates with lots of new content and bug fixes. Today, you can play with friends, build bases, explore abandoned freighters, go on missions, explore world with a plethora of geographic features, find cool flora/fauna, and really experience being an explorer. The NMS Universe no longer feels sterile and empty. Best of all? The company continues to release new updates like companions and even crossplay. No Man's Sky has done something very few games have done and had a tremendous redemption arc.
